_**The Tortured Poets Department**_ is the eleventh studio album by the American singer-songwriter [Taylor Swift](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taylor_Swift "Taylor Swift"). It was released on April 19, 2024, through [Republic Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republic_Records "Republic Records"), followed by a [double album](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Double_album "Double album") issue subtitled _**The Anthology**_ only two hours after the original. Swift wrote and produced the album with [Jack Antonoff](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jack_Antonoff "Jack Antonoff") and [Aaron Dessner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aaron_Dessner "Aaron Dessner") while she was on the American leg of [the Eras Tour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Eras_Tour "The Eras Tour") in 2023.

Using autobiographical songwriting, _The Tortured Poets Department_ reflects Swift's cathartic episode during the tour as she experienced personal upheavals amidst breakups and heightened fame. Its songs depict grief and emotional tumult caused by ill-fated romance in a hyperbolic, confrontational, and [self-aware](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Self-awareness "Self-awareness") manner, exploring themes of mourning, depression, anger, delusion, [erotic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eroticism "Eroticism") desires, and humor. Musically, _The Tortured Poets Department_ features two production styles: the standard set, mainly produced by Antonoff, is largely [minimalist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minimal_music "Minimal music"), [mid-tempo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mid-tempo "Mid-tempo") [synth-pop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Synth-pop "Synth-pop"), characterized by [synthesizers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Synthesizer "Synthesizer"), sustained [bass](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bass_\(sound\) "Bass (sound)"), and [programmed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Programming_\(music\) "Programming (music)") [drums](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Drum_machine "Drum machine"). Dessner was the principal producer of _The Anthology_ tracks, which are mostly mellow and acoustic [chamber pop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chamber_pop "Chamber pop") and [folk-pop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Folk-pop "Folk-pop") [ballads](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sentimental_ballad "Sentimental ballad"), steeped in piano and guitar. Elements of [electronica](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electronica "Electronica"), [country](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Country_music "Country music"), [rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rock_music "Rock music"), [folk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Folk_music "Folk music"), and [western music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Western_music_\(North_America\) "Western music (North America)") are also interspersed throughout the record.

Swift promoted _The Tortured Poets Department_ via social media and [music streaming](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Music_streaming "Music streaming") platforms, and revamped the Eras Tour in 2024 to include the album. It topped charts across Europe, Asia–Pacific, and the Americas; broke streaming and sales records; and became the [global best-selling album of 2024](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_best-selling_albums#Best-selling_album_by_year_worldwide "List of best-selling albums"). In the United States, _The Tortured Poets Department_ became Swift's [seventh album to open with over a million units](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_fastest-selling_albums#United_States "List of fastest-selling albums") and her first to open with two million units. The album spent 17 weeks atop the [_Billboard_ 200](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billboard_200 "Billboard 200") and was [certified](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RIAA_certification "RIAA certification") eight-times platinum by the [Recording Industry Association of America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Recording_Industry_Association_of_America "Recording Industry Association of America"). Its songs made Swift the first artist to monopolize the [_Billboard_ Hot 100](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billboard_Hot_100 "Billboard Hot 100")'s top 14 spots, with the lead single "[Fortnight](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fortnight_\(song\) "Fortnight (song)")" featuring [Post Malone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Post_Malone "Post Malone") topping the chart.

_The Tortured Poets Department_ polarized music critics; positive reviews praised the cathartic narrative songwriting as emotionally resonant and deemed the album one of Swift's finest works, while mixed reviews described the production as redundant and the lyrics as verbose rather than poetic. Within weeks after the initial reviews, several journalists reassessed and appreciated the album's musical and lyrical nuances, opining that the criticism was influenced by Swift's media overexposure and the lengthy tracklist. The album received an [ARIA Music Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ARIA_Music_Award "ARIA Music Award"), a [Premios Odeón](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Premios_Odeón "Premios Odeón"), a [Japan Gold Disc Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japan_Gold_Disc_Award "Japan Gold Disc Award"), and five nominations at the [67th Annual Grammy Awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/67th_Annual_Grammy_Awards "67th Annual Grammy Awards"), including [Album of the Year](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grammy_Award_for_Album_of_the_Year "Grammy Award for Album of the Year").

In March 2023, [Taylor Swift](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taylor_Swift "Taylor Swift") embarked on [the Eras Tour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Eras_Tour "The Eras Tour"), which she conceived as a retrospective tour that paid tribute to all of the albums in [her discography](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taylor_Swift_albums_discography "Taylor Swift albums discography"). The Eras Tour became [the first concert tour to gross $1 billion in revenue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_highest-grossing_concert_tours "List of highest-grossing concert tours"), and its huge success [propelled Swift's global fame to unprecedented levels](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Impact_of_the_Eras_Tour "Impact of the Eras Tour"), becoming a subject of academic studies in marketing, economics, and sociology.[\[1\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTESomvilleBenoit2025437-1) She began working on her eleventh studio album immediately after completing her tenth, _[Midnights](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Midnights "Midnights")_ (2022), and recorded it with longtime collaborators, the producers [Jack Antonoff](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jack_Antonoff "Jack Antonoff") and [Aaron Dessner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aaron_Dessner "Aaron Dessner"), while she was on the American leg of the Eras Tour.[\[2\]](#cite_note-2)[\[3\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEZaleski2024234-3)

Amidst the heightened fame, throughout 2023, Swift's personal life was a subject widely covered and debated by both her fans and the press, who routinely reported on her breakup after a six-year relationship with the actor [Joe Alwyn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Alwyn "Joe Alwyn"), an alleged brief romantic link with the musician [Matty Healy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matty_Healy "Matty Healy"), and a new relationship with the [American football](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_football "American football") player [Travis Kelce](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Travis_Kelce "Travis Kelce").[\[4\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTESomvilleBenoit2025437Zaleski2024234-4)[\[5\]](#cite_note-Abad-Santos-5)[\[6\]](#cite_note-6) At the [66th Annual Grammy Awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/66th_Annual_Grammy_Awards "66th Annual Grammy Awards") on February 4, 2024, during her acceptance speech for the [Best Pop Vocal Album](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Best_Pop_Vocal_Album "Best Pop Vocal Album") award for _Midnights_, Swift announced the title of her eleventh studio album, _The Tortured Poets Department_.[\[7\]](#cite_note-Martoccio-2024-7) Swift shared with her audience at an Eras concert in [Melbourne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Melbourne "Melbourne") on February 16, 2024, that writing _The Tortured Poets Department_ was a "lifeline" for her because it made her reflect on how songwriting was an integral part of her life.[\[8\]](#cite_note-8)

The standard edition of _The Tortured Poets Department_ consists of 16 songs, including two written solely by Swift—"[My Boy Only Breaks His Favorite Toys](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/My_Boy_Only_Breaks_His_Favorite_Toys "My Boy Only Breaks His Favorite Toys")" and "[Who's Afraid of Little Old Me?](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Who's_Afraid_of_Little_Old_Me%3F "Who's Afraid of Little Old Me?"), eight co-written with Antonoff, and five with Dessner. The rapper and singer [Post Malone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Post_Malone "Post Malone") is featured on and co-wrote "[Fortnight](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fortnight_\(song\) "Fortnight (song)")", while the musician [Florence Welch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Florence_Welch "Florence Welch") is featured on "[Florida!!!](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Florida!!! "Florida!!!")".[\[9\]](#cite_note-Liner-9)[\[10\]](#cite_note-Rossignol-2024-10) In a self-written [epilogue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Epilogue "Epilogue") included at the end of the album's packaging, Swift situates herself as the "Chairman of the Tortured Poets Department" and details the overall narrative: she references the end of a long-term relationship, which transitions into a short-lived [rebound](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rebound_\(dating\) "Rebound (dating)") romantic fling that painfully ends.[\[3\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEZaleski2024234-3) In social media posts, she framed _The Tortured Poets Department_ as an introspective album that reflects "events, opinions and sentiments from a fleeting and fatalistic moment in time—one that was both sensational and sorrowful in equal measure".[\[3\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEZaleski2024234-3)[\[11\]](#cite_note-11) According to some critics, by naming the album _The Tortured Poets Department_, Swift situated herself as a songwriter rooted in poetry's tradition of detailing the human experience with lost love and self-torment: from ancient times ([Catullus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catullus "Catullus"), [Sappho](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sappho "Sappho")) and medieval times ([Petrarch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Petrarch "Petrarch")) to the European "_[poète maudit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Poète_maudit "Poète maudit")_" archetype ([Arthur Rimbaud](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arthur_Rimbaud "Arthur Rimbaud"), [Charles Baudelaire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Baudelaire "Charles Baudelaire")).[\[12\]](#cite_note-BurtTime-12)[\[13\]](#cite_note-13)

> _Tortured Poets_ is the culmination of a catalog full of songs in which Swift has taken us into the bedrooms where men pleasured or misled her, the bars where they charmed her, the empty playgrounds where they sat on swings with her and promised something they couldn't give.

Using autobiographical songwriting that combines [country music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Country_music "Country music")'s detail-heavy narratives and [rock music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rock_music "Rock music")'s self-mythologizing,[\[15\]](#cite_note-Brown-2024-15)[\[16\]](#cite_note-16) the songs reference her cathartic phase while dealing with personal upheavals caused by romantic failures and heightened fame.[\[17\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEZaleski2024234Hughes2025128-17)[\[18\]](#cite_note-Savage-2024-18)[\[19\]](#cite_note-Wilson-2024-19) A heavily personal album, _The Tortured Poets Department_ depicts emotions like anger, mourning, confusion, regret, longing, and delusion,[\[3\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEZaleski2024234-3)[\[20\]](#cite_note-20)[\[21\]](#cite_note-Leszkiewicz-21) which are told via lyrical narratives that are messy, unbridled, and unguarded[\[22\]](#cite_note-Lipshutz-2024-22)[\[23\]](#cite_note-Light-2024-23)[\[24\]](#cite_note-Snapes-2024-24)—they mirror the experiences of [grief](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grief "Grief")[\[19\]](#cite_note-Wilson-2024-19)[\[25\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWickmanWeissMcAvoy2025182-25) and explore themes like erotic desires, forbidden love, and escaping from the public eye to extremes, in a hyperbolic and confrontational manner.[\[14\]](#cite_note-Powers-2024-14)[\[24\]](#cite_note-Snapes-2024-24)[\[26\]](#cite_note-Sheffield-26)[\[27\]](#cite_note-27) The music critic [Ann Powers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ann_Powers "Ann Powers") summarized the content as a novel-like song collection about "emotional violence" that is imposed onto women by their male lovers and even by themselves. She further commented that the lyrical details were so personal that they showcased Swift at her most vulnerable but also most ruthless.[\[14\]](#cite_note-Powers-2024-14)

The overall sentiments are grim and sombre, brought by lyrical imagery of death, murder, prison, mental health spirals, narcotics, and alcoholism.[\[3\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEZaleski2024234-3)[\[21\]](#cite_note-Leszkiewicz-21)[\[28\]](#cite_note-28)[\[29\]](#cite_note-29) There are religious undertones, use of [profanity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Profanity "Profanity"),[\[19\]](#cite_note-Wilson-2024-19)[\[30\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTESomvilleBenoit2025437WickmanWeissMcAvoy2025183-30) and [internet culture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Internet_culture "Internet culture")\-inspired [slang](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slang "Slang") in addition to literary allusions. According to the popular-culture academic Eloise Faichney, the writing style combining informal language with formal poetic traditions was emblematic of [Instapoetry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Instapoetry "Instapoetry"), used by her generation of [millennials](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Millennials "Millennials"), particularly women, to convey their experiences in prose or poetry using social media.[\[31\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFaichney202591–92-31) The first major theme, the dissolution of a years-long relationship, is anchored by "[So Long, London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/So_Long,_London "So Long, London")", in which Swift's narrator bids farewell to an ex-partner and their romance in [London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London "London").[\[32\]](#cite_note-BurtNation-32)[\[33\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTESomvilleBenoit2025442-33) She resents how the lost love wasted her youth and how she tried to rescue it to no avail,[\[34\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWickmanWeissMcAvoy2025185-34) a theme that is also detailed in "My Boy Only Breaks His Favorite Toys", in which she is in denial that the relationship is no longer salvageable.[\[35\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTESomvilleBenoit2025440-35) The second major theme, the transition to a passionate fling that abruptly ends, is detailed across most tracks, which combine autobiographical details with fictionalized narratives and use devices like [hyperbole](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hyperbole "Hyperbole") or [melodrama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Melodrama "Melodrama") for impact.[\[3\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEZaleski2024234-3)[\[32\]](#cite_note-BurtNation-32)[\[36\]](#cite_note-Murray-36) "Fortnight" details a two-week-long romance that entails jealousy and murderous thoughts,[\[37\]](#cite_note-Hodgkinson-37) while "[Fresh Out the Slammer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fresh_Out_the_Slammer "Fresh Out the Slammer")" compares the old romance to a suffocating prison and depicts Swift's narrator escaping from it the moment it ends, to get together with an old flame.[\[3\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEZaleski2024234-3)[\[38\]](#cite_note-HunterTilney-2024-38)

[![Swift in a rhinesthoned bodysuit, singing onto a mic](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c9/Taylor_Swift_The_Eras_Tour_Midnights_Era_Set_%2853110003175%29.jpg/250px-Taylor_Swift_The_Eras_Tour_Midnights_Era_Set_%2853110003175%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Taylor_Swift_The_Eras_Tour_Midnights_Era_Set_\(53110003175\).jpg)

Swift's heightened fame and highly publicized breakups during [the Eras Tour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Eras_Tour "The Eras Tour") influenced _The Tortured Poets Department_.

The brief fling sends Swift's narrator into a whirlwind of strong emotions blending desire and pain.[\[14\]](#cite_note-Powers-2024-14)[\[21\]](#cite_note-Leszkiewicz-21) In "[Down Bad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Down_Bad_\(Taylor_Swift_song\) "Down Bad (Taylor Swift song)")", she compares the feelings caused by this short-lived infatuation to being abducted by an extraterrestrial being.[\[39\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTESomvilleBenoit2025441-39) "[Guilty as Sin?](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guilty_as_Sin%3F "Guilty as Sin?")" explores her longing to be intimate with another man while being trapped in an unhappy relationship and the guilt that ensues, comparing her orgasm to death and ocean waves crashing.[\[40\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHughes2025134-40) She declares her devotion to him in "[But Daddy I Love Him](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/But_Daddy_I_Love_Him "But Daddy I Love Him")",[\[32\]](#cite_note-BurtNation-32) and, in "[I Can Fix Him (No Really I Can)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/I_Can_Fix_Him_\(No_Really_I_Can\) "I Can Fix Him (No Really I Can)")", is determined to bring out the sweet nature of this problematic man, until she realizes at the end that she could not.[\[3\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEZaleski2024234-3) The painful ending is the theme of two tracks: "[Loml](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loml "Loml")" and "[The Smallest Man Who Ever Lived](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Smallest_Man_Who_Ever_Lived "The Smallest Man Who Ever Lived")", which both explore the imbalanced dynamic between Swift's narrator and her subject.[\[3\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEZaleski2024234-3)[\[41\]](#cite_note-Snapes-41) In "Loml", Swift's narrator is devastated by this "con-man" who falsely promised her marriage and kids but ultimately abandons her,[\[41\]](#cite_note-Snapes-41)[\[42\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTESomvilleBenoit2025449-42) whereas in "The Smallest Man Who Ever Lived", she directs her anger and condemnation towards him, who [ghosted](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ghosting_\(behavior\) "Ghosting (behavior)") her and thus "didn't measure up in any measure of a man", as depicted in the lyrics.[\[21\]](#cite_note-Leszkiewicz-21)[\[32\]](#cite_note-BurtNation-32)

The album's third major theme revolves around Swift's fame and its impact on her, alluding to how she coped with the breakups while having to perform in the public eye.[\[14\]](#cite_note-Powers-2024-14)[\[32\]](#cite_note-BurtNation-32)[\[43\]](#cite_note-Roberts-2024-43) In these songs, which reference her public image and incorporate self-aware and sometimes self-deprecating humor,[\[44\]](#cite_note-44) she confronts anyone who she thought had wronged her: detractors, music-industry executives, the press, and her fans.[\[12\]](#cite_note-BurtTime-12)[\[14\]](#cite_note-Powers-2024-14)[\[41\]](#cite_note-Snapes-41) In "[The Tortured Poets Department](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Tortured_Poets_Department_\(song\) "The Tortured Poets Department (song)")", which details an impending heartbreak between two musicians,[\[45\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBurt2025-45) she tells her romantic interest that she is not [Patti Smith](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patti_Smith "Patti Smith") and he is not [Dylan Thomas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dylan_Thomas "Dylan Thomas"), both associating with and distancing from the "tortured poet" archetype that the title evokes.[\[12\]](#cite_note-BurtTime-12)[\[46\]](#cite_note-Petrusich-46) In "But Daddy I Love Him", which is set in a religious small town, she criticizes anyone who disapproves of her romance with a troublesome man who may blemish her innocent, good-girl image. Several analyses opined that this was Swift's message to her fans not to interfere with her private life, influenced by their public outcry against her alleged fling with Healy due to his unpopularity.[\[41\]](#cite_note-Snapes-41)[\[47\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTERobb20248Burt2025-47)

"Florida!!!", "Who's Afraid of Little Old Me?", and "I Can Fix Him (No Really I Can)" incorporate elements of [Southern Gothic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Gothic "Southern Gothic") melodrama.[\[41\]](#cite_note-Snapes-41) Both "Florida!!!" and "Who's Afraid of Little Old Me" reflect Swift's anxiety when facing with her fame and identity:[\[45\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBurt2025-45) "Florida!!!" is an [escapist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Escapist_fiction "Escapist fiction") tale about escaping to Florida to reinvent her identity and forget past wrongdoings,[\[37\]](#cite_note-Hodgkinson-37) while "Who's Afraid of Little Old Me?" details her rage and resentment against the culture that she was brought up in, alluding to her early success when she was still a teenager.[\[45\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBurt2025-45)[\[41\]](#cite_note-Snapes-41) In "[I Can Do It with a Broken Heart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/I_Can_Do_It_with_a_Broken_Heart "I Can Do It with a Broken Heart")", Swift claims that she could put on a show despite her depression from being abandoned by her romantic interests.[\[3\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEZaleski2024234-3) The standard edition's penultimate track, "[The Alchemy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Alchemy "The Alchemy")", is about a burgeoning and triumphant romance using American football metaphors—the outlier in an album of heavy emotions.[\[45\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBurt2025-45) The closing track, "[Clara Bow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clara_Bow_\(song\) "Clara Bow (song)")", was named after the 1920s silent-film actress [Clara Bow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clara_Bow "Clara Bow"). In it, Swift explores how women in the music industry are consecutively viewed as replacements for someone before them.[\[14\]](#cite_note-Powers-2024-14)[\[32\]](#cite_note-BurtNation-32)

The [double album](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Double_album "Double album") edition of _The Tortured Poets Department_ is subtitled _The Anthology_ and contains 15 additional songs. Swift wrote three by herself—"[The Black Dog](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Black_Dog_\(song\) "The Black Dog (song)")", "Peter", and "The Manuscript"—ten with Dessner, and two with Antonoff.[\[10\]](#cite_note-Rossignol-2024-10)[\[48\]](#cite_note-Telegraph-48) While the _Anthology_ songs expand on the original edition's themes of heartbreak and emotional tumult, they are less directly autobiographical and use literary subtexts to convey the sentiments via metaphors and character studies.[\[48\]](#cite_note-Telegraph-48)[\[49\]](#cite_note-Sheffield-Anthology-49)[\[50\]](#cite_note-CarrAnthology-50)

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/91/SamuelTaylorColeridge.jpg/250px-SamuelTaylorColeridge.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:SamuelTaylorColeridge.jpg)

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/cd/Cassandra_%28Stratford_Gallery%29.jpg/250px-Cassandra_%28Stratford_Gallery%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Cassandra_\(Stratford_Gallery\).jpg)

Motifs of [mythology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mythology "Mythology") are prominent in _The Anthology_.[\[51\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMills2024233-51) "The Black Dog" and "[The Albatross](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Albatross_\(Taylor_Swift_song\) "The Albatross (Taylor Swift song)")" draw from and reinvent [English folklore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/English_folklore "English folklore") imagery; the literature academic Matthew J. A. Green commented that they also feature influences of [Gothic literature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gothic_literature "Gothic literature").[\[52\]](#cite_note-Green-2024-52) "The Black Dog" references both a London pub and the mythical creature [black dog](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_dog_\(folklore\) "Black dog (folklore)")—Swift's narrator is devastated upon learning that her ex-lover is seducing another woman at the pub and, at the end of the song, compares his act of abandoning her to a dog with its [tail between its legs](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/tail%20between%20one's%20legs "wikt:tail between one's legs").[\[26\]](#cite_note-Sheffield-26)[\[51\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMills2024233-51) In "The Albatross", Swift plays with the [albatross](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albatross_\(metaphor\) "Albatross (metaphor)") metaphor originated in [Samuel Taylor Coleridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Taylor_Coleridge "Samuel Taylor Coleridge")'s 1789 poem _[The Rime of the Ancient Mariner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Rime_of_the_Ancient_Mariner "The Rime of the Ancient Mariner")_. Her narrator compares herself to the albatross as both a sign of danger and an agent of rescue, shifting from third- to first-person narration in the final chorus. The lyrics are ambiguous; according to the philosopher Georgie Mills, they can be interpreted as either Swift's warning to someone who has wronged her or caution for a potential romantic partner.[\[53\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMills2024234–235-53)

Swift similarly switches between first- and third-person storytelling in "[Cassandra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cassandra_\(Taylor_Swift_song\) "Cassandra (Taylor Swift song)")", a reference to the ancient Greek mythological princess [Cassandra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cassandra "Cassandra"), who was a prophetess cursed by the god [Apollo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apollo "Apollo") so that nobody believed in her prophecies. In the song, Swift's narrator details how the townsfolk murder Cassandra for her foresight, contrary to the original mythology that she is just ignored and not killed;[\[51\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMills2024233-51) Burt wrote that Swift's "Cassandra" exerts influences from [Homer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homer "Homer") and [Virgil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Virgil "Virgil").[\[45\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBurt2025-45) In "The Prophecy", Swift's narrator pleads to a higher being to change her destiny of loneliness and begs for a soulmate. According to Mills, the trope of prophecy evokes mythological tales such as Cassandra and [Oedipus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oedipus "Oedipus"), and the lyrics incorporate biblical imagery of [Eve](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eve "Eve") being cursed.[\[54\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMills2024235–236-54)

_The Anthology_ also features influences from literature. "Peter" is based on the narrative of [J. M. Barrie](https:/

    Released: July 2, 2024

_**The Tortured Poets Department**_ is the eleventh studio album by the American singer-songwriter [Taylor Swift](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taylor_Swift "Taylor Swift"). It was released on April 19, 2024, through [Republic Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republic_Records "Republic Records"), followed by a [double album](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Double_album "Double album") issue subtitled _**The Anthology**_ only two hours after the original. Swift wrote and produced the album with [Jack Antonoff](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jack_Antonoff "Jack Antonoff") and [Aaron Dessner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aaron_Dessner "Aaron Dessner") while she was on the American leg of [the Eras Tour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Eras_Tour "The Eras Tour") in 2023.

Using autobiographical songwriting, _The Tortured Poets Department_ reflects Swift's cathartic episode during the tour as she experienced personal upheavals amidst breakups and heightened fame. Its songs depict grief and emotional tumult caused by ill-fated romance in a hyperbolic, confrontational, and [self-aware](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Self-awareness "Self-awareness") manner, exploring themes of mourning, depression, anger, delusion, [erotic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eroticism "Eroticism") desires, and humor. Musically, _The Tortured Poets Department_ features two production styles: the standard set, mainly produced by Antonoff, is largely [minimalist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minimal_music "Minimal music"), [mid-tempo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mid-tempo "Mid-tempo") [synth-pop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Synth-pop "Synth-pop"), characterized by [synthesizers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Synthesizer "Synthesizer"), sustained [bass](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bass_\(sound\) "Bass (sound)"), and [programmed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Programming_\(music\) "Programming (music)") [drums](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Drum_machine "Drum machine"). Dessner was the principal producer of _The Anthology_ tracks, which are mostly mellow and acoustic [chamber pop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chamber_pop "Chamber pop") and [folk-pop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Folk-pop "Folk-pop") [ballads](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sentimental_ballad "Sentimental ballad"), steeped in piano and guitar. Elements of [electronica](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electronica "Electronica"), [country](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Country_music "Country music"), [rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rock_music "Rock music"), [folk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Folk_music "Folk music"), and [western music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Western_music_\(North_America\) "Western music (North America)") are also interspersed throughout the record.

Swift promoted _The Tortured Poets Department_ via social media and [music streaming](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Music_streaming "Music streaming") platforms, and revamped the Eras Tour in 2024 to include the album. It topped charts across Europe, Asia–Pacific, and the Americas; broke streaming and sales records; and became the [global best-selling album of 2024](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_best-selling_albums#Best-selling_album_by_year_worldwide "List of best-selling albums"). In the United States, _The Tortured Poets Department_ became Swift's [seventh album to open with over a million units](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_fastest-selling_albums#United_States "List of fastest-selling albums") and her first to open with two million units. The album spent 17 weeks atop the [_Billboard_ 200](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billboard_200 "Billboard 200") and was [certified](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RIAA_certification "RIAA certification") eight-times platinum by the [Recording Industry Association of America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Recording_Industry_Association_of_America "Recording Industry Association of America"). Its songs made Swift the first artist to monopolize the [_Billboard_ Hot 100](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billboard_Hot_100 "Billboard Hot 100")'s top 14 spots, with the lead single "[Fortnight](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fortnight_\(song\) "Fortnight (song)")" featuring [Post Malone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Post_Malone "Post Malone") topping the chart.

_The Tortured Poets Department_ polarized music critics; positive reviews praised the cathartic narrative songwriting as emotionally resonant and deemed the album one of Swift's finest works, while mixed reviews described the production as redundant and the lyrics as verbose rather than poetic. Within weeks after the initial reviews, several journalists reassessed and appreciated the album's musical and lyrical nuances, opining that the criticism was influenced by Swift's media overexposure and the lengthy tracklist. The album received an [ARIA Music Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ARIA_Music_Award "ARIA Music Award"), a [Premios Odeón](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Premios_Odeón "Premios Odeón"), a [Japan Gold Disc Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japan_Gold_Disc_Award "Japan Gold Disc Award"), and five nominations at the [67th Annual Grammy Awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/67th_Annual_Grammy_Awards "67th Annual Grammy Awards"), including [Album of the Year](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grammy_Award_for_Album_of_the_Year "Grammy Award for Album of the Year").

In March 2023, [Taylor Swift](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taylor_Swift "Taylor Swift") embarked on [the Eras Tour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Eras_Tour "The Eras Tour"), which she conceived as a retrospective tour that paid tribute to all of the albums in [her discography](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taylor_Swift_albums_discography "Taylor Swift albums discography"). The Eras Tour became [the first concert tour to gross $1 billion in revenue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_highest-grossing_concert_tours "List of highest-grossing concert tours"), and its huge success [propelled Swift's global fame to unprecedented levels](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Impact_of_the_Eras_Tour "Impact of the Eras Tour"), becoming a subject of academic studies in marketing, economics, and sociology.[\[1\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTESomvilleBenoit2025437-1) She began working on her eleventh studio album immediately after completing her tenth, _[Midnights](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Midnights "Midnights")_ (2022), and recorded it with longtime collaborators, the producers [Jack Antonoff](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jack_Antonoff "Jack Antonoff") and [Aaron Dessner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aaron_Dessner "Aaron Dessner"), while she was on the American leg of the Eras Tour.[\[2\]](#cite_note-2)[\[3\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEZaleski2024234-3)

Amidst the heightened fame, throughout 2023, Swift's personal life was a subject widely covered and debated by both her fans and the press, who routinely reported on her breakup after a six-year relationship with the actor [Joe Alwyn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Alwyn "Joe Alwyn"), an alleged brief romantic link with the musician [Matty Healy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matty_Healy "Matty Healy"), and a new relationship with the [American football](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_football "American football") player [Travis Kelce](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Travis_Kelce "Travis Kelce").[\[4\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTESomvilleBenoit2025437Zaleski2024234-4)[\[5\]](#cite_note-Abad-Santos-5)[\[6\]](#cite_note-6) At the [66th Annual Grammy Awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/66th_Annual_Grammy_Awards "66th Annual Grammy Awards") on February 4, 2024, during her acceptance speech for the [Best Pop Vocal Album](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Best_Pop_Vocal_Album "Best Pop Vocal Album") award for _Midnights_, Swift announced the title of her eleventh studio album, _The Tortured Poets Department_.[\[7\]](#cite_note-Martoccio-2024-7) Swift shared with her audience at an Eras concert in [Melbourne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Melbourne "Melbourne") on February 16, 2024, that writing _The Tortured Poets Department_ was a "lifeline" for her because it made her reflect on how songwriting was an integral part of her life.[\[8\]](#cite_note-8)

The standard edition of _The Tortured Poets Department_ consists of 16 songs, including two written solely by Swift—"[My Boy Only Breaks His Favorite Toys](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/My_Boy_Only_Breaks_His_Favorite_Toys "My Boy Only Breaks His Favorite Toys")" and "[Who's Afraid of Little Old Me?](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Who's_Afraid_of_Little_Old_Me%3F "Who's Afraid of Little Old Me?"), eight co-written with Antonoff, and five with Dessner. The rapper and singer [Post Malone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Post_Malone "Post Malone") is featured on and co-wrote "[Fortnight](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fortnight_\(song\) "Fortnight (song)")", while the musician [Florence Welch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Florence_Welch "Florence Welch") is featured on "[Florida!!!](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Florida!!! "Florida!!!")".[\[9\]](#cite_note-Liner-9)[\[10\]](#cite_note-Rossignol-2024-10) In a self-written [epilogue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Epilogue "Epilogue") included at the end of the album's packaging, Swift situates herself as the "Chairman of the Tortured Poets Department" and details the overall narrative: she references the end of a long-term relationship, which transitions into a short-lived [rebound](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rebound_\(dating\) "Rebound (dating)") romantic fling that painfully ends.[\[3\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEZaleski2024234-3) In social media posts, she framed _The Tortured Poets Department_ as an introspective album that reflects "events, opinions and sentiments from a fleeting and fatalistic moment in time—one that was both sensational and sorrowful in equal measure".[\[3\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEZaleski2024234-3)[\[11\]](#cite_note-11) According to some critics, by naming the album _The Tortured Poets Department_, Swift situated herself as a songwriter rooted in poetry's tradition of detailing the human experience with lost love and self-torment: from ancient times ([Catullus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catullus "Catullus"), [Sappho](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sappho "Sappho")) and medieval times ([Petrarch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Petrarch "Petrarch")) to the European "_[poète maudit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Poète_maudit "Poète maudit")_" archetype ([Arthur Rimbaud](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arthur_Rimbaud "Arthur Rimbaud"), [Charles Baudelaire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Baudelaire "Charles Baudelaire")).[\[12\]](#cite_note-BurtTime-12)[\[13\]](#cite_note-13)

> _Tortured Poets_ is the culmination of a catalog full of songs in which Swift has taken us into the bedrooms where men pleasured or misled her, the bars where they charmed her, the empty playgrounds where they sat on swings with her and promised something they couldn't give.

Using autobiographical songwriting that combines [country music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Country_music "Country music")'s detail-heavy narratives and [rock music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rock_music "Rock music")'s self-mythologizing,[\[15\]](#cite_note-Brown-2024-15)[\[16\]](#cite_note-16) the songs reference her cathartic phase while dealing with personal upheavals caused by romantic failures and heightened fame.[\[17\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEZaleski2024234Hughes2025128-17)[\[18\]](#cite_note-Savage-2024-18)[\[19\]](#cite_note-Wilson-2024-19) A heavily personal album, _The Tortured Poets Department_ depicts emotions like anger, mourning, confusion, regret, longing, and delusion,[\[3\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEZaleski2024234-3)[\[20\]](#cite_note-20)[\[21\]](#cite_note-Leszkiewicz-21) which are told via lyrical narratives that are messy, unbridled, and unguarded[\[22\]](#cite_note-Lipshutz-2024-22)[\[23\]](#cite_note-Light-2024-23)[\[24\]](#cite_note-Snapes-2024-24)—they mirror the experiences of [grief](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grief "Grief")[\[19\]](#cite_note-Wilson-2024-19)[\[25\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWickmanWeissMcAvoy2025182-25) and explore themes like erotic desires, forbidden love, and escaping from the public eye to extremes, in a hyperbolic and confrontational manner.[\[14\]](#cite_note-Powers-2024-14)[\[24\]](#cite_note-Snapes-2024-24)[\[26\]](#cite_note-Sheffield-26)[\[27\]](#cite_note-27) The music critic [Ann Powers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ann_Powers "Ann Powers") summarized the content as a novel-like song collection about "emotional violence" that is imposed onto women by their male lovers and even by themselves. She further commented that the lyrical details were so personal that they showcased Swift at her most vulnerable but also most ruthless.[\[14\]](#cite_note-Powers-2024-14)

The overall sentiments are grim and sombre, brought by lyrical imagery of death, murder, prison, mental health spirals, narcotics, and alcoholism.[\[3\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEZaleski2024234-3)[\[21\]](#cite_note-Leszkiewicz-21)[\[28\]](#cite_note-28)[\[29\]](#cite_note-29) There are religious undertones, use of [profanity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Profanity "Profanity"),[\[19\]](#cite_note-Wilson-2024-19)[\[30\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTESomvilleBenoit2025437WickmanWeissMcAvoy2025183-30) and [internet culture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Internet_culture "Internet culture")\-inspired [slang](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slang "Slang") in addition to literary allusions. According to the popular-culture academic Eloise Faichney, the writing style combining informal language with formal poetic traditions was emblematic of [Instapoetry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Instapoetry "Instapoetry"), used by her generation of [millennials](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Millennials "Millennials"), particularly women, to convey their experiences in prose or poetry using social media.[\[31\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFaichney202591–92-31) The first major theme, the dissolution of a years-long relationship, is anchored by "[So Long, London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/So_Long,_London "So Long, London")", in which Swift's narrator bids farewell to an ex-partner and their romance in [London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London "London").[\[32\]](#cite_note-BurtNation-32)[\[33\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTESomvilleBenoit2025442-33) She resents how the lost love wasted her youth and how she tried to rescue it to no avail,[\[34\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWickmanWeissMcAvoy2025185-34) a theme that is also detailed in "My Boy Only Breaks His Favorite Toys", in which she is in denial that the relationship is no longer salvageable.[\[35\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTESomvilleBenoit2025440-35) The second major theme, the transition to a passionate fling that abruptly ends, is detailed across most tracks, which combine autobiographical details with fictionalized narratives and use devices like [hyperbole](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hyperbole "Hyperbole") or [melodrama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Melodrama "Melodrama") for impact.[\[3\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEZaleski2024234-3)[\[32\]](#cite_note-BurtNation-32)[\[36\]](#cite_note-Murray-36) "Fortnight" details a two-week-long romance that entails jealousy and murderous thoughts,[\[37\]](#cite_note-Hodgkinson-37) while "[Fresh Out the Slammer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fresh_Out_the_Slammer "Fresh Out the Slammer")" compares the old romance to a suffocating prison and depicts Swift's narrator escaping from it the moment it ends, to get together with an old flame.[\[3\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEZaleski2024234-3)[\[38\]](#cite_note-HunterTilney-2024-38)

[![Swift in a rhinesthoned bodysuit, singing onto a mic](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c9/Taylor_Swift_The_Eras_Tour_Midnights_Era_Set_%2853110003175%29.jpg/250px-Taylor_Swift_The_Eras_Tour_Midnights_Era_Set_%2853110003175%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Taylor_Swift_The_Eras_Tour_Midnights_Era_Set_\(53110003175\).jpg)

Swift's heightened fame and highly publicized breakups during [the Eras Tour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Eras_Tour "The Eras Tour") influenced _The Tortured Poets Department_.

The brief fling sends Swift's narrator into a whirlwind of strong emotions blending desire and pain.[\[14\]](#cite_note-Powers-2024-14)[\[21\]](#cite_note-Leszkiewicz-21) In "[Down Bad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Down_Bad_\(Taylor_Swift_song\) "Down Bad (Taylor Swift song)")", she compares the feelings caused by this short-lived infatuation to being abducted by an extraterrestrial being.[\[39\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTESomvilleBenoit2025441-39) "[Guilty as Sin?](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guilty_as_Sin%3F "Guilty as Sin?")" explores her longing to be intimate with another man while being trapped in an unhappy relationship and the guilt that ensues, comparing her orgasm to death and ocean waves crashing.[\[40\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHughes2025134-40) She declares her devotion to him in "[But Daddy I Love Him](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/But_Daddy_I_Love_Him "But Daddy I Love Him")",[\[32\]](#cite_note-BurtNation-32) and, in "[I Can Fix Him (No Really I Can)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/I_Can_Fix_Him_\(No_Really_I_Can\) "I Can Fix Him (No Really I Can)")", is determined to bring out the sweet nature of this problematic man, until she realizes at the end that she could not.[\[3\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEZaleski2024234-3) The painful ending is the theme of two tracks: "[Loml](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loml "Loml")" and "[The Smallest Man Who Ever Lived](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Smallest_Man_Who_Ever_Lived "The Smallest Man Who Ever Lived")", which both explore the imbalanced dynamic between Swift's narrator and her subject.[\[3\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEZaleski2024234-3)[\[41\]](#cite_note-Snapes-41) In "Loml", Swift's narrator is devastated by this "con-man" who falsely promised her marriage and kids but ultimately abandons her,[\[41\]](#cite_note-Snapes-41)[\[42\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTESomvilleBenoit2025449-42) whereas in "The Smallest Man Who Ever Lived", she directs her anger and condemnation towards him, who [ghosted](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ghosting_\(behavior\) "Ghosting (behavior)") her and thus "didn't measure up in any measure of a man", as depicted in the lyrics.[\[21\]](#cite_note-Leszkiewicz-21)[\[32\]](#cite_note-BurtNation-32)

The album's third major theme revolves around Swift's fame and its impact on her, alluding to how she coped with the breakups while having to perform in the public eye.[\[14\]](#cite_note-Powers-2024-14)[\[32\]](#cite_note-BurtNation-32)[\[43\]](#cite_note-Roberts-2024-43) In these songs, which reference her public image and incorporate self-aware and sometimes self-deprecating humor,[\[44\]](#cite_note-44) she confronts anyone who she thought had wronged her: detractors, music-industry executives, the press, and her fans.[\[12\]](#cite_note-BurtTime-12)[\[14\]](#cite_note-Powers-2024-14)[\[41\]](#cite_note-Snapes-41) In "[The Tortured Poets Department](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Tortured_Poets_Department_\(song\) "The Tortured Poets Department (song)")", which details an impending heartbreak between two musicians,[\[45\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBurt2025-45) she tells her romantic interest that she is not [Patti Smith](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patti_Smith "Patti Smith") and he is not [Dylan Thomas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dylan_Thomas "Dylan Thomas"), both associating with and distancing from the "tortured poet" archetype that the title evokes.[\[12\]](#cite_note-BurtTime-12)[\[46\]](#cite_note-Petrusich-46) In "But Daddy I Love Him", which is set in a religious small town, she criticizes anyone who disapproves of her romance with a troublesome man who may blemish her innocent, good-girl image. Several analyses opined that this was Swift's message to her fans not to interfere with her private life, influenced by their public outcry against her alleged fling with Healy due to his unpopularity.[\[41\]](#cite_note-Snapes-41)[\[47\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTERobb20248Burt2025-47)

"Florida!!!", "Who's Afraid of Little Old Me?", and "I Can Fix Him (No Really I Can)" incorporate elements of [Southern Gothic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Gothic "Southern Gothic") melodrama.[\[41\]](#cite_note-Snapes-41) Both "Florida!!!" and "Who's Afraid of Little Old Me" reflect Swift's anxiety when facing with her fame and identity:[\[45\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBurt2025-45) "Florida!!!" is an [escapist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Escapist_fiction "Escapist fiction") tale about escaping to Florida to reinvent her identity and forget past wrongdoings,[\[37\]](#cite_note-Hodgkinson-37) while "Who's Afraid of Little Old Me?" details her rage and resentment against the culture that she was brought up in, alluding to her early success when she was still a teenager.[\[45\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBurt2025-45)[\[41\]](#cite_note-Snapes-41) In "[I Can Do It with a Broken Heart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/I_Can_Do_It_with_a_Broken_Heart "I Can Do It with a Broken Heart")", Swift claims that she could put on a show despite her depression from being abandoned by her romantic interests.[\[3\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEZaleski2024234-3) The standard edition's penultimate track, "[The Alchemy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Alchemy "The Alchemy")", is about a burgeoning and triumphant romance using American football metaphors—the outlier in an album of heavy emotions.[\[45\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBurt2025-45) The closing track, "[Clara Bow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clara_Bow_\(song\) "Clara Bow (song)")", was named after the 1920s silent-film actress [Clara Bow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clara_Bow "Clara Bow"). In it, Swift explores how women in the music industry are consecutively viewed as replacements for someone before them.[\[14\]](#cite_note-Powers-2024-14)[\[32\]](#cite_note-BurtNation-32)

The [double album](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Double_album "Double album") edition of _The Tortured Poets Department_ is subtitled _The Anthology_ and contains 15 additional songs. Swift wrote three by herself—"[The Black Dog](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Black_Dog_\(song\) "The Black Dog (song)")", "Peter", and "The Manuscript"—ten with Dessner, and two with Antonoff.[\[10\]](#cite_note-Rossignol-2024-10)[\[48\]](#cite_note-Telegraph-48) While the _Anthology_ songs expand on the original edition's themes of heartbreak and emotional tumult, they are less directly autobiographical and use literary subtexts to convey the sentiments via metaphors and character studies.[\[48\]](#cite_note-Telegraph-48)[\[49\]](#cite_note-Sheffield-Anthology-49)[\[50\]](#cite_note-CarrAnthology-50)

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/91/SamuelTaylorColeridge.jpg/250px-SamuelTaylorColeridge.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:SamuelTaylorColeridge.jpg)

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/cd/Cassandra_%28Stratford_Gallery%29.jpg/250px-Cassandra_%28Stratford_Gallery%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Cassandra_\(Stratford_Gallery\).jpg)

Motifs of [mythology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mythology "Mythology") are prominent in _The Anthology_.[\[51\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMills2024233-51) "The Black Dog" and "[The Albatross](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Albatross_\(Taylor_Swift_song\) "The Albatross (Taylor Swift song)")" draw from and reinvent [English folklore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/English_folklore "English folklore") imagery; the literature academic Matthew J. A. Green commented that they also feature influences of [Gothic literature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gothic_literature "Gothic literature").[\[52\]](#cite_note-Green-2024-52) "The Black Dog" references both a London pub and the mythical creature [black dog](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_dog_\(folklore\) "Black dog (folklore)")—Swift's narrator is devastated upon learning that her ex-lover is seducing another woman at the pub and, at the end of the song, compares his act of abandoning her to a dog with its [tail between its legs](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/tail%20between%20one's%20legs "wikt:tail between one's legs").[\[26\]](#cite_note-Sheffield-26)[\[51\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMills2024233-51) In "The Albatross", Swift plays with the [albatross](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albatross_\(metaphor\) "Albatross (metaphor)") metaphor originated in [Samuel Taylor Coleridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Taylor_Coleridge "Samuel Taylor Coleridge")'s 1789 poem _[The Rime of the Ancient Mariner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Rime_of_the_Ancient_Mariner "The Rime of the Ancient Mariner")_. Her narrator compares herself to the albatross as both a sign of danger and an agent of rescue, shifting from third- to first-person narration in the final chorus. The lyrics are ambiguous; according to the philosopher Georgie Mills, they can be interpreted as either Swift's warning to someone who has wronged her or caution for a potential romantic partner.[\[53\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMills2024234–235-53)

Swift similarly switches between first- and third-person storytelling in "[Cassandra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cassandra_\(Taylor_Swift_song\) "Cassandra (Taylor Swift song)")", a reference to the ancient Greek mythological princess [Cassandra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cassandra "Cassandra"), who was a prophetess cursed by the god [Apollo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apollo "Apollo") so that nobody believed in her prophecies. In the song, Swift's narrator details how the townsfolk murder Cassandra for her foresight, contrary to the original mythology that she is just ignored and not killed;[\[51\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMills2024233-51) Burt wrote that Swift's "Cassandra" exerts influences from [Homer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homer "Homer") and [Virgil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Virgil "Virgil").[\[45\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBurt2025-45) In "The Prophecy", Swift's narrator pleads to a higher being to change her destiny of loneliness and begs for a soulmate. According to Mills, the trope of prophecy evokes mythological tales such as Cassandra and [Oedipus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oedipus "Oedipus"), and the lyrics incorporate biblical imagery of [Eve](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eve "Eve") being cursed.[\[54\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMills2024235–236-54)

_The Anthology_ also features influences from literature. "Peter" is based on the narrative of [J. M. Barrie](https:/

"All Too Well"

[Song](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Song "Song") by [Taylor Swift](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taylor_Swift "Taylor Swift")

from the album _[Red](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_\(Taylor_Swift_album\) "Red (Taylor Swift album)")_

Written

2011

Released

[Studio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Recording_studio "Recording studio")

[Genre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Music_genre "Music genre")

*   [arena rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arena_rock "Arena rock")
*   [folk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Folk_music "Folk music")
*   [pop rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pop_rock "Pop rock")

Length

[Label](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Record_label "Record label")

[Songwriters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Songwriter "Songwriter")

[Producers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Record_producer "Record producer")

*   [Nathan Chapman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nathan_Chapman_\(record_producer\) "Nathan Chapman (record producer)")

Audio video

["All Too Well"](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=hnK6CoUZZFc) on [YouTube](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/YouTube_video_\(identifier\) "YouTube video (identifier)")

"**All Too Well**" is a song by the American singer-songwriter [Taylor Swift](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taylor_Swift "Taylor Swift"). Written by Swift and [Liz Rose](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liz_Rose "Liz Rose"), the song was first produced by Swift and [Nathan Chapman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nathan_Chapman_\(record_producer\) "Nathan Chapman (record producer)") for her fourth studio album, _[Red](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_\(Taylor_Swift_album\) "Red (Taylor Swift album)")_ (2012). After a [2019 dispute regarding the ownership of Swift's masters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taylor_Swift_masters_dispute "Taylor Swift masters dispute"), she [re-recorded](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Re-recording_\(music\) "Re-recording (music)") the song as "**All Too Well (Taylor's Version)**" and released an unabridged "**10 Minute Version**" as part of the re-recorded album _[Red (Taylor's Version)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_\(Taylor's_Version\) "Red (Taylor's Version)")_ in November 2021.[\[note 1\]](#cite_note-1)

The lyrics of "All Too Well" narrate a failed romantic relationship, recalling the intimate memories and exploring the painful aftermath. The detail of a scarf that the narrator left at the house of her ex-lover's sister generated widespread interpretations and became a popular culture phenomenon. The 2012 version is a slow-burning [power ballad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Power_ballad "Power ballad") combining styles of [country](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Country_music "Country music") and [rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rock_music "Rock music"). The "10 Minute Version", produced by Swift and [Jack Antonoff](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jack_Antonoff "Jack Antonoff"), has an atmospheric [pop rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pop_rock "Pop rock") production. She performed the song at the [2014 Grammy Awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/56th_Annual_Grammy_Awards "56th Annual Grammy Awards") and included it in the set lists for two of her world tours: [the Red Tour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Red_Tour "The Red Tour") (2013–2014) and [the Eras Tour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Eras_Tour "The Eras Tour") (2023–2024).

"All Too Well" charted in Canada and the United States in 2012, and the "Taylor's Version" re-recording peaked atop the [_Billboard_ Global 200](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billboard_Global_200 "Billboard Global 200") and became the longest song to top the US [_Billboard_ Hot 100](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billboard_Hot_100 "Billboard Hot 100"). The song also charted at number one in Australia, Canada, Ireland, Malaysia, New Zealand, and Singapore. _[Rolling Stone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rolling_Stone "Rolling Stone")_ included it at number 69 in their 2021 revision of the "[500 Greatest Songs of All Time](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rolling_Stone's_500_Greatest_Songs_of_All_Time "Rolling Stone's 500 Greatest Songs of All Time")". Critics praised the "10 Minute Version" for providing a richer context with its additional verses. The short film version of this re-recording received a [Grammy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grammy_Awards "Grammy Awards") nomination for [Song of the Year](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grammy_Award_for_Song_of_the_Year "Grammy Award for Song of the Year") at the [65th Annual Grammy Awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/65th_Annual_Grammy_Awards "65th Annual Grammy Awards"). Swift directed _[All Too Well: The Short Film](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/All_Too_Well:_The_Short_Film "All Too Well: The Short Film")_ to accompany it, which won the [Grammy Award for Best Music Video](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grammy_Award_for_Best_Music_Video "Grammy Award for Best Music Video").

## Background and release

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=All_Too_Well&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Background and release")\]

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/7c/Taylor_Swift_Sydney.jpg/250px-Taylor_Swift_Sydney.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Taylor_Swift_Sydney.jpg)

Swift (pictured in 2012) began writing the song during rehearsals for the [Speak Now World Tour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now_World_Tour "Speak Now World Tour") in February 2011.

[Taylor Swift](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taylor_Swift "Taylor Swift") waѕ inspired by her tumultuous feelings after a breakup while conceiving her fourth studio album, [_Red_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_\(Taylor_Swift_album\) "Red (Taylor Swift album)") (2012).[\[1\]](#cite_note-Bernstein-2020-2) "All Too Well" was the first song Swift wrote for _Red_.[\[2\]](#cite_note-3) During a February 2011 rehearsal of the [Speak Now World Tour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now_World_Tour "Speak Now World Tour"), she [ad-libbed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ad_libitum "Ad libitum") some lyrics to the song while playing a four-[chord](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chord_\(music\) "Chord (music)") guitar [riff](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riff "Riff") as her touring band spontaneously played backing instruments.[\[1\]](#cite_note-Bernstein-2020-2) Swift told _[Rolling Stone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rolling_Stone "Rolling Stone")_ that this relationship caused "a few roller coasters", and she channeled the tumult into the song.[\[1\]](#cite_note-Bernstein-2020-2) She told the _[New York Times](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_New_York_Times "The New York Times")_ that the impromptu performance was "a very emotional rant." She recalled being very sad to the point where "sadness is you, you are sadness."[\[3\]](#cite_note-4) According to the booklets of Swift's 2019 album [_Lover_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lover_\(album\) "Lover (album)"), the final draft was completed a month later.[\[4\]](#cite_note-5)[\[5\]](#cite_note-6)

Swift asked [Liz Rose](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liz_Rose "Liz Rose"), who had co-written songs on her first albums, to co-write "All Too Well". Rose said that it was an unexpected collaboration after not having worked with Swift for some years;[\[6\]](#cite_note-Willman-2014-7) the last time they worked together was on Swift's 2008 album [_Fearless_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fearless_\(Taylor_Swift_album\) "Fearless (Taylor Swift album)").[\[7\]](#cite_note-Jones-2024-8) When Rose agreed to collaborate, she recalled that Swift had come up with the melody.[\[8\]](#cite_note-9) In an interview with _[Good Morning America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Good_Morning_America "Good Morning America")_, Swift said that the song was "the hardest to write on the album", saying that it took her some time "to filter through everything \[she\] wanted to put in the song" without making it lengthy with the help from Rose.[\[9\]](#cite_note-10) Rose said that the song was originally "10, 12 or 15 minutes long" or "probably a 20-minute song" before trimming.[\[6\]](#cite_note-Willman-2014-7)[\[10\]](#cite_note-Skinner-2019-11) The final album version is 5 minutes and 28 seconds long, the longest song on _Red_.[\[11\]](#cite_note-12) It was produced by Swift and [Nathan Chapman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nathan_Chapman_\(record_producer\) "Nathan Chapman (record producer)").[\[12\]](#cite_note-Swift-2012-13)

_Red_ was released on October 22, 2012, by [Big Machine Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Big_Machine_Records "Big Machine Records").[\[13\]](#cite_note-14) After _Red_ was released, "All Too Well" debuted at number 80 on the [_Billboard_ Hot 100](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billboard_Hot_100 "Billboard Hot 100") chart dated November 10, 2012;[\[14\]](#cite_note-Hot100-15) it also charted at number 17 on [Hot Country Songs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hot_Country_Songs "Hot Country Songs")[\[15\]](#cite_note-CountrySongs-16) and number 58 on [Country Airplay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Country_Airplay "Country Airplay").[\[16\]](#cite_note-CountryAirplay-17) The [Recording Industry Association of America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Recording_Industry_Association_of_America "Recording Industry Association of America") (RIAA) in 2018 [certified](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RIAA_certification "RIAA certification") the track gold for crossing 500,000 units based on sales and streams.[\[17\]](#cite_note-RIAA-18) The song also peaked at number 59 on the [Canadian Hot 100](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canadian_Hot_100 "Canadian Hot 100"),[\[18\]](#cite_note-Canada-19) and it was [certified](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_music_recording_certifications "List of music recording certifications") platinum in Australia,[\[19\]](#cite_note-ARIA-20) gold in Brazil[\[20\]](#cite_note-PMB-21) and Portugal,[\[21\]](#cite_note-AFP-22) and silver in the United Kingdom.[\[22\]](#cite_note-BPIOG-23)

![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/cb/Gnome-mime-audio-openclipart.svg/60px-Gnome-mime-audio-openclipart.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)

Chronicling a fallen relationship, "All Too Well" builds up with [overdubbed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Overdub "Overdub") guitars, drums, and strings. Its sound blends styles of [country](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Country_music "Country music"), [folk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Folk_music "Folk music"), and [rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rock_music "Rock music").

"All Too Well" is a [power ballad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Power_ballad "Power ballad")[\[23\]](#cite_note-24)[\[24\]](#cite_note-Braca-2021-25) that is set over a [4/4](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/4/4_time "4/4 time") beat.[\[7\]](#cite_note-Jones-2024-8) The track gradually builds up to a big, eruptive [crescendo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crescendo "Crescendo") in each [refrain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Refrain "Refrain").[\[7\]](#cite_note-Jones-2024-8)[\[25\]](#cite_note-Keefe-2012-26)[\[26\]](#cite_note-Farley-2017-27) Chapman is the sole musician on the track; he played acoustic guitar, electric guitar, bass, and drums, and provided background vocals. The instruments are [overdubbed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Overdubbing "Overdubbing") and [multitracked](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Multitrack_recording "Multitrack recording").[\[27\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPerone201746-28) [Jody Rosen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jody_Rosen "Jody Rosen"), in an article for [_New York_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_\(magazine\) "New York (magazine)"), wrote that the production "rises, like a slow-cresting wave".[\[28\]](#cite_note-Rosen-2013-29)

Bernard Perusse of the _[Edmonton Journal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edmonton_Journal "Edmonton Journal")_ wrote that the song displays influences of [U2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U2 "U2"),[\[29\]](#cite_note-30) while Rosen and [_Spin_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spin_\(magazine\) "Spin (magazine)")'s Michael Robbins thought that its driving [bassline](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bassline "Bassline") was reminiscent of that from U2's "[With or Without You](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/With_or_Without_You "With or Without You")" (1987).[\[28\]](#cite_note-Rosen-2013-29)[\[30\]](#cite_note-Robbins-2012-31) _[Slant Magazine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slant_Magazine "Slant Magazine")_'s Jonathan Keefe wrote that the track progresses from "coffeehouse [folk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Folk_music "Folk music") to [arena rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arena_rock "Arena rock")".[\[25\]](#cite_note-Keefe-2012-26) Bruce Warren, assistant general manager of [programming](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radio_programming "Radio programming") at [WXPN](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WXPN "WXPN"), commented that the track has a [soft rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soft_rock "Soft rock") production.[\[24\]](#cite_note-Braca-2021-25) _[Billboard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billboard_\(magazine\) "Billboard (magazine)")_ and Craig S. Semon of the _[Telegram & Gazette](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Telegram_&_Gazette "Telegram & Gazette")_ described the genre as [country](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Country_music "Country music"),[\[31\]](#cite_note-Billboard-2012-32)[\[32\]](#cite_note-Semon-2012-33) while _[Newsday](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newsday "Newsday")_ said that the song has an "[alt-country](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alt-country "Alt-country") ache".[\[33\]](#cite_note-Newsday-2012-34) Jon Dolan of _Rolling Stone_ opined that "All Too Well" exemplified the "diaristic post-country [rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rock_music "Rock music")" sound of _Red_,[\[34\]](#cite_note-Dolan-2010-35) and in their list of the 50 best albums of 2012, the magazine dubbed the genre "Nashville [pop rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pop_rock "Pop rock")".[\[35\]](#cite_note-36)

## Lyrics and interpretations

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=All_Too_Well&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Lyrics and interpretations")\]

The song is a recount of a fallen relationship[\[7\]](#cite_note-Jones-2024-8)[\[31\]](#cite_note-Billboard-2012-32) that happened in the fall.[\[36\]](#cite_note-Smith-2012-37)[\[37\]](#cite_note-Garrett-2021-38)[\[38\]](#cite_note-Tiffany-2021-39) The verses explore the memories in a loosely chronological order,[\[39\]](#cite_note-Nelson-2019-40) using expository details.[\[40\]](#cite_note-41) The song begins with details of a trip of two ex-lovers to [Upstate New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Upstate_New_York "Upstate New York") ("We're singin' in the car, getting lost upstate")[\[26\]](#cite_note-Farley-2017-27) such as imagery of "autumn leaves falling down like pieces into place".[\[37\]](#cite_note-Garrett-2021-38) When they visit the house of the love interest's sister during the [Thanksgiving](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thanksgiving "Thanksgiving") weekend, the narrator leaves her scarf at that place.[\[26\]](#cite_note-Farley-2017-27)[\[41\]](#cite_note-Rayner-2012-42)[\[42\]](#cite_note-Nelson-2012-43) The narrator then recalls the intimate moments with her ex-lover ("There we are again in the middle of the night/ Dancing around the kitchen in the refrigerator light")[\[39\]](#cite_note-Nelson-2019-40) and the mundane details, such as photo albums, a twin-sized bed, and stopping at red lights.[\[24\]](#cite_note-Braca-2021-25)[\[43\]](#cite_note-Cooney-2024-44) After each refrain, the narrator insists that those moments mattered ("I was there, I remember it all too well").[\[7\]](#cite_note-Jones-2024-8)[\[39\]](#cite_note-Nelson-2019-40)

The [bridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bridge_\(music\) "Bridge (music)") is where the track reaches its climax; Swift sings in her upper [register](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Register_\(music\) "Register (music)")[\[7\]](#cite_note-Jones-2024-8)[\[43\]](#cite_note-Cooney-2024-44) and almost shouts with anger ("You call me up again, just to break me like a promise/ So casually cruel in the name of being honest").[\[44\]](#cite_note-Caramanica-2012-45) Her narrator questions why the relationship fell apart, pondering whether it was because she "asked for too much".[\[45\]](#cite_note-Jagota-2021-46) In the final verse, the narrator mentions the scarf previously detailed in the first verse ("But you keep my old scarf from that very first week/ 'Cause it reminds you of innocence and it smells like me"),[\[39\]](#cite_note-Nelson-2019-40)[\[42\]](#cite_note-Nelson-2012-43) asserting that the love she gave and felt was real and that the ex-partner must have felt the same.[\[45\]](#cite_note-Jagota-2021-46)

Brittany Spanos of _Rolling Stone_ wrote that the song describes "the pain of having to piece one's self back together again" after a crumbled relationship.[\[46\]](#cite_note-47) Brad Nelson, in his reviews for _[The Atlantic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Atlantic "The Atlantic")_ and [_Pitchfork_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pitchfork_\(website\) "Pitchfork (website)"), said that the scarf imagery in the lyrics acts like a [Chekhov's gun](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chekhov's_gun "Chekhov's gun"), symbolizing the persisting emotional flame of the romance long after it has physically ended.[\[39\]](#cite_note-Nelson-2019-40)[\[42\]](#cite_note-Nelson-2012-43) Nelson compared Swift's lyrics mentioning various memories in a loosely chronological timeline to the technique used in [Bob Dylan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Dylan "Bob Dylan")'s "[Tangled Up in Blue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tangled_Up_in_Blue "Tangled Up in Blue")" (1975)[\[39\]](#cite_note-Nelson-2019-40) and wrote that it displayed "ambiguity" in Swift's songwriting about failed relationships by not blaming any sides and instead exploring the dissolution of a romance.[\[42\]](#cite_note-Nelson-2012-43) Meanwhile, J. English of [NPR](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NPR "NPR") thought that Swift's character in "All Too Well" both puts the blame on her "callous" ex-lover and "owns up to her naivete" for the loss of her innocence, departing from the one-sided blame on past songs such as "[Dear John](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dear_John_\(Taylor_Swift_song\) "Dear John (Taylor Swift song)")" (2010).[\[47\]](#cite_note-48)

In reviews of _Red_, critics lauded "All Too Well" for its detail-heavy lyricism[\[48\]](#cite_note-49) and deemed it the album's centerpiece.[\[1\]](#cite_note-Bernstein-2020-2)[\[28\]](#cite_note-Rosen-2013-29) Dolan,[\[34\]](#cite_note-Dolan-2010-35) Robbins,[\[30\]](#cite_note-Robbins-2012-31) and Semon said that the imagery of the couple "dancing around the kitchen in the refrigerator light" was a highlight.[\[32\]](#cite_note-Semon-2012-33) Many reviewers picked "All Too Well" as the album's best track, including Jonathan Keefe for _Slant Magazine_,[\[25\]](#cite_note-Keefe-2012-26) [Sam Lansky](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sam_Lansky "Sam Lansky") for _Billboard_,[\[49\]](#cite_note-50) Grady Smith for _[Entertainment Weekly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Entertainment_Weekly "Entertainment Weekly"),_[\[36\]](#cite_note-Smith-2012-37) and [Ben Rayner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ben_Rayner "Ben Rayner") for the _[Toronto Star](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toronto_Star "Toronto Star")_.[\[41\]](#cite_note-Rayner-2012-42) Rosen wrote that it "takes a special songwriter to craft a sneering kiss-off that's also tender valediction", highlighting the bitter accusations ("You call me up again just to break me like a promise/ So casually cruel in the name of being honest") and the affectionate memories ("Photo album on the counter, your cheeks were turning red/ You used to be a little kid with glasses in a twin-size bed").[\[28\]](#cite_note-Rosen-2013-29)

Some critics highlighted Swift's evolved songwriting. Nelson, in his review for _The Atlantic_, complimented how Swift expressed "ambiguity" and said that the scarf imagery, like a Chekov's gun, makes it "an exhilarating piece of writing". He added that "All Too Well" explores the dissolution of a romance "so delicately" that he found himself contemplating the song similar to how he would do to a [Leonard Cohen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leonard_Cohen "Leonard Cohen") song.[\[42\]](#cite_note-Nelson-2012-43) Keefe highlighted the bridge for featuring one of Swift's "best-ever lines" and how "the song explodes into a full-on bloodletting",[\[25\]](#cite_note-Keefe-2012-26) _[American Songwriter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Songwriter "American Songwriter")_'s Jewly Hight lauded the portrayal of heartbreak using "tangible details",[\[50\]](#cite_note-51) and _[PopMatters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PopMatters "PopMatters")_'s Arnold Pan said the song shows how Swift "has amped things up" by "combining the kind of drama that has come natural to her songwriting with a widescreen guitar-driven approach".[\[51\]](#cite_note-52)

Other reviews also praised the track's sound. Robbins wrote that "All Too Well" is one of the _Red_ tracks that "go down like [pop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pop_music "Pop music") punch spiked by pros".[\[30\]](#cite_note-Robbins-2012-31) Semon described the song as an "acoustic-tinged tearjerker" that has "an alarming intimacy and intense urgency that might even take \[Swift's\] diehard fans off-guard",[\[32\]](#cite_note-Semon-2012-33) and _[The New York Times](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_New_York_Times "The New York Times")_ [Jon Caramanica](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jon_Caramanica "Jon Caramanica") said that the song "swells until it erupts".[\[44\]](#cite_note-Caramanica-2012-45) _Newsday_ hailed "All Too Well" as the album's highlight "both in drama and execution, with Swift's vocals at their most emotional and her lyrics at their sharpest".[\[33\]](#cite_note-Newsday-2012-34) In _[NME](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NME "NME")_, Lucy Harbron selected its bridge as Swift's best and wrote that it was an "ultimate post-breakup big euphoric cry soundtrack".[\[52\]](#cite_note-53)

Swift departed from Big Machine and signed a new contract with [Republic Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republic_Records "Republic Records") in 2018. She began re-recording her first six studio albums in November 2020.[\[59\]](#cite_note-60) The decision followed a [2019 dispute](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taylor_Swift_masters_dispute "Taylor Swift masters dispute") between Swift and the talent manager [Scooter Braun](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scooter_Braun "Scooter Braun"), who acquired Big Machine Records, over the masters of Swift's albums that the label had released.[\[60\]](#cite_note-61)[\[61\]](#cite_note-62) By re-recording the albums, Swift had full ownership of the new masters, which enabled her to encourage licensing of her re-recorded songs for [commercial use](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Synchronization_rights "Synchronization rights") in hopes of substituting the Big Machine-owned masters.[\[62\]](#cite_note-63) She denoted the re-recordings with a "Taylor's Version" subtitle.[\[63\]](#cite_note-64)

_Red_'s re-recorded album, _[Red (Taylor's Version)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_\(Taylor's_Version\) "Red (Taylor's Version)")_, was released on November 12, 2021. It features two versions of "All Too Well": a re-recording of the original album version subtitled "Taylor's Version", and an unabridged version subtitled "10 Minute Version (Taylor's Version) (From the Vault)".[\[64\]](#cite_note-65)[\[65\]](#cite_note-Harris-2021-66) Speaking on _[The Tonight Show Starring Jimmy Fallon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Tonight_Show_Starring_Jimmy_Fallon "The Tonight Show Starring Jimmy Fallon")_ a day prior to the album's release, Swift said that the 10-minute version was recorded by the sound guy at a Speak Now World Tour rehearsal, and her mother Andrea Swift collected a CD recording of it; for the released version, she used notes and new lyricism to flesh out the song, no longer having the soundcheck recording.[\[66\]](#cite_note-67)

Swift wrote and directed _[All Too Well: The Short Film](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/All_Too_Well:_The_Short_Film "All Too Well: The Short Film")_ based on the premise of "All Too Well (10 Minute Version)". It stars [Sadie Sink](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sadie_Sink "Sadie Sink") and [Dylan O'Brien](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dylan_O'Brien "Dylan O'Brien") as a couple in a romantic relationship that ultimately falls apart. Swift premiered the [short film](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Short_film "Short film") at a fan event in New York City on November 12, 2021, the same day that the re-recorded album was released; she also gave a surprise performance of the song there.[\[67\]](#cite_note-68)

"All Too Well (10 Minute Version)" was released via Swift's online store on November 15, 2021, exclusively to US customers.[\[68\]](#cite_note-DL-69) The acoustic "Sad Girl Autumn" version, recorded at [Aaron Dessner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aaron_Dessner "Aaron Dessner")'s Long Pond Studio in the [Hudson Valley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hudson_Valley "Hudson Valley"), was released on November 17.[\[69\]](#cite_note-70) On June 11, 2022, the version used in the short film was made available for download and streaming, and the live performance at the premiere was made available for download, the same day Swift made an appearance at the [Tribeca Film Festival](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tribeca_Film_Festival "Tribeca Film Festival") to discuss her approach to making the film.[\[70\]](#cite_note-71)[\[71\]](#cite_note-72)[\[72\]](#cite_note-acoustic-73)

A sample of the final verse and [outro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Outro_\(music\) "Outro (music)") of "All Too Well (10 Minute Version)", showing the atmospheric production of synths, strings, percussion, distant violins and acoustic guitar [arpeggios](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arpeggio "Arpeggio"), and layered vocal harmonies
