"**All Too Well**" is a song by the American singer-songwriter [Taylor Swift](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taylor_Swift "Taylor Swift"). Written by Swift and [Liz Rose](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liz_Rose "Liz Rose"), the song was first produced by Swift and [Nathan Chapman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nathan_Chapman_\(record_producer\) "Nathan Chapman (record producer)") for her fourth studio album, _[Red](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_\(Taylor_Swift_album\) "Red (Taylor Swift album)")_ (2012). After a [2019 dispute regarding the ownership of Swift's masters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taylor_Swift_masters_dispute "Taylor Swift masters dispute"), she [re-recorded](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Re-recording_\(music\) "Re-recording (music)") the song as "**All Too Well (Taylor's Version)**" and released an unabridged "**10 Minute Version**" as part of the re-recorded album _[Red (Taylor's Version)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_\(Taylor's_Version\) "Red (Taylor's Version)")_ in November 2021.[\[note 1\]](#cite_note-1)

The lyrics of "All Too Well" narrate a failed romantic relationship, recalling the intimate memories and exploring the painful aftermath. The detail of a scarf that the narrator left at the house of her ex-lover's sister generated widespread interpretations and became a popular culture phenomenon. The 2012 version is a slow-burning [power ballad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Power_ballad "Power ballad") combining styles of [country](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Country_music "Country music") and [rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rock_music "Rock music"). The "10 Minute Version", produced by Swift and [Jack Antonoff](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jack_Antonoff "Jack Antonoff"), has an atmospheric [pop rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pop_rock "Pop rock") production. She performed the song at the [2014 Grammy Awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/56th_Annual_Grammy_Awards "56th Annual Grammy Awards") and included it in the set lists for two of her world tours: [the Red Tour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Red_Tour "The Red Tour") (2013–2014) and [the Eras Tour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Eras_Tour "The Eras Tour") (2023–2024).

"All Too Well" charted in Canada and the United States in 2012, and the "Taylor's Version" re-recording peaked atop the [_Billboard_ Global 200](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billboard_Global_200 "Billboard Global 200") and became the longest song to top the US [_Billboard_ Hot 100](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billboard_Hot_100 "Billboard Hot 100"). The song also charted at number one in Australia, Canada, Ireland, Malaysia, New Zealand, and Singapore. _[Rolling Stone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rolling_Stone "Rolling Stone")_ included it at number 69 in their 2021 revision of the "[500 Greatest Songs of All Time](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rolling_Stone's_500_Greatest_Songs_of_All_Time "Rolling Stone's 500 Greatest Songs of All Time")". Critics praised the "10 Minute Version" for providing a richer context with its additional verses. The short film version of this re-recording received a [Grammy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grammy_Awards "Grammy Awards") nomination for [Song of the Year](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grammy_Award_for_Song_of_the_Year "Grammy Award for Song of the Year") at the [65th Annual Grammy Awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/65th_Annual_Grammy_Awards "65th Annual Grammy Awards"). Swift directed _[All Too Well: The Short Film](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/All_Too_Well:_The_Short_Film "All Too Well: The Short Film")_ to accompany it, which won the [Grammy Award for Best Music Video](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grammy_Award_for_Best_Music_Video "Grammy Award for Best Music Video").

## Background and release

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=All_Too_Well&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Background and release")\]

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/7c/Taylor_Swift_Sydney.jpg/250px-Taylor_Swift_Sydney.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Taylor_Swift_Sydney.jpg)

Swift (pictured in 2012) began writing the song during rehearsals for the [Speak Now World Tour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now_World_Tour "Speak Now World Tour") in February 2011.

[Taylor Swift](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taylor_Swift "Taylor Swift") waѕ inspired by her tumultuous feelings after a breakup while conceiving her fourth studio album, [_Red_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_\(Taylor_Swift_album\) "Red (Taylor Swift album)") (2012).[\[1\]](#cite_note-Bernstein-2020-2) "All Too Well" was the first song Swift wrote for _Red_.[\[2\]](#cite_note-3) During a February 2011 rehearsal of the [Speak Now World Tour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now_World_Tour "Speak Now World Tour"), she [ad-libbed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ad_libitum "Ad libitum") some lyrics to the song while playing a four-[chord](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chord_\(music\) "Chord (music)") guitar [riff](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riff "Riff") as her touring band spontaneously played backing instruments.[\[1\]](#cite_note-Bernstein-2020-2) Swift told _[Rolling Stone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rolling_Stone "Rolling Stone")_ that this relationship caused "a few roller coasters", and she channeled the tumult into the song.[\[1\]](#cite_note-Bernstein-2020-2) She told the _[New York Times](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_New_York_Times "The New York Times")_ that the impromptu performance was "a very emotional rant." She recalled being very sad to the point where "sadness is you, you are sadness."[\[3\]](#cite_note-4) According to the booklets of Swift's 2019 album [_Lover_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lover_\(album\) "Lover (album)"), the final draft was completed a month later.[\[4\]](#cite_note-5)[\[5\]](#cite_note-6)

Swift asked [Liz Rose](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liz_Rose "Liz Rose"), who had co-written songs on her first albums, to co-write "All Too Well". Rose said that it was an unexpected collaboration after not having worked with Swift for some years;[\[6\]](#cite_note-Willman-2014-7) the last time they worked together was on Swift's 2008 album [_Fearless_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fearless_\(Taylor_Swift_album\) "Fearless (Taylor Swift album)").[\[7\]](#cite_note-Jones-2024-8) When Rose agreed to collaborate, she recalled that Swift had come up with the melody.[\[8\]](#cite_note-9) In an interview with _[Good Morning America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Good_Morning_America "Good Morning America")_, Swift said that the song was "the hardest to write on the album", saying that it took her some time "to filter through everything \[she\] wanted to put in the song" without making it lengthy with the help from Rose.[\[9\]](#cite_note-10) Rose said that the song was originally "10, 12 or 15 minutes long" or "probably a 20-minute song" before trimming.[\[6\]](#cite_note-Willman-2014-7)[\[10\]](#cite_note-Skinner-2019-11) The final album version is 5 minutes and 28 seconds long, the longest song on _Red_.[\[11\]](#cite_note-12) It was produced by Swift and [Nathan Chapman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nathan_Chapman_\(record_producer\) "Nathan Chapman (record producer)").[\[12\]](#cite_note-Swift-2012-13)

_Red_ was released on October 22, 2012, by [Big Machine Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Big_Machine_Records "Big Machine Records").[\[13\]](#cite_note-14) After _Red_ was released, "All Too Well" debuted at number 80 on the [_Billboard_ Hot 100](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billboard_Hot_100 "Billboard Hot 100") chart dated November 10, 2012;[\[14\]](#cite_note-Hot100-15) it also charted at number 17 on [Hot Country Songs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hot_Country_Songs "Hot Country Songs")[\[15\]](#cite_note-CountrySongs-16) and number 58 on [Country Airplay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Country_Airplay "Country Airplay").[\[16\]](#cite_note-CountryAirplay-17) The [Recording Industry Association of America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Recording_Industry_Association_of_America "Recording Industry Association of America") (RIAA) in 2018 [certified](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RIAA_certification "RIAA certification") the track gold for crossing 500,000 units based on sales and streams.[\[17\]](#cite_note-RIAA-18) The song also peaked at number 59 on the [Canadian Hot 100](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canadian_Hot_100 "Canadian Hot 100"),[\[18\]](#cite_note-Canada-19) and it was [certified](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_music_recording_certifications "List of music recording certifications") platinum in Australia,[\[19\]](#cite_note-ARIA-20) gold in Brazil[\[20\]](#cite_note-PMB-21) and Portugal,[\[21\]](#cite_note-AFP-22) and silver in the United Kingdom.[\[22\]](#cite_note-BPIOG-23)

![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/cb/Gnome-mime-audio-openclipart.svg/60px-Gnome-mime-audio-openclipart.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)

Chronicling a fallen relationship, "All Too Well" builds up with [overdubbed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Overdub "Overdub") guitars, drums, and strings. Its sound blends styles of [country](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Country_music "Country music"), [folk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Folk_music "Folk music"), and [rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rock_music "Rock music").

"All Too Well" is a [power ballad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Power_ballad "Power ballad")[\[23\]](#cite_note-24)[\[24\]](#cite_note-Braca-2021-25) that is set over a [4/4](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/4/4_time "4/4 time") beat.[\[7\]](#cite_note-Jones-2024-8) The track gradually builds up to a big, eruptive [crescendo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crescendo "Crescendo") in each [refrain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Refrain "Refrain").[\[7\]](#cite_note-Jones-2024-8)[\[25\]](#cite_note-Keefe-2012-26)[\[26\]](#cite_note-Farley-2017-27) Chapman is the sole musician on the track; he played acoustic guitar, electric guitar, bass, and drums, and provided background vocals. The instruments are [overdubbed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Overdubbing "Overdubbing") and [multitracked](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Multitrack_recording "Multitrack recording").[\[27\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPerone201746-28) [Jody Rosen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jody_Rosen "Jody Rosen"), in an article for [_New York_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_\(magazine\) "New York (magazine)"), wrote that the production "rises, like a slow-cresting wave".[\[28\]](#cite_note-Rosen-2013-29)

Bernard Perusse of the _[Edmonton Journal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edmonton_Journal "Edmonton Journal")_ wrote that the song displays influences of [U2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U2 "U2"),[\[29\]](#cite_note-30) while Rosen and [_Spin_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spin_\(magazine\) "Spin (magazine)")'s Michael Robbins thought that its driving [bassline](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bassline "Bassline") was reminiscent of that from U2's "[With or Without You](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/With_or_Without_You "With or Without You")" (1987).[\[28\]](#cite_note-Rosen-2013-29)[\[30\]](#cite_note-Robbins-2012-31) _[Slant Magazine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slant_Magazine "Slant Magazine")_'s Jonathan Keefe wrote that the track progresses from "coffeehouse [folk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Folk_music "Folk music") to [arena rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arena_rock "Arena rock")".[\[25\]](#cite_note-Keefe-2012-26) Bruce Warren, assistant general manager of [programming](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radio_programming "Radio programming") at [WXPN](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WXPN "WXPN"), commented that the track has a [soft rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soft_rock "Soft rock") production.[\[24\]](#cite_note-Braca-2021-25) _[Billboard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billboard_\(magazine\) "Billboard (magazine)")_ and Craig S. Semon of the _[Telegram & Gazette](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Telegram_&_Gazette "Telegram & Gazette")_ described the genre as [country](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Country_music "Country music"),[\[31\]](#cite_note-Billboard-2012-32)[\[32\]](#cite_note-Semon-2012-33) while _[Newsday](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newsday "Newsday")_ said that the song has an "[alt-country](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alt-country "Alt-country") ache".[\[33\]](#cite_note-Newsday-2012-34) Jon Dolan of _Rolling Stone_ opined that "All Too Well" exemplified the "diaristic post-country [rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rock_music "Rock music")" sound of _Red_,[\[34\]](#cite_note-Dolan-2010-35) and in their list of the 50 best albums of 2012, the magazine dubbed the genre "Nashville [pop rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pop_rock "Pop rock")".[\[35\]](#cite_note-36)

## Lyrics and interpretations

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=All_Too_Well&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Lyrics and interpretations")\]

The song is a recount of a fallen relationship[\[7\]](#cite_note-Jones-2024-8)[\[31\]](#cite_note-Billboard-2012-32) that happened in the fall.[\[36\]](#cite_note-Smith-2012-37)[\[37\]](#cite_note-Garrett-2021-38)[\[38\]](#cite_note-Tiffany-2021-39) The verses explore the memories in a loosely chronological order,[\[39\]](#cite_note-Nelson-2019-40) using expository details.[\[40\]](#cite_note-41) The song begins with details of a trip of two ex-lovers to [Upstate New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Upstate_New_York "Upstate New York") ("We're singin' in the car, getting lost upstate")[\[26\]](#cite_note-Farley-2017-27) such as imagery of "autumn leaves falling down like pieces into place".[\[37\]](#cite_note-Garrett-2021-38) When they visit the house of the love interest's sister during the [Thanksgiving](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thanksgiving "Thanksgiving") weekend, the narrator leaves her scarf at that place.[\[26\]](#cite_note-Farley-2017-27)[\[41\]](#cite_note-Rayner-2012-42)[\[42\]](#cite_note-Nelson-2012-43) The narrator then recalls the intimate moments with her ex-lover ("There we are again in the middle of the night/ Dancing around the kitchen in the refrigerator light")[\[39\]](#cite_note-Nelson-2019-40) and the mundane details, such as photo albums, a twin-sized bed, and stopping at red lights.[\[24\]](#cite_note-Braca-2021-25)[\[43\]](#cite_note-Cooney-2024-44) After each refrain, the narrator insists that those moments mattered ("I was there, I remember it all too well").[\[7\]](#cite_note-Jones-2024-8)[\[39\]](#cite_note-Nelson-2019-40)

The [bridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bridge_\(music\) "Bridge (music)") is where the track reaches its climax; Swift sings in her upper [register](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Register_\(music\) "Register (music)")[\[7\]](#cite_note-Jones-2024-8)[\[43\]](#cite_note-Cooney-2024-44) and almost shouts with anger ("You call me up again, just to break me like a promise/ So casually cruel in the name of being honest").[\[44\]](#cite_note-Caramanica-2012-45) Her narrator questions why the relationship fell apart, pondering whether it was because she "asked for too much".[\[45\]](#cite_note-Jagota-2021-46) In the final verse, the narrator mentions the scarf previously detailed in the first verse ("But you keep my old scarf from that very first week/ 'Cause it reminds you of innocence and it smells like me"),[\[39\]](#cite_note-Nelson-2019-40)[\[42\]](#cite_note-Nelson-2012-43) asserting that the love she gave and felt was real and that the ex-partner must have felt the same.[\[45\]](#cite_note-Jagota-2021-46)

Brittany Spanos of _Rolling Stone_ wrote that the song describes "the pain of having to piece one's self back together again" after a crumbled relationship.[\[46\]](#cite_note-47) Brad Nelson, in his reviews for _[The Atlantic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Atlantic "The Atlantic")_ and [_Pitchfork_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pitchfork_\(website\) "Pitchfork (website)"), said that the scarf imagery in the lyrics acts like a [Chekhov's gun](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chekhov's_gun "Chekhov's gun"), symbolizing the persisting emotional flame of the romance long after it has physically ended.[\[39\]](#cite_note-Nelson-2019-40)[\[42\]](#cite_note-Nelson-2012-43) Nelson compared Swift's lyrics mentioning various memories in a loosely chronological timeline to the technique used in [Bob Dylan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Dylan "Bob Dylan")'s "[Tangled Up in Blue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tangled_Up_in_Blue "Tangled Up in Blue")" (1975)[\[39\]](#cite_note-Nelson-2019-40) and wrote that it displayed "ambiguity" in Swift's songwriting about failed relationships by not blaming any sides and instead exploring the dissolution of a romance.[\[42\]](#cite_note-Nelson-2012-43) Meanwhile, J. English of [NPR](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NPR "NPR") thought that Swift's character in "All Too Well" both puts the blame on her "callous" ex-lover and "owns up to her naivete" for the loss of her innocence, departing from the one-sided blame on past songs such as "[Dear John](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dear_John_\(Taylor_Swift_song\) "Dear John (Taylor Swift song)")" (2010).[\[47\]](#cite_note-48)

In reviews of _Red_, critics lauded "All Too Well" for its detail-heavy lyricism[\[48\]](#cite_note-49) and deemed it the album's centerpiece.[\[1\]](#cite_note-Bernstein-2020-2)[\[28\]](#cite_note-Rosen-2013-29) Dolan,[\[34\]](#cite_note-Dolan-2010-35) Robbins,[\[30\]](#cite_note-Robbins-2012-31) and Semon said that the imagery of the couple "dancing around the kitchen in the refrigerator light" was a highlight.[\[32\]](#cite_note-Semon-2012-33) Many reviewers picked "All Too Well" as the album's best track, including Jonathan Keefe for _Slant Magazine_,[\[25\]](#cite_note-Keefe-2012-26) [Sam Lansky](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sam_Lansky "Sam Lansky") for _Billboard_,[\[49\]](#cite_note-50) Grady Smith for _[Entertainment Weekly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Entertainment_Weekly "Entertainment Weekly"),_[\[36\]](#cite_note-Smith-2012-37) and [Ben Rayner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ben_Rayner "Ben Rayner") for the _[Toronto Star](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toronto_Star "Toronto Star")_.[\[41\]](#cite_note-Rayner-2012-42) Rosen wrote that it "takes a special songwriter to craft a sneering kiss-off that's also tender valediction", highlighting the bitter accusations ("You call me up again just to break me like a promise/ So casually cruel in the name of being honest") and the affectionate memories ("Photo album on the counter, your cheeks were turning red/ You used to be a little kid with glasses in a twin-size bed").[\[28\]](#cite_note-Rosen-2013-29)

Some critics highlighted Swift's evolved songwriting. Nelson, in his review for _The Atlantic_, complimented how Swift expressed "ambiguity" and said that the scarf imagery, like a Chekov's gun, makes it "an exhilarating piece of writing". He added that "All Too Well" explores the dissolution of a romance "so delicately" that he found himself contemplating the song similar to how he would do to a [Leonard Cohen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leonard_Cohen "Leonard Cohen") song.[\[42\]](#cite_note-Nelson-2012-43) Keefe highlighted the bridge for featuring one of Swift's "best-ever lines" and how "the song explodes into a full-on bloodletting",[\[25\]](#cite_note-Keefe-2012-26) _[American Songwriter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Songwriter "American Songwriter")_'s Jewly Hight lauded the portrayal of heartbreak using "tangible details",[\[50\]](#cite_note-51) and _[PopMatters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PopMatters "PopMatters")_'s Arnold Pan said the song shows how Swift "has amped things up" by "combining the kind of drama that has come natural to her songwriting with a widescreen guitar-driven approach".[\[51\]](#cite_note-52)

Other reviews also praised the track's sound. Robbins wrote that "All Too Well" is one of the _Red_ tracks that "go down like [pop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pop_music "Pop music") punch spiked by pros".[\[30\]](#cite_note-Robbins-2012-31) Semon described the song as an "acoustic-tinged tearjerker" that has "an alarming intimacy and intense urgency that might even take \[Swift's\] diehard fans off-guard",[\[32\]](#cite_note-Semon-2012-33) and _[The New York Times](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_New_York_Times "The New York Times")_ [Jon Caramanica](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jon_Caramanica "Jon Caramanica") said that the song "swells until it erupts".[\[44\]](#cite_note-Caramanica-2012-45) _Newsday_ hailed "All Too Well" as the album's highlight "both in drama and execution, with Swift's vocals at their most emotional and her lyrics at their sharpest".[\[33\]](#cite_note-Newsday-2012-34) In _[NME](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NME "NME")_, Lucy Harbron selected its bridge as Swift's best and wrote that it was an "ultimate post-breakup big euphoric cry soundtrack".[\[52\]](#cite_note-53)

Swift departed from Big Machine and signed a new contract with [Republic Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republic_Records "Republic Records") in 2018. She began re-recording her first six studio albums in November 2020.[\[59\]](#cite_note-60) The decision followed a [2019 dispute](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taylor_Swift_masters_dispute "Taylor Swift masters dispute") between Swift and the talent manager [Scooter Braun](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scooter_Braun "Scooter Braun"), who acquired Big Machine Records, over the masters of Swift's albums that the label had released.[\[60\]](#cite_note-61)[\[61\]](#cite_note-62) By re-recording the albums, Swift had full ownership of the new masters, which enabled her to encourage licensing of her re-recorded songs for [commercial use](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Synchronization_rights "Synchronization rights") in hopes of substituting the Big Machine-owned masters.[\[62\]](#cite_note-63) She denoted the re-recordings with a "Taylor's Version" subtitle.[\[63\]](#cite_note-64)

_Red_'s re-recorded album, _[Red (Taylor's Version)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_\(Taylor's_Version\) "Red (Taylor's Version)")_, was released on November 12, 2021. It features two versions of "All Too Well": a re-recording of the original album version subtitled "Taylor's Version", and an unabridged version subtitled "10 Minute Version (Taylor's Version) (From the Vault)".[\[64\]](#cite_note-65)[\[65\]](#cite_note-Harris-2021-66) Speaking on _[The Tonight Show Starring Jimmy Fallon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Tonight_Show_Starring_Jimmy_Fallon "The Tonight Show Starring Jimmy Fallon")_ a day prior to the album's release, Swift said that the 10-minute version was recorded by the sound guy at a Speak Now World Tour rehearsal, and her mother Andrea Swift collected a CD recording of it; for the released version, she used notes and new lyricism to flesh out the song, no longer having the soundcheck recording.[\[66\]](#cite_note-67)

Swift wrote and directed _[All Too Well: The Short Film](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/All_Too_Well:_The_Short_Film "All Too Well: The Short Film")_ based on the premise of "All Too Well (10 Minute Version)". It stars [Sadie Sink](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sadie_Sink "Sadie Sink") and [Dylan O'Brien](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dylan_O'Brien "Dylan O'Brien") as a couple in a romantic relationship that ultimately falls apart. Swift premiered the [short film](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Short_film "Short film") at a fan event in New York City on November 12, 2021, the same day that the re-recorded album was released; she also gave a surprise performance of the song there.[\[67\]](#cite_note-68)

"All Too Well (10 Minute Version)" was released via Swift's online store on November 15, 2021, exclusively to US customers.[\[68\]](#cite_note-DL-69) The acoustic "Sad Girl Autumn" version, recorded at [Aaron Dessner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aaron_Dessner "Aaron Dessner")'s Long Pond Studio in the [Hudson Valley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hudson_Valley "Hudson Valley"), was released on November 17.[\[69\]](#cite_note-70) On June 11, 2022, the version used in the short film was made available for download and streaming, and the live performance at the premiere was made available for download, the same day Swift made an appearance at the [Tribeca Film Festival](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tribeca_Film_Festival "Tribeca Film Festival") to discuss her approach to making the film.[\[70\]](#cite_note-71)[\[71\]](#cite_note-72)[\[72\]](#cite_note-acoustic-73)

A sample of the final verse and [outro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Outro_\(music\) "Outro (music)") of "All Too Well (10 Minute Version)", showing the atmospheric production of synths, strings, percussion, distant violins and acoustic guitar [arpeggios](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arpeggio "Arpeggio"), and layered vocal harmonies

"All Too Well (10 Minute Version)" has an atmospheric pop rock production by Swift and [Jack Antonoff](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jack_Antonoff "Jack Antonoff").[\[73\]](#cite_note-74) Compared to the shorter version, the guitars in the 10 Minute Version are more atmospheric and subdued, and the production is driven more prominently by keyboards and synths.[\[74\]](#cite_note-Carson-2021-75)[\[75\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTESomvilleBenoit2025198-76) From the 7:15 mark, the [outro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Outro_\(music\) "Outro (music)") begins,

"**Cruel Summer**" is a song by the American singer-songwriter [Taylor Swift](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taylor_Swift "Taylor Swift") from her seventh studio album, _[Lover](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lover_\(album\) "Lover (album)")_ (2019). Swift and [Jack Antonoff](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jack_Antonoff "Jack Antonoff") produced the song, and they wrote it with [St. Vincent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Vincent_\(musician\) "St. Vincent (musician)"). "Cruel Summer" is an [electropop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electropop "Electropop"), [synth-pop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Synth-pop "Synth-pop"), [bubblegum pop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bubblegum_pop "Bubblegum pop"), and [industrial pop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Industrial_pop "Industrial pop") song composed of [synths](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Synths "Synths"), wobbling beats, and [vocoder](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vocoder "Vocoder")\-manipulated vocals. The lyrics are about an intense and painful summer romance.

Initial reviews of _Lover_ lauded "Cruel Summer" for its melodic composition and [catchy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catchy "Catchy") sound, specifically highlighting the [hook](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hook_\(music\) "Hook (music)") and [bridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bridge_\(music\) "Bridge (music)"); many deemed it a highlight on the album. Retrospective reviews have considered "Cruel Summer" one of Swift's best songs, and it was placed on the 2024 revision of [_Rolling Stone_'s 500 Greatest Songs of All Time](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rolling_Stone's_500_Greatest_Songs_of_All_Time "Rolling Stone's 500 Greatest Songs of All Time"). "Cruel Summer" debuted in the top 30 of various singles charts in 2019 and became a fan favorite over time, prompting [fans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swifties "Swifties") and publications to question why Swift did not release the track as a single.

After being included in the set list of Swift's sixth concert tour, [the Eras Tour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Eras_Tour "The Eras Tour"), in 2023, "Cruel Summer" became [viral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Viral_video "Viral video") on social media, leading [Republic Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republic_Records "Republic Records") to release it as a single on June 20, 2023. In the United States, the single peaked atop the [_Billboard_ Hot 100](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billboard_Hot_100 "Billboard Hot 100") for four weeks and helped Swift become the solo artist with the most number-one songs on the [Pop Airplay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pop_Airplay "Pop Airplay") and [Adult Pop Airplay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adult_Pop_Airplay "Adult Pop Airplay") radio charts. It also topped the [_Billboard_ Global 200](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billboard_Global_200 "Billboard Global 200") and the singles charts in Australia, Canada, the Philippines, and Singapore. The song has been [certified](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Music_recording_certification "Music recording certification") diamond in France, and multi-platinum in Australia, Brazil, New Zealand, Poland, Portugal, Spain, Switzerland, and the United Kingdom.

## Background and composition

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Cruel_Summer_\(Taylor_Swift_song\)&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Background and composition")\]

[Taylor Swift](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taylor_Swift "Taylor Swift") described her seventh studio album, _[Lover](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lover_\(album\) "Lover (album)")_, as a "love letter to love" itself with all the feelings evoked by it.[\[1\]](#cite_note-1) The album was released on August 23, 2019, via [Republic Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republic_Records "Republic Records").[\[2\]](#cite_note-2) _Lover_ consists of 18 tracks, and "Cruel Summer" is track number two.[\[3\]](#cite_note-LinerNotes-3) According to Swift, the track is about an uncertain summer romance with elements of pain and desperation in it.[\[4\]](#cite_note-iHeart-4) The relationship in question is "where you're yearning for something that you don't quite have yet, it's just right there, and you just can't reach it".[\[4\]](#cite_note-iHeart-4)

![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/cb/Gnome-mime-audio-openclipart.svg/60px-Gnome-mime-audio-openclipart.svg.png)

A sample of the [refrain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Refrain "Refrain"), instrumented by pulsing [synths](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Synths "Synths") and fluctuating vocals singing "ooooh"

"Cruel Summer" is an [electropop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electropop "Electropop"),[\[5\]](#cite_note-5)[\[6\]](#cite_note-6)[\[7\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEZaleski2024151-7) [synth-pop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Synth-pop "Synth-pop"),[\[8\]](#cite_note-independent-8)[\[9\]](#cite_note-9)[\[10\]](#cite_note-10) [bubblegum pop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bubblegum_pop "Bubblegum pop"),[\[11\]](#cite_note-11) and [industrial pop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Industrial_pop "Industrial pop") song.[\[12\]](#cite_note-12) Critics described its production as melancholic[\[13\]](#cite_note-13) or dreamy.[\[14\]](#cite_note-14) It has a "ranting" [bridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bridge_\(music\) "Bridge (music)") underscored by skittering synths,[\[15\]](#cite_note-Bruner-2019-15)[\[16\]](#cite_note-The_Spinoff-2019-16)[\[17\]](#cite_note-17)[\[18\]](#cite_note-18) distorted vocals[\[8\]](#cite_note-independent-8) manipulated by a [vocoder](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vocoder "Vocoder"),[\[19\]](#cite_note-19) and a hook that consists of a long, high, fluctuating "ooooh".[\[20\]](#cite_note-20) The song has a fast [tempo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tempo "Tempo") of 170 beats per minute with a time signature of **4**  
**4**. It is played in the key of [A major](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_major "A major") and follows a chord progression of A–C♯m–F♯m–D.[\[21\]](#cite_note-21)[\[22\]](#cite_note-22) Swift's vocals range from A2 to E5. "Cruel Summer" was written by Swift, [Jack Antonoff](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jack_Antonoff "Jack Antonoff") and [St. Vincent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Vincent_\(musician\) "St. Vincent (musician)"),[\[23\]](#cite_note-23) with a "burbling" production from Swift and Antonoff;[\[24\]](#cite_note-Sayles-2019-24) St. Vincent also took part in the production of the song, playing the guitar.[\[25\]](#cite_note-25)

Lyrically, the song is about a summer romance that entails strong feelings, including romantic ecstasy, anxiety, and pain.[\[26\]](#cite_note-26)[\[27\]](#cite_note-27) David Penn of _Hit Songs Deconstructed_ opined that the song's vocals, instrumentation and lyrics work "in tandem to create a unified expression, a combination known as [prosody](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prosody_\(linguistics\) "Prosody (linguistics)")".[\[28\]](#cite_note-28) According to [_Time_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Time_\(magazine\) "Time (magazine)")'s Raina Bruner, the song also portrays the challenges faced by pop stars in the public spotlight, similar to the theme of Swift's 2017 song "[Delicate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Delicate_\(Taylor_Swift_song\) "Delicate (Taylor Swift song)")".[\[15\]](#cite_note-Bruner-2019-15) Justin Styles of [_The Ringer_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ringer_\(website\) "The Ringer (website)") wrote that the song tells a "more humanizing version" of Swift's "ill-fated period three years ago", adding that Swift sings about "falling in love with then-current boyfriend [Joe Alwyn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Alwyn "Joe Alwyn") while her public life was in shambles".[\[24\]](#cite_note-Sayles-2019-24) Anna Gaca, writing for [_Pitchfork_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pitchfork_\(website\) "Pitchfork (website)"), called the song a "drama-free delight" with "magnetic pink glow".[\[29\]](#cite_note-29) _[The Spinoff](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Spinoff "The Spinoff")_ pointed out that Swift's vocals in "Cruel Summer" are "most notable for the modern [country](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Country_music "Country music") cadence".[\[16\]](#cite_note-The_Spinoff-2019-16)

## Release and commercial performance

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Cruel_Summer_\(Taylor_Swift_song\)&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Release and commercial performance")\]

"Cruel Summer" was released as the second track on _Lover_, on August 23, 2019, via [Republic Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republic_Records "Republic Records").[\[30\]](#cite_note-30) The track originally charted as an album cut within the top 30 in Singapore (8),[\[31\]](#cite_note-Singapore-31) Malaysia (13),[\[32\]](#cite_note-Malaysia-32) Ireland (20),[\[33\]](#cite_note-33) New Zealand (20),[\[34\]](#cite_note-34) Australia (23),[\[35\]](#cite_note-Australia19-35) the United Kingdom (27),[\[36\]](#cite_note-uk-36) and Canada (28).[\[37\]](#cite_note-Canada19-37) In the United States, the song debuted at number 29 on the [_Billboard_ Hot 100](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billboard_Hot_100 "Billboard Hot 100") dated September 7, 2019; it is one of the seven tracks from _Lover_ to reach the top 40[\[38\]](#cite_note-38) and remained on the chart for two weeks.[\[39\]](#cite_note-Zellner-2023-39) The song became a widespread fan favorite over time[\[40\]](#cite_note-40)[\[41\]](#cite_note-41) and critics and fans questioned Swift's decision over not having released "Cruel Summer" as a single.[\[42\]](#cite_note-Spanos-2023-42)[\[43\]](#cite_note-RadioDate-43)

[![Swift singing onstage dressed in a sparkling bodysuite](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/57/Eras_Tour_-_Arlington%2C_TX_-_Lover_Act_2_%28cropped%29.jpg/250px-Eras_Tour_-_Arlington%2C_TX_-_Lover_Act_2_%28cropped%29.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Eras_Tour_-_Arlington,_TX_-_Lover_Act_2_\(cropped\).jpg)

"Cruel Summer" resurged in popularity after Swift included it in the setlist of [the Eras Tour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Eras_Tour "The Eras Tour") in 2023.

Beginning March 2023, Swift embarked on [the Eras Tour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Eras_Tour "The Eras Tour"), her sixth headlining concert tour, as a tribute to all of her "musical eras".[\[44\]](#cite_note-44) The show begins with the _Lover_ act, during which "Cruel Summer" is the second song performed.[\[43\]](#cite_note-RadioDate-43) Around this time, the song began to resurge in popularity and [streaming](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Streaming "Streaming") after it became viral on social media.[\[42\]](#cite_note-Spanos-2023-42)[\[45\]](#cite_note-45) In the U.S., the single re-entered the _Billboard_ Hot 100 at number 49 on the chart dated June 3, 2023.[\[39\]](#cite_note-Zellner-2023-39) It began gaining airplay spins on US radio by mid-June,[\[46\]](#cite_note-46) leading Republic Records to release it as a single to US [contemporary hit radio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Contemporary_hit_radio "Contemporary hit radio") on June 20, 2023.[\[43\]](#cite_note-RadioDate-43)[\[47\]](#cite_note-Iasimone-2023-47) The song also impacted [hot adult contemporary radio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hot_adult_contemporary_radio "Hot adult contemporary radio") on June 26.[\[48\]](#cite_note-HotAC-48) On June 17, at an Eras Tour show in [Pittsburgh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pittsburgh "Pittsburgh"), Swift said she had intended to release "Cruel Summer" as a single in 2020 during the promotional cycle for _Lover_ but she abandoned the plan after the outbreak of the [COVID-19 pandemic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/COVID-19_pandemic_in_the_United_States "COVID-19 pandemic in the United States"), instead shifting her artistic direction and releasing her next album, _[Folklore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Folklore_\(Taylor_Swift_album\) "Folklore (Taylor Swift album)")_.[\[47\]](#cite_note-Iasimone-2023-47)[\[49\]](#cite_note-49)

"Cruel Summer" became Swift's record-extending 41st song to reach the top 10 on the _Billboard_ Hot 100 and the fourth _Lover_ track to do so.[\[50\]](#cite_note-50) After the release of the Eras Tour's [accompanying concert film](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taylor_Swift:_The_Eras_Tour "Taylor Swift: The Eras Tour"), a live recording of the song and a remix by [LP Giobbi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/LP_Giobbi "LP Giobbi") were released as part of a streaming compilation, titled _The Cruelest Summer,_ on October 18, 2023.[\[51\]](#cite_note-Atkinson-2023-51) "Cruel Summer" topped the _Billboard_ Hot 100, marking _Lover_'s first and Swift's 10th number-one single.[\[52\]](#cite_note-52) It was replaced by, and in turn replaced, Swift's "[Is It Over Now?](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Is_It_Over_Now%3F "Is It Over Now?")" atop the Hot 100 for one week,[\[53\]](#cite_note-53) spending a total of four non-consecutive weeks at number one and making Swift the first female artist to succeed herself at the top spot twice and thrice.[\[54\]](#cite_note-54)[\[55\]](#cite_note-Trust-2024a-55)

On US [_Billboard_ airplay charts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billboard_charts "Billboard charts") in 2023, "Cruel Summer" became Swift's eighth number-one single on [Radio Songs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radio_Songs_\(chart\) "Radio Songs (chart)"), where it reigned for 12 non-consecutive weeks surpassing "[Blank Space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blank_Space "Blank Space")" as her longest running number one.[\[56\]](#cite_note-Trust-2023-56) It became her 12th number-one single on [Pop Airplay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pop_Airplay "Pop Airplay"), and her 11th number-one single on [Adult Pop Airplay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adult_Pop_Airplay "Adult Pop Airplay"), making her the solo artist with the most chart toppers on the latter two charts.[\[57\]](#cite_note-57)[\[58\]](#cite_note-58) The song also spent 10 weeks atop Pop Airplay and 23 weeks atop Adult Pop Airplay, becoming her longest-running number-one song on both[\[56\]](#cite_note-Trust-2023-56) and the longest-running number-one song by a solo artist and female artist on the latter.[\[55\]](#cite_note-Trust-2024a-55)[\[59\]](#cite_note-Trust-2024b-59) Jason Lipshutz of _Billboard_ commented that the single's resurgent success "simply demonstrates Swift's current ubiquity, unprecedented in the modern music era".[\[60\]](#cite_note-60) In January 2024, the song topped the [Adult Contemporary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adult_Contemporary_\(chart\) "Adult Contemporary (chart)") chart, marking Swift's ninth number-one single. As such, it made Swift the first artist in history to release six singles that topped the Adult Contemporary, Adult Pop Airplay and Pop Airplay charts individually, surpassing [Adele](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adele "Adele") (five).[\[59\]](#cite_note-Trust-2024b-59) Additionally, the song spent 34 weeks in the top ten of the Hot 100, becoming the first song by a solo female artist to do so.[\[61\]](#cite_note-61) In total, "Cruel Summer" spent 54 weeks on the Hot 100, becoming Swift's longest-charting Hot 100 hit, surpassing "[Anti-Hero](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anti-Hero_\(song\) "Anti-Hero (song)")".[\[62\]](#cite_note-62)

Elsewhere, "Cruel Summer" reached new peaks in Australia (1),[\[63\]](#cite_note-aus-63) Canada (1),[\[64\]](#cite_note-Canada2023-64) Singapore (1),[\[65\]](#cite_note-65) New Zealand (3),[\[66\]](#cite_note-NZ2023-66) Ireland (4),[\[67\]](#cite_note-67) Malaysia (6),[\[68\]](#cite_note-68) and Brazil (54) as well.[\[69\]](#cite_note-69) It peaked at number one in the Philippines[\[70\]](#cite_note-Philippines-70) and entered the top 10 in Indonesia, as well in few Europeans countries, including Switzerland and Iceland, top twenty for most of them, including Norway, Sweden, Austria, Portugal, the Netherlands and Luxembourg and top forty in Denmark and Slovakia.[\[71\]](#cite_note-Indonesia-71) In France, from the general surprise, due to massive broadcasting radio plays, the song didn't reached the top fifty and reached number 52. However, the song spent 55 weeks and peaked at number 9 on French airplay and was certified diamond, becoming Swift fifth diamond single at the time.[\[72\]](#cite_note-72) The song was [certified](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Music_recording_certification "Music recording certification") thirteen-times platinum in Australia;[\[73\]](#cite_note-ARIA-73) seven-times platinum in New Zealand;[\[74\]](#cite_note-RMNZ-74) quadruple platinum in Portugal[\[75\]](#cite_note-afp-75) and the United Kingdom;[\[76\]](#cite_note-bpi-76) triple platinum in Switzerland;[\[77\]](#cite_note-IFPI_Switzerland-77) and double platinum in Brazil,[\[78\]](#cite_note-Brazil-78) Poland,[\[79\]](#cite_note-zpav-79) and Spain.[\[80\]](#cite_note-PROMUSICAE-80) It reached number one on the [_Billboard_ Global 200](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billboard_Global_200 "Billboard Global 200"),[\[81\]](#cite_note-global200-81) and was the sixth-most-streamed song globally on [Spotify](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spotify "Spotify") in 2023.[\[82\]](#cite_note-82) The song was the seventh-biggest song of 2023 according to the [International Federation of the Phonographic Industry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Federation_of_the_Phonographic_Industry "International Federation of the Phonographic Industry") (IFPI), with an equivalent of 1.39 billion global subscription streams.[\[83\]](#cite_note-83) Within the first half of 2024, according to [Luminate Data](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luminate_Data "Luminate Data"), the single was the third-most-streamed song globally with 1.012 billion streams.[\[84\]](#cite_note-84) St. Vincent described the resurgent success of "Cruel Summer" as "crazy", "so wild and so modern".[\[85\]](#cite_note-85)

In reviews of _Lover_, "Cruel Summer" received rave reviews from music critics, particularly for its production, bridge and hook. [Jon Caramanica](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jon_Caramanica "Jon Caramanica") of _[The New York Times](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_New_York_Times "The New York Times")_ commended the "thick, ethereal" production and Swift's signature vocal motifs such as the "question-mark syllables" and the "hard-felt smears".[\[86\]](#cite_note-86) Mikael Wood of the _[Los Angeles Times](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Angeles_Times "Los Angeles Times")_ proclaimed "Cruel Summer" to be the best song of _Lover_ and said the bridge where Swift "shrieks about the devil might be the punkest thing you'll hear all year".[\[87\]](#cite_note-87) Alex Abad-Santos, writing for [_Vox_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vox_\(website\) "Vox (website)"), listed "Cruel Summer" as one of his top-three best _Lover_ tracks, writing that the song is an "aquatic robot bop" featuring "wobbly" synths.[\[88\]](#cite_note-88) _The Spinoff_ stated that Swift "absolutely pulls it off" and compared it to [Bananarama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bananarama "Bananarama")'s [1983 song of the same name](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cruel_Summer_\(Bananarama_song\) "Cruel Summer (Bananarama song)").[\[16\]](#cite_note-The_Spinoff-2019-16) Writing for _The Ringer_, Justin Sayles praised the song as a "better rebuke of her personal drama than anything on her last album", and added that Swift "shakes off the bad vibes" with "Cruel Summer"; Sayles named it Swift's "most infectious song since that run of singles from _[1989](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1989_\(Taylor_Swift_album\) "1989 (Taylor Swift album)")_", and opined that song "sets the tone" for the "warmer, more inviting vibes" of _Lover_.[\[24\]](#cite_note-Sayles-2019-24) Also calling it "infectious", Nick Levine of _[NME](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NME "NME")_ termed the track as a "brilliant pop song".[\[89\]](#cite_note-89) Natalia Barr, writing for _[Consequence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Consequence_\(publication\) "Consequence (publication)")_, highlighted Swift's vocal delivery in the song's bridge ("He looks up, grinning like a devil"), calling it "simultaneously funny, agonizing, and thrilling, and needs to be created into a viral [YouTube](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/YouTube "YouTube") loop immediately". Barr further labeled "Cruel Summer" as one of the "most perfect" pop songs of 2019.[\[90\]](#cite_note-90) "Cruel Summer" featured on year-end lists of the best songs of 2019 by _Rolling Stone_ (4th)[\[91\]](#cite_note-91) and _Billboard_ (10th).[\[92\]](#cite_note-92)

Retrospectively, "Cruel Summer" continued to receive high acclaim, and has been deemed the signature track of _Lover_. In a 2021 list ranking the best bridges of the 21st-century, _Billboard_ placed "Cruel Summer" at number 11.[\[93\]](#cite_note-93) The song has ranked highly on critics' rankings of Swift's songs in her discography, appearing on such lists by [Rob Sheffield](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rob_Sheffield "Rob Sheffield") of _Rolling Stone_ (2021) at number 11 out of 229,[\[94\]](#cite_note-94) and Hannah Mylrea of _NME_ (2020), number 6 out of 161.[\[95\]](#cite_note-95) [_Clash_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clash_\(magazine\) "Clash (magazine)") critics picked the song as one of Swift's 15 best, citing its "highly addictive" [song structure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Song_structure "Song structure").[\[96\]](#cite_note-96) In 2022, _[Exclaim!](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Exclaim! "Exclaim!")_'s Alex Hudson and Megan LaPierre ranked it second on another list of the best 20 songs by Swift, praising how St. Vincent's artistic input complements Swift's.[\[97\]](#cite_note-97) Allaire Nuss of _[Entertainment Weekly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Entertainment_Weekly "Entertainment Weekly")_ described it as a "buzzer-beating, angst-wielding anthem".[\[98\]](#cite_note-98) Brittany Spanos of _Rolling Stone_ wrote in 2023, "Swift flaunts a rock-star edge alongside a grand sense of romantic urgency" in "Cruel Summer", making it one of her best songs.[\[42\]](#cite_note-Spanos-2023-42) _Billboard_ opined in 2023 that "Cruel Summer" is both a fan and a critics' favorite.[\[99\]](#cite_note-99) In 2024, _Rolling Stone_ ranked the song at number 400 in their updated list of the [500 Greatest Songs of All Time](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/500_Greatest_Songs_of_All_Time "500 Greatest Songs of All Time").[\[100\]](#cite_note-100)

"**Cruel Summer**" is a song by the American singer-songwriter [Taylor Swift](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taylor_Swift "Taylor Swift") from her seventh studio album, _[Lover](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lover_\(album\) "Lover (album)")_ (2019). Swift and [Jack Antonoff](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jack_Antonoff "Jack Antonoff") produced the song, and they wrote it with [St. Vincent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Vincent_\(musician\) "St. Vincent (musician)"). "Cruel Summer" is an [electropop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electropop "Electropop"), [synth-pop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Synth-pop "Synth-pop"), [bubblegum pop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bubblegum_pop "Bubblegum pop"), and [industrial pop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Industrial_pop "Industrial pop") song composed of [synths](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Synths "Synths"), wobbling beats, and [vocoder](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vocoder "Vocoder")\-manipulated vocals. The lyrics are about an intense and painful summer romance.

Initial reviews of _Lover_ lauded "Cruel Summer" for its melodic composition and [catchy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catchy "Catchy") sound, specifically highlighting the [hook](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hook_\(music\) "Hook (music)") and [bridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bridge_\(music\) "Bridge (music)"); many deemed it a highlight on the album. Retrospective reviews have considered "Cruel Summer" one of Swift's best songs, and it was placed on the 2024 revision of [_Rolling Stone_'s 500 Greatest Songs of All Time](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rolling_Stone's_500_Greatest_Songs_of_All_Time "Rolling Stone's 500 Greatest Songs of All Time"). "Cruel Summer" debuted in the top 30 of various singles charts in 2019 and became a fan favorite over time, prompting [fans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swifties "Swifties") and publications to question why Swift did not release the track as a single.

After being included in the set list of Swift's sixth concert tour, [the Eras Tour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Eras_Tour "The Eras Tour"), in 2023, "Cruel Summer" became [viral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Viral_video "Viral video") on social media, leading [Republic Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republic_Records "Republic Records") to release it as a single on June 20, 2023. In the United States, the single peaked atop the [_Billboard_ Hot 100](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billboard_Hot_100 "Billboard Hot 100") for four weeks and helped Swift become the solo artist with the most number-one songs on the [Pop Airplay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pop_Airplay "Pop Airplay") and [Adult Pop Airplay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adult_Pop_Airplay "Adult Pop Airplay") radio charts. It also topped the [_Billboard_ Global 200](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billboard_Global_200 "Billboard Global 200") and the singles charts in Australia, Canada, the Philippines, and Singapore. The song has been [certified](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Music_recording_certification "Music recording certification") diamond in France, and multi-platinum in Australia, Brazil, New Zealand, Poland, Portugal, Spain, Switzerland, and the United Kingdom.

## Background and composition

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Cruel_Summer_\(Taylor_Swift_song\)&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Background and composition")\]

[Taylor Swift](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taylor_Swift "Taylor Swift") described her seventh studio album, _[Lover](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lover_\(album\) "Lover (album)")_, as a "love letter to love" itself with all the feelings evoked by it.[\[1\]](#cite_note-1) The album was released on August 23, 2019, via [Republic Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republic_Records "Republic Records").[\[2\]](#cite_note-2) _Lover_ consists of 18 tracks, and "Cruel Summer" is track number two.[\[3\]](#cite_note-LinerNotes-3) According to Swift, the track is about an uncertain summer romance with elements of pain and desperation in it.[\[4\]](#cite_note-iHeart-4) The relationship in question is "where you're yearning for something that you don't quite have yet, it's just right there, and you just can't reach it".[\[4\]](#cite_note-iHeart-4)

![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/cb/Gnome-mime-audio-openclipart.svg/60px-Gnome-mime-audio-openclipart.svg.png)

A sample of the [refrain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Refrain "Refrain"), instrumented by pulsing [synths](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Synths "Synths") and fluctuating vocals singing "ooooh"

"Cruel Summer" is an [electropop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electropop "Electropop"),[\[5\]](#cite_note-5)[\[6\]](#cite_note-6)[\[7\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEZaleski2024151-7) [synth-pop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Synth-pop "Synth-pop"),[\[8\]](#cite_note-independent-8)[\[9\]](#cite_note-9)[\[10\]](#cite_note-10) [bubblegum pop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bubblegum_pop "Bubblegum pop"),[\[11\]](#cite_note-11) and [industrial pop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Industrial_pop "Industrial pop") song.[\[12\]](#cite_note-12) Critics described its production as melancholic[\[13\]](#cite_note-13) or dreamy.[\[14\]](#cite_note-14) It has a "ranting" [bridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bridge_\(music\) "Bridge (music)") underscored by skittering synths,[\[15\]](#cite_note-Bruner-2019-15)[\[16\]](#cite_note-The_Spinoff-2019-16)[\[17\]](#cite_note-17)[\[18\]](#cite_note-18) distorted vocals[\[8\]](#cite_note-independent-8) manipulated by a [vocoder](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vocoder "Vocoder"),[\[19\]](#cite_note-19) and a hook that consists of a long, high, fluctuating "ooooh".[\[20\]](#cite_note-20) The song has a fast [tempo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tempo "Tempo") of 170 beats per minute with a time signature of **4**  
**4**. It is played in the key of [A major](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_major "A major") and follows a chord progression of A–C♯m–F♯m–D.[\[21\]](#cite_note-21)[\[22\]](#cite_note-22) Swift's vocals range from A2 to E5. "Cruel Summer" was written by Swift, [Jack Antonoff](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jack_Antonoff "Jack Antonoff") and [St. Vincent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Vincent_\(musician\) "St. Vincent (musician)"),[\[23\]](#cite_note-23) with a "burbling" production from Swift and Antonoff;[\[24\]](#cite_note-Sayles-2019-24) St. Vincent also took part in the production of the song, playing the guitar.[\[25\]](#cite_note-25)

Lyrically, the song is about a summer romance that entails strong feelings, including romantic ecstasy, anxiety, and pain.[\[26\]](#cite_note-26)[\[27\]](#cite_note-27) David Penn of _Hit Songs Deconstructed_ opined that the song's vocals, instrumentation and lyrics work "in tandem to create a unified expression, a combination known as [prosody](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prosody_\(linguistics\) "Prosody (linguistics)")".[\[28\]](#cite_note-28) According to [_Time_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Time_\(magazine\) "Time (magazine)")'s Raina Bruner, the song also portrays the challenges faced by pop stars in the public spotlight, similar to the theme of Swift's 2017 song "[Delicate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Delicate_\(Taylor_Swift_song\) "Delicate (Taylor Swift song)")".[\[15\]](#cite_note-Bruner-2019-15) Justin Styles of [_The Ringer_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ringer_\(website\) "The Ringer (website)") wrote that the song tells a "more humanizing version" of Swift's "ill-fated period three years ago", adding that Swift sings about "falling in love with then-current boyfriend [Joe Alwyn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Alwyn "Joe Alwyn") while her public life was in shambles".[\[24\]](#cite_note-Sayles-2019-24) Anna Gaca, writing for [_Pitchfork_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pitchfork_\(website\) "Pitchfork (website)"), called the song a "drama-free delight" with "magnetic pink glow".[\[29\]](#cite_note-29) _[The Spinoff](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Spinoff "The Spinoff")_ pointed out that Swift's vocals in "Cruel Summer" are "most notable for the modern [country](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Country_music "Country music") cadence".[\[16\]](#cite_note-The_Spinoff-2019-16)

## Release and commercial performance

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Cruel_Summer_\(Taylor_Swift_song\)&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Release and commercial performance")\]

"Cruel Summer" was released as the second track on _Lover_, on August 23, 2019, via [Republic Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republic_Records "Republic Records").[\[30\]](#cite_note-30) The track originally charted as an album cut within the top 30 in Singapore (8),[\[31\]](#cite_note-Singapore-31) Malaysia (13),[\[32\]](#cite_note-Malaysia-32) Ireland (20),[\[33\]](#cite_note-33) New Zealand (20),[\[34\]](#cite_note-34) Australia (23),[\[35\]](#cite_note-Australia19-35) the United Kingdom (27),[\[36\]](#cite_note-uk-36) and Canada (28).[\[37\]](#cite_note-Canada19-37) In the United States, the song debuted at number 29 on the [_Billboard_ Hot 100](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billboard_Hot_100 "Billboard Hot 100") dated September 7, 2019; it is one of the seven tracks from _Lover_ to reach the top 40[\[38\]](#cite_note-38) and remained on the chart for two weeks.[\[39\]](#cite_note-Zellner-2023-39) The song became a widespread fan favorite over time[\[40\]](#cite_note-40)[\[41\]](#cite_note-41) and critics and fans questioned Swift's decision over not having released "Cruel Summer" as a single.[\[42\]](#cite_note-Spanos-2023-42)[\[43\]](#cite_note-RadioDate-43)

[![Swift singing onstage dressed in a sparkling bodysuite](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/57/Eras_Tour_-_Arlington%2C_TX_-_Lover_Act_2_%28cropped%29.jpg/250px-Eras_Tour_-_Arlington%2C_TX_-_Lover_Act_2_%28cropped%29.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Eras_Tour_-_Arlington,_TX_-_Lover_Act_2_\(cropped\).jpg)

"Cruel Summer" resurged in popularity after Swift included it in the setlist of [the Eras Tour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Eras_Tour "The Eras Tour") in 2023.

Beginning March 2023, Swift embarked on [the Eras Tour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Eras_Tour "The Eras Tour"), her sixth headlining concert tour, as a tribute to all of her "musical eras".[\[44\]](#cite_note-44) The show begins with the _Lover_ act, during which "Cruel Summer" is the second song performed.[\[43\]](#cite_note-RadioDate-43) Around this time, the song began to resurge in popularity and [streaming](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Streaming "Streaming") after it became viral on social media.[\[42\]](#cite_note-Spanos-2023-42)[\[45\]](#cite_note-45) In the U.S., the single re-entered the _Billboard_ Hot 100 at number 49 on the chart dated June 3, 2023.[\[39\]](#cite_note-Zellner-2023-39) It began gaining airplay spins on US radio by mid-June,[\[46\]](#cite_note-46) leading Republic Records to release it as a single to US [contemporary hit radio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Contemporary_hit_radio "Contemporary hit radio") on June 20, 2023.[\[43\]](#cite_note-RadioDate-43)[\[47\]](#cite_note-Iasimone-2023-47) The song also impacted [hot adult contemporary radio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hot_adult_contemporary_radio "Hot adult contemporary radio") on June 26.[\[48\]](#cite_note-HotAC-48) On June 17, at an Eras Tour show in [Pittsburgh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pittsburgh "Pittsburgh"), Swift said she had intended to release "Cruel Summer" as a single in 2020 during the promotional cycle for _Lover_ but she abandoned the plan after the outbreak of the [COVID-19 pandemic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/COVID-19_pandemic_in_the_United_States "COVID-19 pandemic in the United States"), instead shifting her artistic direction and releasing her next album, _[Folklore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Folklore_\(Taylor_Swift_album\) "Folklore (Taylor Swift album)")_.[\[47\]](#cite_note-Iasimone-2023-47)[\[49\]](#cite_note-49)

"Cruel Summer" became Swift's record-extending 41st song to reach the top 10 on the _Billboard_ Hot 100 and the fourth _Lover_ track to do so.[\[50\]](#cite_note-50) After the release of the Eras Tour's [accompanying concert film](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taylor_Swift:_The_Eras_Tour "Taylor Swift: The Eras Tour"), a live recording of the song and a remix by [LP Giobbi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/LP_Giobbi "LP Giobbi") were released as part of a streaming compilation, titled _The Cruelest Summer,_ on October 18, 2023.[\[51\]](#cite_note-Atkinson-2023-51) "Cruel Summer" topped the _Billboard_ Hot 100, marking _Lover_'s first and Swift's 10th number-one single.[\[52\]](#cite_note-52) It was replaced by, and in turn replaced, Swift's "[Is It Over Now?](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Is_It_Over_Now%3F "Is It Over Now?")" atop the Hot 100 for one week,[\[53\]](#cite_note-53) spending a total of four non-consecutive weeks at number one and making Swift the first female artist to succeed herself at the top spot twice and thrice.[\[54\]](#cite_note-54)[\[55\]](#cite_note-Trust-2024a-55)

On US [_Billboard_ airplay charts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billboard_charts "Billboard charts") in 2023, "Cruel Summer" became Swift's eighth number-one single on [Radio Songs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radio_Songs_\(chart\) "Radio Songs (chart)"), where it reigned for 12 non-consecutive weeks surpassing "[Blank Space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blank_Space "Blank Space")" as her longest running number one.[\[56\]](#cite_note-Trust-2023-56) It became her 12th number-one single on [Pop Airplay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pop_Airplay "Pop Airplay"), and her 11th number-one single on [Adult Pop Airplay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adult_Pop_Airplay "Adult Pop Airplay"), making her the solo artist with the most chart toppers on the latter two charts.[\[57\]](#cite_note-57)[\[58\]](#cite_note-58) The song also spent 10 weeks atop Pop Airplay and 23 weeks atop Adult Pop Airplay, becoming her longest-running number-one song on both[\[56\]](#cite_note-Trust-2023-56) and the longest-running number-one song by a solo artist and female artist on the latter.[\[55\]](#cite_note-Trust-2024a-55)[\[59\]](#cite_note-Trust-2024b-59) Jason Lipshutz of _Billboard_ commented that the single's resurgent success "simply demonstrates Swift's current ubiquity, unprecedented in the modern music era".[\[60\]](#cite_note-60) In January 2024, the song topped the [Adult Contemporary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adult_Contemporary_\(chart\) "Adult Contemporary (chart)") chart, marking Swift's ninth number-one single. As such, it made Swift the first artist in history to release six singles that topped the Adult Contemporary, Adult Pop Airplay and Pop Airplay charts individually, surpassing [Adele](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adele "Adele") (five).[\[59\]](#cite_note-Trust-2024b-59) Additionally, the song spent 34 weeks in the top ten of the Hot 100, becoming the first song by a solo female artist to do so.[\[61\]](#cite_note-61) In total, "Cruel Summer" spent 54 weeks on the Hot 100, becoming Swift's longest-charting Hot 100 hit, surpassing "[Anti-Hero](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anti-Hero_\(song\) "Anti-Hero (song)")".[\[62\]](#cite_note-62)

Elsewhere, "Cruel Summer" reached new peaks in Australia (1),[\[63\]](#cite_note-aus-63) Canada (1),[\[64\]](#cite_note-Canada2023-64) Singapore (1),[\[65\]](#cite_note-65) New Zealand (3),[\[66\]](#cite_note-NZ2023-66) Ireland (4),[\[67\]](#cite_note-67) Malaysia (6),[\[68\]](#cite_note-68) and Brazil (54) as well.[\[69\]](#cite_note-69) It peaked at number one in the Philippines[\[70\]](#cite_note-Philippines-70) and entered the top 10 in Indonesia, as well in few Europeans countries, including Switzerland and Iceland, top twenty for most of them, including Norway, Sweden, Austria, Portugal, the Netherlands and Luxembourg and top forty in Denmark and Slovakia.[\[71\]](#cite_note-Indonesia-71) In France, from the general surprise, due to massive broadcasting radio plays, the song didn't reached the top fifty and reached number 52. However, the song spent 55 weeks and peaked at number 9 on French airplay and was certified diamond, becoming Swift fifth diamond single at the time.[\[72\]](#cite_note-72) The song was [certified](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Music_recording_certification "Music recording certification") thirteen-times platinum in Australia;[\[73\]](#cite_note-ARIA-73) seven-times platinum in New Zealand;[\[74\]](#cite_note-RMNZ-74) quadruple platinum in Portugal[\[75\]](#cite_note-afp-75) and the United Kingdom;[\[76\]](#cite_note-bpi-76) triple platinum in Switzerland;[\[77\]](#cite_note-IFPI_Switzerland-77) and double platinum in Brazil,[\[78\]](#cite_note-Brazil-78) Poland,[\[79\]](#cite_note-zpav-79) and Spain.[\[80\]](#cite_note-PROMUSICAE-80) It reached number one on the [_Billboard_ Global 200](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billboard_Global_200 "Billboard Global 200"),[\[81\]](#cite_note-global200-81) and was the sixth-most-streamed song globally on [Spotify](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spotify "Spotify") in 2023.[\[82\]](#cite_note-82) The song was the seventh-biggest song of 2023 according to the [International Federation of the Phonographic Industry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Federation_of_the_Phonographic_Industry "International Federation of the Phonographic Industry") (IFPI), with an equivalent of 1.39 billion global subscription streams.[\[83\]](#cite_note-83) Within the first half of 2024, according to [Luminate Data](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luminate_Data "Luminate Data"), the single was the third-most-streamed song globally with 1.012 billion streams.[\[84\]](#cite_note-84) St. Vincent described the resurgent success of "Cruel Summer" as "crazy", "so wild and so modern".[\[85\]](#cite_note-85)

In reviews of _Lover_, "Cruel Summer" received rave reviews from music critics, particularly for its production, bridge and hook. [Jon Caramanica](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jon_Caramanica "Jon Caramanica") of _[The New York Times](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_New_York_Times "The New York Times")_ commended the "thick, ethereal" production and Swift's signature vocal motifs such as the "question-mark syllables" and the "hard-felt smears".[\[86\]](#cite_note-86) Mikael Wood of the _[Los Angeles Times](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Angeles_Times "Los Angeles Times")_ proclaimed "Cruel Summer" to be the best song of _Lover_ and said the bridge where Swift "shrieks about the devil might be the punkest thing you'll hear all year".[\[87\]](#cite_note-87) Alex Abad-Santos, writing for [_Vox_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vox_\(website\) "Vox (website)"), listed "Cruel Summer" as one of his top-three best _Lover_ tracks, writing that the song is an "aquatic robot bop" featuring "wobbly" synths.[\[88\]](#cite_note-88) _The Spinoff_ stated that Swift "absolutely pulls it off" and compared it to [Bananarama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bananarama "Bananarama")'s [1983 song of the same name](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cruel_Summer_\(Bananarama_song\) "Cruel Summer (Bananarama song)").[\[16\]](#cite_note-The_Spinoff-2019-16) Writing for _The Ringer_, Justin Sayles praised the song as a "better rebuke of her personal drama than anything on her last album", and added that Swift "shakes off the bad vibes" with "Cruel Summer"; Sayles named it Swift's "most infectious song since that run of singles from _[1989](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1989_\(Taylor_Swift_album\) "1989 (Taylor Swift album)")_", and opined that song "sets the tone" for the "warmer, more inviting vibes" of _Lover_.[\[24\]](#cite_note-Sayles-2019-24) Also calling it "infectious", Nick Levine of _[NME](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NME "NME")_ termed the track as a "brilliant pop song".[\[89\]](#cite_note-89) Natalia Barr, writing for _[Consequence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Consequence_\(publication\) "Consequence (publication)")_, highlighted Swift's vocal delivery in the song's bridge ("He looks up, grinning like a devil"), calling it "simultaneously funny, agonizing, and thrilling, and needs to be created into a viral [YouTube](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/YouTube "YouTube") loop immediately". Barr further labeled "Cruel Summer" as one of the "most perfect" pop songs of 2019.[\[90\]](#cite_note-90) "Cruel Summer" featured on year-end lists of the best songs of 2019 by _Rolling Stone_ (4th)[\[91\]](#cite_note-91) and _Billboard_ (10th).[\[92\]](#cite_note-92)

Retrospectively, "Cruel Summer" continued to receive high acclaim, and has been deemed the signature track of _Lover_. In a 2021 list ranking the best bridges of the 21st-century, _Billboard_ placed "Cruel Summer" at number 11.[\[93\]](#cite_note-93) The song has ranked highly on critics' rankings of Swift's songs in her discography, appearing on such lists by [Rob Sheffield](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rob_Sheffield "Rob Sheffield") of _Rolling Stone_ (2021) at number 11 out of 229,[\[94\]](#cite_note-94) and Hannah Mylrea of _NME_ (2020), number 6 out of 161.[\[95\]](#cite_note-95) [_Clash_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clash_\(magazine\) "Clash (magazine)") critics picked the song as one of Swift's 15 best, citing its "highly addictive" [song structure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Song_structure "Song structure").[\[96\]](#cite_note-96) In 2022, _[Exclaim!](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Exclaim! *   The first song that Swift wrote for **Red**, she penned the tune in 2011 with Liz Rose, one of her co-writers on her first three albums. The heart-rending breakup tune came after a six-month writing block that followed a particularly painful ending of a relationship. "There's a kind of bad that gets so overpowering you can't even write about it," she told _USA Today_ of that time. "When you feel pain that is so far past dysfunctional, that leaves you with so many emotions that you can't filter them down to simple emotions to write about, that's when you know you really need to get out."
    
*   Swift was asked by The Daily Beast if she ever felt guilty regarding writing about an ex. She replied: "I take these songs and these people who inspire these songs on a case-by-case basis. If there were someone who was a good person, I'm not going to write something bad about them. But if they handle a situation in a way that really messed up my life for a while, that's what I'm going to write about. For me, I've never changed the reason I write a song. Songs for me are like a message in a bottle. You send them out to the world and maybe the person who you feel that way about will hear about it someday."
    
*   Taylor is a noted fan of singer/songwriter Matt Nathanson of "[Come On Get Higher](https://www.songfacts.com/facts/matt-nathanson/come-on-get-higher)" and "[Run](https://www.songfacts.com/facts/matt-nathanson/run)" fame, to the extent that she has been known to perform with the lyrics of his song "Modern Love" written on her arm. Fans have pointed out the similarity between a lyric in this song ("And I forget about you long enough to forget why I needed to"), and a line from Nathanson's 2003 tune "I Saw," ("And I'll forget about you long enough to forget why I need to").
    
    Maybe Taylor wanted to pay homage to Nathanson or it may be simply unconscious plagiarism on her part. However, Nathanson seems to believe it to be plagiarism. According to Gawker site, he posted a tweet after the rumors first surfaced that was subsequently deleted in which he wrote, "She's definitely a fan, and now she's a thief."
    
*   "All Too Well" is said to be based on Taylor's relationship with actor Jake Gyllenhaal, whom she dated for three months in 2010. During the song, she sings:
    
    _Left my scarf there at your sister's house,  
    And you still got it in your drawer even now_
    
    When Jake's sister Maggie Gyllenhaal sat down with Andy Cohen on _Watch What Happens Live_, she was asked whether Taylor once left a scarf at her house. The actress looked bewildered and replied, "You know, I never understood why everybody asked me about this scarf. What is this? I am in the dark about the scarf."
    
*   The song was originally a vitriolic and bitter 10-minute tirade Swift spat out during a soundtrack on her 2011 Speak Now tour. She then edited it with the help of collaborator Liz Rose.
    
    "I was just feeling terrible about what was going on in my personal life," she explained during an appearance on _Rolling Stone's 500 Greatest Albums_ podcast. "I just started singing and riffing and ad-libbing this song that basically was 'All Too Well.' It literally just was that song, but it had probably seven extra verses... and it included the F-word."
    
    A sound guy burned her rant onto a CD, and Swift took her demo home and got some perspective after listening back to it. "I was like, 'I actually really like this, but it definitely is, like, 10 minutes long and I need to pare it down, so I'm going to call Liz Rose,'" she recalled.
    
*   This is the fifth track on **Red**. It follows the track five pattern on all of Swift's albums where she traditionally places her most anguish-filled songs. Previous fifth tracks had been "[Cold As You](https://www.songfacts.com/facts/taylor-swift/cold-as-you)" and "[White Horse](https://www.songfacts.com/facts/taylor-swift/white-horse)."
    
*   Swift re-recorded her first six albums – originally released on Big Machine Records – in order to regain ownership of her lucrative master recordings following their sale. The pop star released the uncut, 10-minute version on November 12, 2021, as part of her re-recorded album, **Red (Taylor's Version)**.
    
*   In one of her additional verses, Swift brings up the incident where Gyllenhaal missed her 21st birthday party - a transgression she detailed in another **Red** track, "[The Moment I Knew](https://www.songfacts.com/facts/taylor-swift/the-moment-i-knew)."
    
    _You who charmed my dad with self-effacing jokes  
    Sipping coffee like you're on a late-night show  
    But then he watched me watch the front door all night, willing you to come  
    And he said, "It's supposed to be fun turning twenty-one"_
    
    When Gyllenhaal didn't show up for her birthday bash, it proved to be the final nail in the coffin.
    
*   Swift released a self-directed short film to accompany the 10-minute version. Also titled _All Too Well_, it stars _Stranger Things_' Sadie Sink and _Maze Runner_'s Dylan O'Brien. The 15-minute visual is split into seven chapters, each chronicling a period in Sink and O'Brien's relationship. Swift cameos in the film's epilogue as an older version of Sink's character.
    
*   Swift gave the [debut live performance](https://youtu.be/Kds56tbF0FE) of "All Too Well (10 Minute Version) (Taylor's Version)" following the premiere of the _All Too Well_ film at Manhattan's AMC 13 Lincoln Square cinema on November 12, 2012.
    
*   Taylor Swift performed the 10-minute version of the song on the November 3, 2021 episode of _Saturday Night Live_. Swift sang the track, accompanying herself on acoustic guitar, as the _All Too Well_ film played behind her on a screen.
    
*   Fans and critics have long dubbed **Red**, the "Sad Girl Autumn" album for its autumnal heartbreak themes. Examples in this song include the cold air, falling autumn leaves, and need for a scarf.
    
    A few days after releasing the 10-minute version of "All Too Well," Swift drove up to Aaron Dessner's Long Pond Studios and recorded a ["Sad Girl Autumn" version](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=r0yq_yXFQhg) of this song. Sharing her rendition on social media, Swift wrote: "One of the saddest songs I've ever written just got sadder."
    
*   "All Too Well (10 Minute Version)" debuted at #1 on the Hot 100 in the week after the release of **Red (Taylor's Version)**. The song became the longest track to ever top the chart, usurping Don McLean, whose 8:32 single "[American Pie](https://www.songfacts.com/facts/don-mclean/american-pie)" spent four weeks at the summit in 1972.
    
*   Jake Gyllenhaal has no hard feelings towards Swift over her dissing him. "It's her way of expressing herself," he told _Esquire Italia_ magazine. "Artists draw on their personal experiences to write songs and I'm not angry with her."
    

*   Swift says "All Too Well" is a prime example of her "fountain pen" lyricism, where she sets the scene with vivid descriptions and lots of emotional intensity. It's as if she's writing in a diary with a fountain pen.
    
    Her other lyric styles are "quill pen" (old-timey, poetic) and "glitter gel pen" (upbeat, fun, a little goofy).
    
*   "All Too Well (10 Minute Version)" won Best Video and Best Longform Video at the MTV Europe Music Awards 2022. Swift also took home the prizes for Best Artist and Best Pop.
    
*   The short film won the Favorite Music Video prize at the 2022 American Music Awards. Swift also took home the night's biggest honor, Artist of the Year, as well as Favorite Female Pop Artist and Favorite Female Country Artist, while **Red (Taylor's Version)** won the Favorite Country Album and Favorite Pop Album awards.
    
*   "All Too Well" won for Best Music Video at the Grammy Awards in 2023. It was nominated for Song Of The Year but lost to "[Just Like That](https://www.songfacts.com/facts/bonnie-raitt/just-like-that)" by "Bonnie Raitt."
    
*   "All Too Well" plays a part in the 2024 movie _The Fall Guy_, directed by David Leitch. The film follows a stuntman (Ryan Gosling) reuniting with his ex-girlfriend Jody Moreno (Emily Blunt) on the set of her directorial debut. There's a twist, though: Colt ghosted Jody 18 months prior after a nasty injury. Now, forced to work together, tensions simmer.
    
    In one scene, Colt finds himself alone in his car after a rough day, seeking solace in "All Too Well." Jody catches him in the act: "Have you been crying to Taylor Swift?" she asks, to which Colt replies, "Doesn't everyone?"
    
    This musical choice came from producer Emily McCormick, Leitch's wife. Initially, Leitch envisioned a different song for the scene, but McCormick felt it lacked the right touch. A trip to see Swift's Eras tour in Las Vegas changed everything.
    
    "She sang the 10-minute version," [McCormick recalled to Vanity Fare](https://www.vanityfair.com/hollywood/story/how-the-fall-guy-got-all-too-well). "David was blown away." They knew that the pop star's **Red** ballad was the perfect fit, but securing the rights wasn't guaranteed. Swift's approval, along with potential licensing costs, were hurdles to overcome.
    
    "The first time we dropped it in, we knew there was no going back," said McCormick, "and we were going to be really upset if we couldn't get it."
    
    "We showed her what we had cut, and there were no notes," she added. "Thankfully, she's open to the process, and didn't price herself so far out of our budget that we weren't able to include her."
    
*   Stanford University students could take a very deep dive into this song in 2023 with a course called "All Too Well (Ten Week Version)." It's far from the first college course on Taylor Swift (New York University, Arizona State University and the University Of South Carolina also ran courses on Swift) but it's the only one we know of dedicated to a specific song.
