_**Folklore**_ (stylized in [all lowercase](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/All_lowercase "All lowercase")) is the eighth studio album by the American singer-songwriter [Taylor Swift](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taylor_Swift "Taylor Swift"). It was [surprise-released](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Surprise_album "Surprise album") on July 24, 2020, through [Republic Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republic_Records "Republic Records"). Conceived during [quarantine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/COVID-19_lockdowns "COVID-19 lockdowns") in early 2020, amidst the [COVID-19 pandemic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/COVID-19_pandemic "COVID-19 pandemic"), the album explores themes of [escapism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Escapism "Escapism"), nostalgia, and [romanticism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Romanticism "Romanticism"). Swift recorded her vocals in her Los Angeles home studio and worked virtually with the producers [Aaron Dessner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aaron_Dessner "Aaron Dessner") and [Jack Antonoff](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jack_Antonoff "Jack Antonoff"), who operated from their studios in the [Hudson Valley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hudson_Valley "Hudson Valley") and New York City.

Using a set of characters and story arcs to depict fictional narratives, the album departs from the autobiographical songwriting that had characterized Swift's past albums. Experimenting with new musical styles, _Folklore_ consists of mellow [ballads](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sentimental_ballad "Sentimental ballad") driven by [piano](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Piano "Piano"), [strings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/String_instrument "String instrument"), [orchestration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orchestration "Orchestration"), and muted [percussion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Percussion "Percussion"). Music critics classified the genre into various styles of [folk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Folk_music "Folk music"), [pop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pop_music "Pop music"), and indie, namely [chamber pop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chamber_pop "Chamber pop"), [indie folk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indie_folk "Indie folk"), [electro-folk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electro-folk "Electro-folk"), [folk rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Folk_rock "Folk rock"), and [indie rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indie_rock "Indie rock"). The album's title was inspired by the lasting legacy of folktales, and its visual aesthetic adopts [cottagecore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cottagecore "Cottagecore").

_Folklore_ was accompanied by the concert documentary _[Folklore: The Long Pond Studio Sessions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Folklore:_The_Long_Pond_Studio_Sessions "Folklore: The Long Pond Studio Sessions")_, featuring Swift's commentary and performances. The album topped the charts in Australasia and various European countries and was [certified platinum or higher](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Music_recording_certification "Music recording certification") in Australia, Austria, Denmark, France, Germany, Italy, New Zealand, Norway, Poland, Portugal, and the United Kingdom. In the United States, it spent eight weeks atop the [_Billboard_ 200](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billboard_200 "Billboard 200"), was the best-selling album of 2020, and was certified six-times platinum by the [Recording Industry Association of America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Recording_Industry_Association_of_America "Recording Industry Association of America"). Three songs, "[Cardigan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cardigan_\(song\) "Cardigan (song)")", "[The 1](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_1 "The 1")", and "[Exile](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Exile_\(song\) "Exile (song)")" featuring [Bon Iver](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bon_Iver "Bon Iver"), reached the top 10 on international singles charts, with "Cardigan" peaking at number one on the [_Billboard_ Hot 100](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billboard_Hot_100 "Billboard Hot 100").

_Folklore_ received widespread critical acclaim for its emotional weight and intricate lyricism; some journalists commented that its introspective tone was timely for the pandemic, and they regarded its sound as a bold reinvention of Swift's artistry. Many publications featured the album on their 2020 year-end rankings, and _[Rolling Stone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rolling_Stone "Rolling Stone")_ included it in their 2023 revision of their "[500 Greatest Albums of All Time](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rolling_Stone's_500_Greatest_Albums_of_All_Time "Rolling Stone's 500 Greatest Albums of All Time")" list. _Folklore_ won [Album of the Year](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grammy_Award_for_Album_of_the_Year "Grammy Award for Album of the Year") at the [63rd Annual Grammy Awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/63rd_Annual_Grammy_Awards "63rd Annual Grammy Awards"), making Swift the first woman to win the award three times. The album informed the concept of Swift's next record, _[Evermore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Evermore "Evermore")_ (2020), and has inspired other artists' works.

In April 2020, [Taylor Swift](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taylor_Swift "Taylor Swift") was set to embark on Lover Fest, a concert tour in support of her seventh studio album _[Lover](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lover_\(album\) "Lover (album)")_ (2019), which was cancelled following the [COVID-19 pandemic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/COVID-19_pandemic "COVID-19 pandemic").[\[1\]](#cite_note-Lipshutz-1) On July 23, 2020, nine photos were uploaded to Swift's [Instagram](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Instagram "Instagram") account, all without captions, forming a black and white image of her standing alone in a forest. Subsequently, Swift made another post across all her social media accounts, announcing that her eighth studio album would be released at midnight; Swift stated: "Most of the things I had planned this summer didn't end up happening, but there is something I hadn't planned on that DID happen. And that thing is my 8th studio album, _Folklore_". She confirmed the image as the album's cover artwork and revealed the track list.[\[2\]](#cite_note-2) _[The Wall Street Journal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Wall_Street_Journal "The Wall Street Journal")_ opined that the surprise announcement "caught fans and the music business off-guard".[\[3\]](#cite_note-3) _[Billboard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billboard_\(magazine\) "Billboard (magazine)")_ stated that it "blindsided the pop music world", arriving as "exciting news" during [lockdown](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/COVID-19_lockdowns "COVID-19 lockdowns").[\[4\]](#cite_note-Billboard_List-4) _Folklore_ was released eleven months after _Lover_—the fastest turnaround for a Swift studio album at the time, beating the one year and nine-month gap between _[Reputation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reputation_\(Taylor_Swift_album\) "Reputation (Taylor Swift album)")_ (2017) and _Lover_. In another post, Swift announced that the music video for the track "[Cardigan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cardigan_\(song\) "Cardigan (song)")" would be released at the same time as the album.[\[5\]](#cite_note-Reilly-5)

During the [YouTube](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/YouTube "YouTube") premiere countdown to the "Cardigan" music video, Swift hinted that the album lyrics contained many of her signature [Easter eggs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Easter_egg_\(media\) "Easter egg (media)"): "One thing I did purposely on this album was put the Easter eggs in the lyrics, more than just the videos. I created character arcs and recurring themes that map out who is singing about who... For example, there's a collection of three songs I refer to as the Teenage Love Triangle. These three songs explore a love triangle from all three people's perspectives at different times in their lives".[\[6\]](#cite_note-Rolling_Stone-6) She referred to the album as "[wistful](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Melancholia "Melancholia") and full of [escapism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Escapism "Escapism"). Sad, beautiful, tragic. Like a photo album full of imagery, and all the stories behind that imagery",[\[7\]](#cite_note-E!-7) described "Cardigan" as a song that explores "lost romance and why young love is often fixed so permanently in our memories,"[\[8\]](#cite_note-8) and identified the self-written track, "[My Tears Ricochet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/My_Tears_Ricochet "My Tears Ricochet")", as the first song she wrote for the album.[\[7\]](#cite_note-E!-7) _[Uproxx](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uproxx "Uproxx")_ narrated, "on Thursday night, that hand-drawn 'T' and 'S' could be seen up and down the timeline. Music fans and critics across genres unveiled hot takes, quoted lyrics like [Myspace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Myspace "Myspace") teens writing on the back of textbooks or crafting the perfect [AIM away message](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AIM_\(software\) "AIM (software)"), and debated _Folklore_'s place in the unimpeachable Taylor Swift canon."[\[9\]](#cite_note-9)

Swift did not expect to create an album in early 2020.[\[10\]](#cite_note-Suskind-2020-10) After the cancellation of Lover Fest,[\[1\]](#cite_note-Lipshutz-1) Swift [quarantined](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quarantine "Quarantine") herself, during which she watched numerous films and shows, such as _[Rear Window](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rear_Window "Rear Window")_ (1954), _[L.A. Confidential](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/L.A._Confidential_\(film\) "L.A. Confidential (film)")_ (1997), _[Pan's Labyrinth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pan's_Labyrinth "Pan's Labyrinth")_ (2006), _[Jane Eyre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jane_Eyre_\(2011_film\) "Jane Eyre (2011 film)")_ (2011), _[Marriage Story](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marriage_Story "Marriage Story")_ (2019),[\[10\]](#cite_note-Suskind-2020-10) and _[The Last Dance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Last_Dance_\(miniseries\) "The Last Dance (miniseries)")_ (2020),[\[11\]](#cite_note-11) and read more books than she ever did, books that "dealt with times past, a world that doesn't exist anymore", such as _[Rebecca](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rebecca_\(novel\) "Rebecca (novel)")_ (1938) by [Daphne du Maurier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daphne_du_Maurier "Daphne du Maurier").[\[12\]](#cite_note-Doyle-2020-12) The fictions inspired Swift to venture beyond her usual autobiographical style of songwriting and experiment with different narrative standpoints.[\[10\]](#cite_note-Suskind-2020-10) In isolation during the lockdown, she let her imagination "run wild", ensuing in a set of imagery and visuals that consequently became _Folklore_.[\[13\]](#cite_note-Primer-13)

> It started with imagery. Visuals that popped into my mind and piqued my curiosity. Stars drawn around scars. A [cardigan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cardigan_\(sweater\) "Cardigan (sweater)") that still bears the scent of loss twenty years later. [Battleships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battleship "Battleship") sinking into the ocean, down, down, down. The tree swing in the woods of my childhood. Hushed tones of "let's run away" and never doing it. The sun drenched month of August, sipped away like a bottle of wine. A mirrored disco ball hovering above a dance floor. A [whiskey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whiskey "Whiskey") bottle beckoning. Hands held through plastic. A single thread that, for better or for worse, ties you to your fate. Pretty soon these images in my head grew faces or names and became characters. I found myself not only writing my own stories, but also writing about or from the perspective of people I've never met, people I've known, or those I wish I hadn't.

— Swift on developing _Folklore_, _Billboard_[\[13\]](#cite_note-Primer-13)

Some of the imagery the singer developed includes: "An exiled man walking the bluffs of a land that isn't his own, wondering how it all went so terribly, terribly wrong. An embittered tormentor showing up at the funeral of his fallen object of obsession. A seventeen-year-old standing on a porch, learning to apologize. Lovestruck kids wandering up and down the evergreen [High Line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/High_Line "High Line"). My grandfather, Dean, [landing at Guadalcanal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guadalcanal_campaign "Guadalcanal campaign") in 1942. A misfit widow getting gleeful revenge on the town that cast her out".[\[13\]](#cite_note-Primer-13) Swift "poured all of \[her\] whims, dreams, fears, and musings" into the songs, and reached out to her "musical heroes" to collaborate with.[\[14\]](#cite_note-14) She initially planned to release _Folklore_ in early 2021, but it "ended up being done" sooner, and released in July 2020 without giving it second thoughts. She approached the album's creation without subjecting herself to any rules, and explained that she "used to put all these parameters on \[herself\], like, "How will this song sound in a stadium? How will this song sound on radio?" If you take away all the parameters, what do you make? And I guess the answer is _Folklore_."[\[12\]](#cite_note-Doyle-2020-12)

## Writing and recording

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Folklore_\(Taylor_Swift_album\)&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Writing and recording")\]

Swift's songwriting drifted towards escapism and [romanticism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Romanticism "Romanticism") for _Folklore_.[\[12\]](#cite_note-Doyle-2020-12) She enlisted two producers to achieve her desired sound—her longtime collaborator, [Jack Antonoff](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jack_Antonoff "Jack Antonoff"), who worked with her on _[1989](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1989_\(Taylor_Swift_album\) "1989 (Taylor Swift album)")_ (2014), _Reputation_, and _Lover_, and first-time collaborator [Aaron Dessner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aaron_Dessner "Aaron Dessner"), guitarist of American [indie rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indie_rock "Indie rock") band [the National](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_National_\(band\) "The National (band)").[\[15\]](#cite_note-PitchforkCredits-15) Due to COVID-19 concerns, Swift, Antonoff, and Dessner quarantined remotely, separate from each other, creating _Folklore_ by continually exchanging digital files of instrumentals and vocals.[\[16\]](#cite_note-Blistein-2020-16) The album ensued from a [DIY](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DIY "DIY") process,[\[17\]](#cite_note-17) [mixed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mixing_engineer "Mixing engineer") and [engineered](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Audio_engineer "Audio engineer") by personnel scattered across the US.[\[4\]](#cite_note-Billboard_List-4)

[![Man playing a guitar on stage](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a3/Aaron_Dessner_at_Way_Out_West_2014.jpg/250px-Aaron_Dessner_at_Way_Out_West_2014.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Aaron_Dessner_at_Way_Out_West_2014.jpg)

[![Man playing a red guitar](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/89/Antonoff_in_Tucson_%28cropped%29.jpg/250px-Antonoff_in_Tucson_%28cropped%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Antonoff_in_Tucson_\(cropped\).jpg)

_Folklore_ features production from [Aaron Dessner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aaron_Dessner "Aaron Dessner") (_pictured_ left) and [Jack Antonoff](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jack_Antonoff "Jack Antonoff") (right); Dessner produced the majority of tracks.

Swift had previously met the National on a _[Saturday Night Live](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saturday_Night_Live "Saturday Night Live")_ episode in 2014, and attended one of their concerts in 2019, where she talked to Dessner and his twin brother [Bryce](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bryce_Dessner "Bryce Dessner").[\[18\]](#cite_note-DessnerPitchfork-18) She asked Aaron Dessner about his songwriting technique, because it is her "favorite thing to ask people who I'm a fan of", and he replied his band members live in different parts of the world, and that he would make instrumental tracks and send them to the lead singer, [Matt Berninger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matt_Berninger "Matt Berninger"), who would write the lyrics—this ignited Swift's idea to create music in quarantine.[\[12\]](#cite_note-Doyle-2020-12)

Due to the pandemic, all recording studios were closed, so Swift built a home studio at her [Los Angeles residence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Goldwyn_Estate "Samuel Goldwyn Estate"), named Kitty Committee, with help from engineer Laura Sisk.[\[10\]](#cite_note-Suskind-2020-10) Antonoff, with whom Swift worked on five songs from the album, operated from New York City while Sisk recorded Swift's vocals in Los Angeles. "My Tears Ricochet" was the first song written for _Folklore_. Swift wrote it about her ties with [Scott Borchetta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scott_Borchetta "Scott Borchetta"), founder of [her old record label](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Big_Machine_Records "Big Machine Records"), coming to an abrupt end.[\[10\]](#cite_note-Suskind-2020-10) Antonoff compared the writing process of "[Mirrorball](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mirrorball_\(song\) "Mirrorball (song)")" and "[August](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/August_\(song\) "August (song)")" to that of "[Out of the Woods](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Out_of_the_Woods "Out of the Woods")" (2014).[\[19\]](#cite_note-19) Swift wrote "Mirrorball" following the cancellation of Lover Fest, as an ode to fans who find solace in her music and concerts.[\[20\]](#cite_note-20) She wrote "August" about a fictitious [mistress](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mistress_\(lover\) "Mistress (lover)"), and "[This Is Me Trying](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/This_Is_Me_Trying "This Is Me Trying")" based on multiple narratives, such as dealing with addiction, and her own mental health in 2016 and 2017 when she felt she was "worth absolutely nothing."[\[10\]](#cite_note-Suskind-2020-10)

In late April, Swift approached Dessner to co-write some songs remotely. He worked on eleven of the album's 16 tracks over the next few months.[\[21\]](#cite_note-BB_Announcement-21) Dessner "thought it would take a while for song ideas to come" and "had no expectations as far as what we could accomplish remotely", but was surprised that "a few hours after sharing music, my phone lit up with a voice memo from Taylor of a fully written song—the momentum never really stopped."[\[22\]](#cite_note-DessnerVulture-22) Swift and Dessner "were pretty much in touch daily for three or four months by text and phone calls."[\[18\]](#cite_note-DessnerPitchfork-18) He would mail her folders of instrumentals, and she would write the "entire top line"—melody and lyrics, and "he wouldn't know what the song would be about, what it was going to be called, where \[she\] was going to put the chorus."[\[12\]](#cite_note-Doyle-2020-12) The first song the duo wrote was "Cardigan", which is based on one of Dessner's sketches called "Maple".[\[22\]](#cite_note-DessnerVulture-22) "Cardigan" was followed by "[Seven](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seven_\(Taylor_Swift_song\) "Seven (Taylor Swift song)")" and "[Peace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peace_\(Taylor_Swift_song\) "Peace (Taylor Swift song)")".[\[23\]](#cite_note-DessnerRS-23) Upon hearing the composition of "Peace", Swift felt an "immediate sense of serenity" that roused the feeling of being peaceful, but felt it would be "too on-the-nose" to sing about finding peace; she instead wrote about complex "conflicted" feelings contrasting the track's calming sound,[\[10\]](#cite_note-Suskind-2020-10) and recorded it in one vocal take.[\[18\]](#cite_note-DessnerPitchfork-18)

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c2/Rebekah_Harkness_publicity_photo.jpg/250px-Rebekah_Harkness_publicity_photo.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Rebekah_Harkness_publicity_photo.jpg)

[Rebekah Harkness](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rebekah_Harkness "Rebekah Harkness"), the former owner of [Swift's Rhode Island house](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Holiday_House_\(Watch_Hill\) "Holiday House (Watch Hill)"), is the muse behind the third track, "[The Last Great American Dynasty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Last_Great_American_Dynasty "The Last Great American Dynasty")".

A few weeks later, when Swift and Dessner had written "six or seven" songs, she explained him her concept of _Folklore_.[\[23\]](#cite_note-DessnerRS-23) She told him about the work she had done earlier with Antonoff, concluding that both of her works resonate as an album.[\[22\]](#cite_note-DessnerVulture-22) Swift and Dessner also wrote "[The Last Great American Dynasty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Last_Great_American_Dynasty "The Last Great American Dynasty")", "[Mad Woman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mad_Woman "Mad Woman")", and "[Epiphany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Epiphany_\(Taylor_Swift_song\) "Epiphany (Taylor Swift song)")", the first of which has an array of electric guitars inspired by [Radiohead](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radiohead "Radiohead")'s 2007 surprise album _[In Rainbows](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/In_Rainbows "In Rainbows")_.[\[22\]](#cite_note-DessnerVulture-22) The lyrics document American socialite [Rebekah Harkness](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rebekah_Harkness "Rebekah Harkness"), whom Swift had been wanting to write about ever since she bought the [Holiday House](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Holiday_House_\(Watch_Hill\) "Holiday House (Watch Hill)") in 2013.[\[10\]](#cite_note-Suskind-2020-10) Dessner composed the piano melody for "Mad Woman" with his earlier work on "Cardigan" and "Seven" in mind.[\[23\]](#cite_note-DessnerRS-23) On "Epiphany", he slowed down and reversed the sounds of different instruments to create a "giant stack of harmony", and added piano for a cinematic trope.[\[22\]](#cite_note-DessnerVulture-22) Swift wrote the song based on the experiences of her [veteran](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Veteran "Veteran") grandfather, and healthcare workers in the pandemic.[\[10\]](#cite_note-Suskind-2020-10)

Swift wrote two songs, "[Exile](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Exile_\(song\) "Exile (song)")" and "[Betty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Betty_\(Taylor_Swift_song\) "Betty (Taylor Swift song)")", with her then-boyfriend, English actor [Joe Alwyn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Alwyn "Joe Alwyn"). She developed "Exile" as a [duet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duet "Duet"), and Dessner recorded a draft of her singing both the male and female parts.[\[23\]](#cite_note-DessnerRS-23) Swift and Dessner ran through candidates for the male partner, and Swift liked the voice of [Bon Iver](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bon_Iver "Bon Iver")'s [Justin Vernon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Justin_Vernon "Justin Vernon"), who is one half of the American indie rock band [Big Red Machine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Big_Red_Machine_\(band\) "Big Red Machine (band)"), along with Dessner.[\[18\]](#cite_note-DessnerPitchfork-18) Dessner sent the song to Vernon, who liked the song, added his own lyrics, and sang his part.[\[22\]](#cite_note-DessnerVulture-22) "Betty" is the only song on the album produced by both Dessner and Antonoff; Swift was influenced by [Bob Dylan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Dylan "Bob Dylan")'s _[The Freewheelin' Bob Dylan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Freewheelin'_Bob_Dylan "The Freewheelin' Bob Dylan")_ (1963) and _[John Wesley Harding](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Wesley_Harding "John Wesley Harding")_ (1967) for its composition.[\[23\]](#cite_note-DessnerRS-23)[\[22\]](#cite_note-DessnerVulture-22) Alwyn used the pseudonym William Bowery for his credits. Upon the album's release, [mainstream media](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mainstream_media "Mainstream media") and fans pointed out Bowery's lack of online presence,[\[24\]](#cite_note-24)[\[21\]](#cite_note-BB_Announcement-21) and presumed that it was actually a pseudonym for Alwyn, which was later ultimately confirmed by Swift.[\[25\]](#cite_note-25)[\[26\]](#cite_note-26)[\[27\]](#cite_note-Aubrey-27) Swift added that he also penned the chorus of "Betty", and the piano line and first verse in "Exile".[\[28\]](#cite_note-28) The last two songs written were "[The 1](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_1 "The 1")" and "[Hoax](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hoax_\(song\) "Hoax (song)")", the first and last songs on the album respectively; Swift wrote both in a span of a few hours.[\[22\]](#cite_note-DessnerVulture-22) Speaking about his collaboration with her, Dessner commented, "there's a palpable humanity and warmth and raw emotion in these songs that I hope you'll love and take comfort in as much as I do."[\[29\]](#cite_note-29)

In a November 2020 _Rolling Stone_ interview with [Paul McCartney](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_McCartney "Paul McCartney"), Swift stated she began using words in the album's lyrics that she always wanted to use, not worrying about whether it would suit radio. She used "bigger, flowerier, prettier" words such as "[epiphany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Epiphany_\(feeling\) "Epiphany (feeling)")", "[elegies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elegies "Elegies")", and "divorcée", just because they "sound beautiful". Swift disclosed that she maintains lists of such words, and recalled using one such, "[kaleidoscope](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kaleidoscope "Kaleidoscope")", in "[Welcome to New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Welcome_to_New_York_\(song\) "Welcome to New York (song)")" (2014).[\[12\]](#cite_note-Doyle-2020-12) In a December 2020 _[Entertainment Weekly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Entertainment_Weekly "Entertainment Weekly")_ interview, Swift said the lyrics, melodies, and production of _Folklore_ are the way she wanted them, without subjecting to others' expectations.[\[10\]](#cite_note-Suskind-2020-10)

> Taylor has opened the door for artists to not feel pressure to have "the bop". To make the record that she made, while running against what is programmed in radio at the highest levels of [pop music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pop_music "Pop music")—she has kind of made an anti-pop record.

— Dessner on Swift's new sonic direction in _Folklore_, _Billboard_[\[30\]](#cite_note-30)

_Folklore_ was written and recorded in secrecy. Swift, her boyfriend, family, management team, Antonoff, and Dessner were aware of the album's creation; she did not disclose the news or play the album to her friends as she did with her previous works.[\[10\]](#cite_note-Suskind-2020-10) Near the end of _Folklore_'s recording process, Dessner reached out to his regular collaborators, including the National bandmates, to provide instrumentation remotely.[\[23\]](#cite_note-DessnerRS-23) Bryce [orchestrated](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orchestrated "Orchestrated") several songs, while [Bryan Devendorf](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bryan_Devendorf "Bryan Devendorf") performed the drums in "Seven".[\[15\]](#

_**Folklore**_ (stylized in [all lowercase](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/All_lowercase "All lowercase")) is the eighth studio album by the American singer-songwriter [Taylor Swift](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taylor_Swift "Taylor Swift"). It was [surprise-released](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Surprise_album "Surprise album") on July 24, 2020, through [Republic Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republic_Records "Republic Records"). Conceived during [quarantine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/COVID-19_lockdowns "COVID-19 lockdowns") in early 2020, amidst the [COVID-19 pandemic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/COVID-19_pandemic "COVID-19 pandemic"), the album explores themes of [escapism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Escapism "Escapism"), nostalgia, and [romanticism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Romanticism "Romanticism"). Swift recorded her vocals in her Los Angeles home studio and worked virtually with the producers [Aaron Dessner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aaron_Dessner "Aaron Dessner") and [Jack Antonoff](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jack_Antonoff "Jack Antonoff"), who operated from their studios in the [Hudson Valley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hudson_Valley "Hudson Valley") and New York City.

Using a set of characters and story arcs to depict fictional narratives, the album departs from the autobiographical songwriting that had characterized Swift's past albums. Experimenting with new musical styles, _Folklore_ consists of mellow [ballads](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sentimental_ballad "Sentimental ballad") driven by [piano](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Piano "Piano"), [strings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/String_instrument "String instrument"), [orchestration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orchestration "Orchestration"), and muted [percussion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Percussion "Percussion"). Music critics classified the genre into various styles of [folk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Folk_music "Folk music"), [pop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pop_music "Pop music"), and indie, namely [chamber pop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chamber_pop "Chamber pop"), [indie folk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indie_folk "Indie folk"), [electro-folk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electro-folk "Electro-folk"), [folk rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Folk_rock "Folk rock"), and [indie rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indie_rock "Indie rock"). The album's title was inspired by the lasting legacy of folktales, and its visual aesthetic adopts [cottagecore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cottagecore "Cottagecore").

_Folklore_ was accompanied by the concert documentary _[Folklore: The Long Pond Studio Sessions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Folklore:_The_Long_Pond_Studio_Sessions "Folklore: The Long Pond Studio Sessions")_, featuring Swift's commentary and performances. The album topped the charts in Australasia and various European countries and was [certified platinum or higher](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Music_recording_certification "Music recording certification") in Australia, Austria, Denmark, France, Germany, Italy, New Zealand, Norway, Poland, Portugal, and the United Kingdom. In the United States, it spent eight weeks atop the [_Billboard_ 200](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billboard_200 "Billboard 200"), was the best-selling album of 2020, and was certified six-times platinum by the [Recording Industry Association of America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Recording_Industry_Association_of_America "Recording Industry Association of America"). Three songs, "[Cardigan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cardigan_\(song\) "Cardigan (song)")", "[The 1](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_1 "The 1")", and "[Exile](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Exile_\(song\) "Exile (song)")" featuring [Bon Iver](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bon_Iver "Bon Iver"), reached the top 10 on international singles charts, with "Cardigan" peaking at number one on the [_Billboard_ Hot 100](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billboard_Hot_100 "Billboard Hot 100").

_Folklore_ received widespread critical acclaim for its emotional weight and intricate lyricism; some journalists commented that its introspective tone was timely for the pandemic, and they regarded its sound as a bold reinvention of Swift's artistry. Many publications featured the album on their 2020 year-end rankings, and _[Rolling Stone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rolling_Stone "Rolling Stone")_ included it in their 2023 revision of their "[500 Greatest Albums of All Time](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rolling_Stone's_500_Greatest_Albums_of_All_Time "Rolling Stone's 500 Greatest Albums of All Time")" list. _Folklore_ won [Album of the Year](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grammy_Award_for_Album_of_the_Year "Grammy Award for Album of the Year") at the [63rd Annual Grammy Awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/63rd_Annual_Grammy_Awards "63rd Annual Grammy Awards"), making Swift the first woman to win the award three times. The album informed the concept of Swift's next record, _[Evermore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Evermore "Evermore")_ (2020), and has inspired other artists' works.

In April 2020, [Taylor Swift](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taylor_Swift "Taylor Swift") was set to embark on Lover Fest, a concert tour in support of her seventh studio album _[Lover](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lover_\(album\) "Lover (album)")_ (2019), which was cancelled following the [COVID-19 pandemic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/COVID-19_pandemic "COVID-19 pandemic").[\[1\]](#cite_note-Lipshutz-1) On July 23, 2020, nine photos were uploaded to Swift's [Instagram](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Instagram "Instagram") account, all without captions, forming a black and white image of her standing alone in a forest. Subsequently, Swift made another post across all her social media accounts, announcing that her eighth studio album would be released at midnight; Swift stated: "Most of the things I had planned this summer didn't end up happening, but there is something I hadn't planned on that DID happen. And that thing is my 8th studio album, _Folklore_". She confirmed the image as the album's cover artwork and revealed the track list.[\[2\]](#cite_note-2) _[The Wall Street Journal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Wall_Street_Journal "The Wall Street Journal")_ opined that the surprise announcement "caught fans and the music business off-guard".[\[3\]](#cite_note-3) _[Billboard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billboard_\(magazine\) "Billboard (magazine)")_ stated that it "blindsided the pop music world", arriving as "exciting news" during [lockdown](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/COVID-19_lockdowns "COVID-19 lockdowns").[\[4\]](#cite_note-Billboard_List-4) _Folklore_ was released eleven months after _Lover_—the fastest turnaround for a Swift studio album at the time, beating the one year and nine-month gap between _[Reputation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reputation_\(Taylor_Swift_album\) "Reputation (Taylor Swift album)")_ (2017) and _Lover_. In another post, Swift announced that the music video for the track "[Cardigan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cardigan_\(song\) "Cardigan (song)")" would be released at the same time as the album.[\[5\]](#cite_note-Reilly-5)

During the [YouTube](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/YouTube "YouTube") premiere countdown to the "Cardigan" music video, Swift hinted that the album lyrics contained many of her signature [Easter eggs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Easter_egg_\(media\) "Easter egg (media)"): "One thing I did purposely on this album was put the Easter eggs in the lyrics, more than just the videos. I created character arcs and recurring themes that map out who is singing about who... For example, there's a collection of three songs I refer to as the Teenage Love Triangle. These three songs explore a love triangle from all three people's perspectives at different times in their lives".[\[6\]](#cite_note-Rolling_Stone-6) She referred to the album as "[wistful](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Melancholia "Melancholia") and full of [escapism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Escapism "Escapism"). Sad, beautiful, tragic. Like a photo album full of imagery, and all the stories behind that imagery",[\[7\]](#cite_note-E!-7) described "Cardigan" as a song that explores "lost romance and why young love is often fixed so permanently in our memories,"[\[8\]](#cite_note-8) and identified the self-written track, "[My Tears Ricochet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/My_Tears_Ricochet "My Tears Ricochet")", as the first song she wrote for the album.[\[7\]](#cite_note-E!-7) _[Uproxx](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uproxx "Uproxx")_ narrated, "on Thursday night, that hand-drawn 'T' and 'S' could be seen up and down the timeline. Music fans and critics across genres unveiled hot takes, quoted lyrics like [Myspace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Myspace "Myspace") teens writing on the back of textbooks or crafting the perfect [AIM away message](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AIM_\(software\) "AIM (software)"), and debated _Folklore_'s place in the unimpeachable Taylor Swift canon."[\[9\]](#cite_note-9)

Swift did not expect to create an album in early 2020.[\[10\]](#cite_note-Suskind-2020-10) After the cancellation of Lover Fest,[\[1\]](#cite_note-Lipshutz-1) Swift [quarantined](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quarantine "Quarantine") herself, during which she watched numerous films and shows, such as _[Rear Window](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rear_Window "Rear Window")_ (1954), _[L.A. Confidential](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/L.A._Confidential_\(film\) "L.A. Confidential (film)")_ (1997), _[Pan's Labyrinth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pan's_Labyrinth "Pan's Labyrinth")_ (2006), _[Jane Eyre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jane_Eyre_\(2011_film\) "Jane Eyre (2011 film)")_ (2011), _[Marriage Story](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marriage_Story "Marriage Story")_ (2019),[\[10\]](#cite_note-Suskind-2020-10) and _[The Last Dance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Last_Dance_\(miniseries\) "The Last Dance (miniseries)")_ (2020),[\[11\]](#cite_note-11) and read more books than she ever did, books that "dealt with times past, a world that doesn't exist anymore", such as _[Rebecca](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rebecca_\(novel\) "Rebecca (novel)")_ (1938) by [Daphne du Maurier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daphne_du_Maurier "Daphne du Maurier").[\[12\]](#cite_note-Doyle-2020-12) The fictions inspired Swift to venture beyond her usual autobiographical style of songwriting and experiment with different narrative standpoints.[\[10\]](#cite_note-Suskind-2020-10) In isolation during the lockdown, she let her imagination "run wild", ensuing in a set of imagery and visuals that consequently became _Folklore_.[\[13\]](#cite_note-Primer-13)

> It started with imagery. Visuals that popped into my mind and piqued my curiosity. Stars drawn around scars. A [cardigan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cardigan_\(sweater\) "Cardigan (sweater)") that still bears the scent of loss twenty years later. [Battleships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battleship "Battleship") sinking into the ocean, down, down, down. The tree swing in the woods of my childhood. Hushed tones of "let's run away" and never doing it. The sun drenched month of August, sipped away like a bottle of wine. A mirrored disco ball hovering above a dance floor. A [whiskey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whiskey "Whiskey") bottle beckoning. Hands held through plastic. A single thread that, for better or for worse, ties you to your fate. Pretty soon these images in my head grew faces or names and became characters. I found myself not only writing my own stories, but also writing about or from the perspective of people I've never met, people I've known, or those I wish I hadn't.

— Swift on developing _Folklore_, _Billboard_[\[13\]](#cite_note-Primer-13)

Some of the imagery the singer developed includes: "An exiled man walking the bluffs of a land that isn't his own, wondering how it all went so terribly, terribly wrong. An embittered tormentor showing up at the funeral of his fallen object of obsession. A seventeen-year-old standing on a porch, learning to apologize. Lovestruck kids wandering up and down the evergreen [High Line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/High_Line "High Line"). My grandfather, Dean, [landing at Guadalcanal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guadalcanal_campaign "Guadalcanal campaign") in 1942. A misfit widow getting gleeful revenge on the town that cast her out".[\[13\]](#cite_note-Primer-13) Swift "poured all of \[her\] whims, dreams, fears, and musings" into the songs, and reached out to her "musical heroes" to collaborate with.[\[14\]](#cite_note-14) She initially planned to release _Folklore_ in early 2021, but it "ended up being done" sooner, and released in July 2020 without giving it second thoughts. She approached the album's creation without subjecting herself to any rules, and explained that she "used to put all these parameters on \[herself\], like, "How will this song sound in a stadium? How will this song sound on radio?" If you take away all the parameters, what do you make? And I guess the answer is _Folklore_."[\[12\]](#cite_note-Doyle-2020-12)

## Writing and recording

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Folklore_\(Taylor_Swift_album\)&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Writing and recording")\]

Swift's songwriting drifted towards escapism and [romanticism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Romanticism "Romanticism") for _Folklore_.[\[12\]](#cite_note-Doyle-2020-12) She enlisted two producers to achieve her desired sound—her longtime collaborator, [Jack Antonoff](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jack_Antonoff "Jack Antonoff"), who worked with her on _[1989](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1989_\(Taylor_Swift_album\) "1989 (Taylor Swift album)")_ (2014), _Reputation_, and _Lover_, and first-time collaborator [Aaron Dessner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aaron_Dessner "Aaron Dessner"), guitarist of American [indie rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indie_rock "Indie rock") band [the National](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_National_\(band\) "The National (band)").[\[15\]](#cite_note-PitchforkCredits-15) Due to COVID-19 concerns, Swift, Antonoff, and Dessner quarantined remotely, separate from each other, creating _Folklore_ by continually exchanging digital files of instrumentals and vocals.[\[16\]](#cite_note-Blistein-2020-16) The album ensued from a [DIY](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DIY "DIY") process,[\[17\]](#cite_note-17) [mixed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mixing_engineer "Mixing engineer") and [engineered](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Audio_engineer "Audio engineer") by personnel scattered across the US.[\[4\]](#cite_note-Billboard_List-4)

[![Man playing a guitar on stage](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a3/Aaron_Dessner_at_Way_Out_West_2014.jpg/250px-Aaron_Dessner_at_Way_Out_West_2014.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Aaron_Dessner_at_Way_Out_West_2014.jpg)

[![Man playing a red guitar](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/89/Antonoff_in_Tucson_%28cropped%29.jpg/250px-Antonoff_in_Tucson_%28cropped%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Antonoff_in_Tucson_\(cropped\).jpg)

_Folklore_ features production from [Aaron Dessner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aaron_Dessner "Aaron Dessner") (_pictured_ left) and [Jack Antonoff](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jack_Antonoff "Jack Antonoff") (right); Dessner produced the majority of tracks.

Swift had previously met the National on a _[Saturday Night Live](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saturday_Night_Live "Saturday Night Live")_ episode in 2014, and attended one of their concerts in 2019, where she talked to Dessner and his twin brother [Bryce](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bryce_Dessner "Bryce Dessner").[\[18\]](#cite_note-DessnerPitchfork-18) She asked Aaron Dessner about his songwriting technique, because it is her "favorite thing to ask people who I'm a fan of", and he replied his band members live in different parts of the world, and that he would make instrumental tracks and send them to the lead singer, [Matt Berninger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matt_Berninger "Matt Berninger"), who would write the lyrics—this ignited Swift's idea to create music in quarantine.[\[12\]](#cite_note-Doyle-2020-12)

Due to the pandemic, all recording studios were closed, so Swift built a home studio at her [Los Angeles residence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Goldwyn_Estate "Samuel Goldwyn Estate"), named Kitty Committee, with help from engineer Laura Sisk.[\[10\]](#cite_note-Suskind-2020-10) Antonoff, with whom Swift worked on five songs from the album, operated from New York City while Sisk recorded Swift's vocals in Los Angeles. "My Tears Ricochet" was the first song written for _Folklore_. Swift wrote it about her ties with [Scott Borchetta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scott_Borchetta "Scott Borchetta"), founder of [her old record label](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Big_Machine_Records "Big Machine Records"), coming to an abrupt end.[\[10\]](#cite_note-Suskind-2020-10) Antonoff compared the writing process of "[Mirrorball](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mirrorball_\(song\) "Mirrorball (song)")" and "[August](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/August_\(song\) "August (song)")" to that of "[Out of the Woods](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Out_of_the_Woods "Out of the Woods")" (2014).[\[19\]](#cite_note-19) Swift wrote "Mirrorball" following the cancellation of Lover Fest, as an ode to fans who find solace in her music and concerts.[\[20\]](#cite_note-20) She wrote "August" about a fictitious [mistress](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mistress_\(lover\) "Mistress (lover)"), and "[This Is Me Trying](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/This_Is_Me_Trying "This Is Me Trying")" based on multiple narratives, such as dealing with addiction, and her own mental health in 2016 and 2017 when she felt she was "worth absolutely nothing."[\[10\]](#cite_note-Suskind-2020-10)

In late April, Swift approached Dessner to co-write some songs remotely. He worked on eleven of the album's 16 tracks over the next few months.[\[21\]](#cite_note-BB_Announcement-21) Dessner "thought it would take a while for song ideas to come" and "had no expectations as far as what we could accomplish remotely", but was surprised that "a few hours after sharing music, my phone lit up with a voice memo from Taylor of a fully written song—the momentum never really stopped."[\[22\]](#cite_note-DessnerVulture-22) Swift and Dessner "were pretty much in touch daily for three or four months by text and phone calls."[\[18\]](#cite_note-DessnerPitchfork-18) He would mail her folders of instrumentals, and she would write the "entire top line"—melody and lyrics, and "he wouldn't know what the song would be about, what it was going to be called, where \[she\] was going to put the chorus."[\[12\]](#cite_note-Doyle-2020-12) The first song the duo wrote was "Cardigan", which is based on one of Dessner's sketches called "Maple".[\[22\]](#cite_note-DessnerVulture-22) "Cardigan" was followed by "[Seven](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seven_\(Taylor_Swift_song\) "Seven (Taylor Swift song)")" and "[Peace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peace_\(Taylor_Swift_song\) "Peace (Taylor Swift song)")".[\[23\]](#cite_note-DessnerRS-23) Upon hearing the composition of "Peace", Swift felt an "immediate sense of serenity" that roused the feeling of being peaceful, but felt it would be "too on-the-nose" to sing about finding peace; she instead wrote about complex "conflicted" feelings contrasting the track's calming sound,[\[10\]](#cite_note-Suskind-2020-10) and recorded it in one vocal take.[\[18\]](#cite_note-DessnerPitchfork-18)

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c2/Rebekah_Harkness_publicity_photo.jpg/250px-Rebekah_Harkness_publicity_photo.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Rebekah_Harkness_publicity_photo.jpg)

[Rebekah Harkness](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rebekah_Harkness "Rebekah Harkness"), the former owner of [Swift's Rhode Island house](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Holiday_House_\(Watch_Hill\) "Holiday House (Watch Hill)"), is the muse behind the third track, "[The Last Great American Dynasty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Last_Great_American_Dynasty "The Last Great American Dynasty")".

A few weeks later, when Swift and Dessner had written "six or seven" songs, she explained him her concept of _Folklore_.[\[23\]](#cite_note-DessnerRS-23) She told him about the work she had done earlier with Antonoff, concluding that both of her works resonate as an album.[\[22\]](#cite_note-DessnerVulture-22) Swift and Dessner also wrote "[The Last Great American Dynasty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Last_Great_American_Dynasty "The Last Great American Dynasty")", "[Mad Woman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mad_Woman "Mad Woman")", and "[Epiphany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Epiphany_\(Taylor_Swift_song\) "Epiphany (Taylor Swift song)")", the first of which has an array of electric guitars inspired by [Radiohead](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radiohead "Radiohead")'s 2007 surprise album _[In Rainbows](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/In_Rainbows "In Rainbows")_.[\[22\]](#cite_note-DessnerVulture-22) The lyrics document American socialite [Rebekah Harkness](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rebekah_Harkness "Rebekah Harkness"), whom Swift had been wanting to write about ever since she bought the [Holiday House](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Holiday_House_\(Watch_Hill\) "Holiday House (Watch Hill)") in 2013.[\[10\]](#cite_note-Suskind-2020-10) Dessner composed the piano melody for "Mad Woman" with his earlier work on "Cardigan" and "Seven" in mind.[\[23\]](#cite_note-DessnerRS-23) On "Epiphany", he slowed down and reversed the sounds of different instruments to create a "giant stack of harmony", and added piano for a cinematic trope.[\[22\]](#cite_note-DessnerVulture-22) Swift wrote the song based on the experiences of her [veteran](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Veteran "Veteran") grandfather, and healthcare workers in the pandemic.[\[10\]](#cite_note-Suskind-2020-10)

Swift wrote two songs, "[Exile](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Exile_\(song\) "Exile (song)")" and "[Betty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Betty_\(Taylor_Swift_song\) "Betty (Taylor Swift song)")", with her then-boyfriend, English actor [Joe Alwyn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Alwyn "Joe Alwyn"). She developed "Exile" as a [duet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duet "Duet"), and Dessner recorded a draft of her singing both the male and female parts.[\[23\]](#cite_note-DessnerRS-23) Swift and Dessner ran through candidates for the male partner, and Swift liked the voice of [Bon Iver](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bon_Iver "Bon Iver")'s [Justin Vernon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Justin_Vernon "Justin Vernon"), who is one half of the American indie rock band [Big Red Machine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Big_Red_Machine_\(band\) "Big Red Machine (band)"), along with Dessner.[\[18\]](#cite_note-DessnerPitchfork-18) Dessner sent the song to Vernon, who liked the song, added his own lyrics, and sang his part.[\[22\]](#cite_note-DessnerVulture-22) "Betty" is the only song on the album produced by both Dessner and Antonoff; Swift was influenced by [Bob Dylan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Dylan "Bob Dylan")'s _[The Freewheelin' Bob Dylan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Freewheelin'_Bob_Dylan "The Freewheelin' Bob Dylan")_ (1963) and _[John Wesley Harding](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Wesley_Harding "John Wesley Harding")_ (1967) for its composition.[\[23\]](#cite_note-DessnerRS-23)[\[22\]](#cite_note-DessnerVulture-22) Alwyn used the pseudonym William Bowery for his credits. Upon the album's release, [mainstream media](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mainstream_media "Mainstream media") and fans pointed out Bowery's lack of online presence,[\[24\]](#cite_note-24)[\[21\]](#cite_note-BB_Announcement-21) and presumed that it was actually a pseudonym for Alwyn, which was later ultimately confirmed by Swift.[\[25\]](#cite_note-25)[\[26\]](#cite_note-26)[\[27\]](#cite_note-Aubrey-27) Swift added that he also penned the chorus of "Betty", and the piano line and first verse in "Exile".[\[28\]](#cite_note-28) The last two songs written were "[The 1](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_1 "The 1")" and "[Hoax](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hoax_\(song\) "Hoax (song)")", the first and last songs on the album respectively; Swift wrote both in a span of a few hours.[\[22\]](#cite_note-DessnerVulture-22) Speaking about his collaboration with her, Dessner commented, "there's a palpable humanity and warmth and raw emotion in these songs that I hope you'll love and take comfort in as much as I do."[\[29\]](#cite_note-29)

In a November 2020 _Rolling Stone_ interview with [Paul McCartney](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_McCartney "Paul McCartney"), Swift stated she began using words in the album's lyrics that she always wanted to use, not worrying about whether it would suit radio. She used "bigger, flowerier, prettier" words such as "[epiphany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Epiphany_\(feeling\) "Epiphany (feeling)")", "[elegies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elegies "Elegies")", and "divorcée", just because they "sound beautiful". Swift disclosed that she maintains lists of such words, and recalled using one such, "[kaleidoscope](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kaleidoscope "Kaleidoscope")", in "[Welcome to New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Welcome_to_New_York_\(song\) "Welcome to New York (song)")" (2014).[\[12\]](#cite_note-Doyle-2020-12) In a December 2020 _[Entertainment Weekly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Entertainment_Weekly "Entertainment Weekly")_ interview, Swift said the lyrics, melodies, and production of _Folklore_ are the way she wanted them, without subjecting to others' expectations.[\[10\]](#cite_note-Suskind-2020-10)

> Taylor has opened the door for artists to not feel pressure to have "the bop". To make the record that she made, while running against what is programmed in radio at the highest levels of [pop music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pop_music "Pop music")—she has kind of made an anti-pop record.

— Dessner on Swift's new sonic direction in _Folklore_, _Billboard_[\[30\]](#cite_note-30)

_Folklore_ was written and recorded in secrecy. After almost 10 years, it’s finally here. Taylor Swift’s long-rumored, never-before-heard 10-minute version of her 2012 hit “All Too Well” is finally seeing the light of day [as Swift releases her fully re-recorded _Red_](/culture/22278732/taylor-swift-re-recording-fearless-love-story-master-rights-scooter-braun). The full version is a strikingly vulnerable piece of songcraft, even for heartbreak queen Taylor Swift. It surpasses the original.

“All Too Well” has always been a bit of an oddity as a Taylor Swift hit. _Red_ was the album in which Swift began transitioning from country pop star to pure pop star, collaborating with Swedish pop master Max Martin to turn out sharp-edged earworms like “We Are Never Ever Getting Back Together” and “I Knew You Were Trouble.” “All Too Well,” in contrast, is shaggier and looser than its peers on the album, and was never released as a single. It was in a way a throwback even in 2012: It saw Swift returning to her early songwriting partner Liz Rose, with whom she wrote her first singles “Tim McGraw” and “Teardrops on My Guitar” as a teenager and with whom she hasn’t worked since.

Regardless, “All Too Well” became a fan favorite and a popular choice for Swift’s best song. It’s a breakup song, rumored to be about Swift’s split with Jake Gyllenhaal, and it shows off Swift’s ability to build a whole love story around a single telling detail — in this case, the scarf Swift’s narrator leaves with her ex, still in a drawer at his sister’s house. (That would be, I suppose, [Maggie Gyllenhaal’s house](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=xlNC8Q62imU). And I would be remiss not to note that [Swift is selling a version of the much-mythologized scarf](https://store.taylorswift.com/products/the-all-too-well-knit-scarf).) What’s most touching about the song is Swift’s insistence on her own dignity even at age 21, her repeated assertion that even if her older ex refuses to admit their relationship was meaningful, “I was there, I remember it all too well.”

In the years since “All Too Well” first dropped, both Rose and Swift have talked about a longer version of the song, a first draft that clocked in at 10 minutes long, that served as a catharsis for all that Swift wanted to get out about her ex. And now, she’s finally given it a proper studio recording and included it as a bonus track on the newly re-released _Red_. Improbably, it lives up to the years of teases and hype-building.

While the first “All Too Well” worked because it demanded that we give Swift the respect she is due, the 10-minute “All Too Well” improves upon the original by making us privy to her humiliations first. The new verses include descriptions of her ex condescending to her about their age gap, of him charming Swift’s dad “like you’re on a late-night show” before standing her up on her 21st birthday, of Swift crying in the bathroom at a Hollywood party. “That made me want to die,” she sings, and it’s hard not to believe her.

Swift has written a lot of songs about the ways her exes have wronged her, but she’s rarely been quite as vulnerable and open as she is here. Like: Imagine dating a movie star when you were 20 and he was 30, feeling really grown-up and sophisticated and like maybe you’d found the one, and then having him tell you that maybe it would have worked out if you weren’t 10 years younger than him. _God!_ The sheer cringing awfulness of the idea, the infuriating passing of the blame. She says, “You kept me like a secret but I kept you like an oath,” and, well, _right_? That’s how those relationships work, in those moments when one person is fully invested and the other ashamed and wary.

There’s just enough detail in Swift’s songwriting to give her story the ring of truth — and the ex she’s conjuring up here is so condescending, so glib and casually cruel, that it lands harder than ever when Swift insists, with understandable fervor, “It was rare, I was there, I remember it all too well.” She’s shown herself to us at her lowest, and that means the respect she demands in the chorus feels absolutely fully earned.

text:
# Midnights

er from _[Billboard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billboard_\(magazine\) "Billboard (magazine)")_ described it as "[alt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alternative_pop "Alternative pop")\-leaning synth-pop".[\[75\]](#cite_note-Unterberger-2022a-79) Ilana Kaplam of the [_Alternative Press_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alternative_Press_\(magazine\) "Alternative Press (magazine)") and [Stephen Thomas Erlewine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_Thomas_Erlewine "Stephen Thomas Erlewine") of [AllMusic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AllMusic "AllMusic") said that in addition to the electronic sound, _Midnights_ incorporated alternative elements and contemplative lyricism that evoked _Folklore_ and _Evermore_.[\[30\]](#cite_note-Kaplan-2022-31)[\[61\]](#cite_note-Erlewine-2022-63)

## Artwork and aesthetics

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Midnights&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Artwork and aesthetics")\]

Employing a [minimalist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minimalism_\(visual_arts\) "Minimalism (visual arts)") design, the standard edition's cover artwork contains a square photo of Swift in blue [eye shadow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eye_shadow "Eye shadow"), black [eye liner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eye_liner "Eye liner"), and red lipstick, holding the flame of a lighter close to her face.[\[76\]](#cite_note-Sanchez-2022-80)[\[77\]](#cite_note-Dailey-2022-81) The photo is at the bottom right corner, occupying half of the cover, and bordered on the top and left sides by off-white [negative space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Negative_space "Negative space").[\[77\]](#cite_note-Dailey-2022-81) The tracklist is on the bottom left, and the title _Midnights_ is written in a blue gradient, printed on top of Swift's photo.[\[76\]](#cite_note-Sanchez-2022-80) The [typeface](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Typeface "Typeface") used on the album cover is [Neue Haas Grotesk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neue_Haas_Grotesk "Neue Haas Grotesk").[\[78\]](#cite_note-82)

The tracklist presentation is reminiscent of vinyl [album jackets](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Record_sleeve "Record sleeve") common in the 1970s.[\[79\]](#cite_note-83)[\[80\]](#cite_note-Willman-2022a-84) Several 1970s cultural items that were listed by journalists as potential reference points for the _Midnights_ cover include the English band [Roxy Music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roxy_Music "Roxy Music")'s 1974 album _[Country Life](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Country_Life_\(Roxy_Music_album\) "Country Life (Roxy Music album)")_, the French artist [Guy Bourdin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guy_Bourdin "Guy Bourdin")'s photographs for _[Vogue France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vogue_France "Vogue France")_, and the English model [Jean Shrimpton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jean_Shrimpton "Jean Shrimpton"), as discussed by [Jess Cartner-Morley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jess_Cartner-Morley "Jess Cartner-Morley")[\[2\]](#cite_note-Snapes-2022-2) and [Alex Bilmes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alex_Bilmes "Alex Bilmes").[\[31\]](#cite_note-Bilmes-2022-32) Several other analyses aligned the _Midnights_ cover with the [indie sleaze](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indie_sleaze "Indie sleaze") trend of the 2000s decade;[\[e\]](#cite_note-87) [Rob Sheffield](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rob_Sheffield "Rob Sheffield") of _[Rolling Stone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rolling_Stone "Rolling Stone")_ named the _Ultra Chilled_ [dance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dance_music "Dance music") CD compilations from the early 2000s as a potential influence.[\[83\]](#cite_note-88) The cover created a trend and was parodied by many brands, celebrities, and athletic teams.[\[84\]](#cite_note-89)[\[85\]](#cite_note-90)

Other promotional visuals for _Midnights_ also feature 1970s aesthetics.[\[86\]](#cite_note-91)[\[87\]](#cite_note-92) The photographs and videos that Swift posted onto social media featured a clock face, family-room furniture with retro [upholstery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Upholstery "Upholstery"), and a [rust](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rust_\(color\) "Rust (color)") velvet curtain in the background.[\[42\]](#cite_note-Willman-2022c-43)[\[88\]](#cite_note-93)[\[89\]](#cite_note-94) Her wardrobe incorporated embellishments that [_Vogue_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vogue_\(magazine\) "Vogue (magazine)") identified as "disco [sequins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sequin "Sequin")" and "[corduroy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corduroy "Corduroy") flare".[\[90\]](#cite_note-95) The covers for three other physical editions all feature 1970s memorabilia: a retro piano, a [push-button telephone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Push-button_telephone "Push-button telephone"), and a [wood-paneled](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Panelling "Panelling") wall.[\[76\]](#cite_note-Sanchez-2022-80)[\[80\]](#cite_note-Willman-2022a-84) Their reverse sides each portray a quarter sector of a dial and, when assembled together and combined with a [clock mechanism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clockwork "Clockwork") sold separately, form a functioning clock.[\[91\]](#cite_note-96) The [music videos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Music_video "Music video") for "Anti-Hero", "Bejeweled", and "Lavender Haze" feature Swift in [1970s fashion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1970s_fashion "1970s fashion"): [houndstooth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Houndstooth "Houndstooth") polo sweaters, ribbed knit trousers, and sequined bodysuits.[\[f\]](#cite_note-100)

Swift extensively used social media to promote _Midnights_.[\[1\]](#cite_note-Lutz-2022-1)[\[8\]](#cite_note-Martoccio-2022-8) After the announcement at the MTV Video Music Awards, Swift's website and the canvases of her songs on [Spotify](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spotify "Spotify") were updated with images of a clock.[\[95\]](#cite_note-101) Using the video-sharing platform [TikTok](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TikTok "TikTok"), from September 21 to October 7, 2022, she released a 13-episode video series called _Midnights Mayhem with Me_, where she announced the title of each track in a randomized order per episode.[\[96\]](#cite_note-Jones-2022-102) In each episode, Swift rolled a [lottery cage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lottery_machine#Gravity_Pick "Lottery machine") containing 13 ping pong balls numbered from 1 to 13, each representing a track of the album; when a ball dropped out, she disclosed the title of the corresponding track through a telephone.[\[97\]](#cite_note-103)[\[96\]](#cite_note-Jones-2022-102) On October 17, Swift posted on her social media an itinerary titled _Midnights Manifest_, which included promotional events she had planned.[\[98\]](#cite_note-104) Swift partnered with Spotify to display some lyrics from _Midnights_ on billboards in five cities: New York, London, [São Paulo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/São_Paulo "São Paulo"), Nashville, and Mexico City.[\[99\]](#cite_note-105) Another partnership with [Apple Fitness+](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fitness_\(Apple\) "Fitness (Apple)") included three exercise programs designed around Swift's music, featuring tracks from _Midnights_.[\[100\]](#cite_note-106)

Although Swift extensively promoted _Midnights_ and announced multiple release pre-orders, she did not conduct press interviews or preview music prior to the album's release.[\[2\]](#cite_note-Snapes-2022-2) [Republic Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republic_Records "Republic Records") released _Midnights_ on October 21, 2022.[\[48\]](#cite_note-Sisario-2022-49) The standard edition was made available for streaming, download, cassette, four CD variants, and four [vinyl LP](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vinyl_LP "Vinyl LP") variants.[\[101\]](#cite_note-107) [Target](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Target_Corporation "Target Corporation") stores exclusively sold a _Lavender Edition_ on CD and vinyl LP, and [Capital One](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capital_One "Capital One") distributed a [box set](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Box_set "Box set") that contained the CD and a Swift-branded T-shirt.[\[102\]](#cite_note-Caulfield-2022b-108) The _3am Edition_ was surprise-released onto streaming and digital services three hours after the standard edition.[\[102\]](#cite_note-Caulfield-2022b-108) From October 21 to 26, [iHeartRadio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IHeartRadio "IHeartRadio") aired a program called _iHeartRadio Brings You Midnights with Taylor_, which featured tracks from the album and stories behind the songs told by Swift herself.[\[103\]](#cite_note-109) She appeared, but did not perform, on the talk shows _[The Tonight Show Starring Jimmy Fallon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Tonight_Show_Starring_Jimmy_Fallon "The Tonight Show Starring Jimmy Fallon")_ on October 24[\[104\]](#cite_note-110) and _[The Graham Norton Show](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Graham_Norton_Show "The Graham Norton Show")_ on October 28.[\[105\]](#cite_note-111)

[![Swift, dressed in a rhinestoned bodysuite, singing into a mic](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/5d/Taylor_Swift_The_Eras_Tour_Midnights_Era_Set_%2853109799784%29_%28cropped%29.jpg/250px-Taylor_Swift_The_Eras_Tour_Midnights_Era_Set_%2853109799784%29_%28cropped%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Taylor_Swift_The_Eras_Tour_Midnights_Era_Set_\(53109799784\)_\(cropped\).jpg)

Swift performing on [the Eras Tour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Eras_Tour "The Eras Tour") at [SoFi Stadium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SoFi_Stadium "SoFi Stadium") in August 2023

"Anti-Hero" was released as the album's lead single on October 21, 2022.[\[106\]](#cite_note-112) In the United States, it became the best-selling song of 2022[\[107\]](#cite_note-Caulfield-2023a-113) and made Swift the first artist to have a number-one song on the [Radio Songs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radio_Songs_\(chart\) "Radio Songs (chart)") chart in the 2000s, 2010s, and 2020s decades.[\[108\]](#cite_note-114) "Bejeweled" and "Question...?" were released for limited-time digital download exclusively through Swift's website on October 25.[\[109\]](#cite_note-115) "Snow on the Beach" was issued to US [triple-A](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adult_album_alternative "Adult album alternative") radio as a single on November 7, 2022,[\[110\]](#cite_note-116) followed by the US [pop radio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pop_radio "Pop radio") releases of "Lavender Haze" on November 29, 2022,[\[111\]](#cite_note-117)[\[112\]](#cite_note-118) and "Karma" on May 1, 2023.[\[113\]](#cite_note-119)[\[114\]](#cite_note-120) A remix of "Karma" featuring the rapper [Ice Spice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ice_Spice "Ice Spice") was released on May 26, 2023.[\[115\]](#cite_note-121) On the US [_Billboard_ Hot 100](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billboard_Hot_100 "Billboard Hot 100"), "Anti-Hero" reached number one, "Lavender Haze" and "Karma" both peaked at number two, and "Snow on the Beach" charted at number four.[\[116\]](#cite_note-122)[\[117\]](#cite_note-Trust-2022-123)

The promotional rollout of _Midnights_ received media commentary. Unterberger and [_Slate_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slate_\(magazine\) "Slate (magazine)")'s Chris Molanphy described it as a middle ground between a traditional album rollout and the surprise-release strategy of _Folklore_ and _Evermore_.[\[118\]](#cite_note-Unterberger-2022b-124)[\[119\]](#cite_note-Molanphy-2022-125) Molanphy argued that _Midnights_ employed an optimal promotion for every consumption metric: the multiple CD and LP offers would boost physical sales, the limited-time download tracks would increase digital sales, and the surprise _3am Edition_ release would prompt higher streams.[\[119\]](#cite_note-Molanphy-2022-125) The fact that there were no pre-release singles prompted speculation on the album's sound and content,[\[2\]](#cite_note-Snapes-2022-2)[\[118\]](#cite_note-Unterberger-2022b-124)[\[120\]](#cite_note-126) and the TikTok video series prompted Swift's fans to interpret possible [Easter eggs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Easter_egg_\(media\) "Easter egg (media)"), heightening the anticipation for the album.[\[121\]](#cite_note-127)

To support _Midnights_ and her other albums, Swift embarked on [the Eras Tour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Eras_Tour "The Eras Tour"), which she described as a retrospective journey through her "musical eras".[\[122\]](#cite_note-128) Running from March 2023 to December 2024, the tour spanned 149 dates and visited five continents.[\[123\]](#cite_note-129) It became the first concert tour to gross over $1 billion, totaling $2 billion, the [highest-grossing in history](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_highest-grossing_concert_tours "List of highest-grossing concert tours").[\[124\]](#cite_note-130) During the run of the tour, a _Til Dawn Edition_ of _Midnights_ containing the bonus track "[Hits Different](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hits_Different "Hits Different")" was released to digital platforms, and a _Late Night Edition_ containing the bonus track "[You're Losing Me](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/You're_Losing_Me "You're Losing Me")" was sold as concert–exclusive merchandise starting from the [East Rutherford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_Rutherford "East Rutherford") show on May 26, 2023.[\[125\]](#cite_note-Caulfield-2023b-131)

## Commercial performance

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Midnights&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Commercial performance")\]

_Midnights_ was a commercial success across all consumption metrics: streaming, digital sales, and physical sales.[\[75\]](#cite_note-Unterberger-2022a-79)[\[126\]](#cite_note-132) It broke various records on music streaming platforms.[\[127\]](#cite_note-133) On Spotify, _Midnights_ broke records for the [highest single-day streams](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_most-streamed_songs_on_Spotify#Most_streamed_albums_in_a_single_day "List of most-streamed songs on Spotify") and the highest single-week streams.[\[128\]](#cite_note-134)[\[129\]](#cite_note-Jericho-2022-135) It also claimed the highest single-day streams for a pop album and an album released in [Dolby Atmos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dolby_Atmos "Dolby Atmos") on [Apple Music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_Music "Apple Music"), the highest single-week streams for an album on [Amazon Music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amazon_Music "Amazon Music"), and the highest single-day requests on [Amazon Alexa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amazon_Alexa "Amazon Alexa").[\[130\]](#cite_note-Young-2022-136) All of its tracks entered the [_Billboard_ Global 200](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billboard_Global_200 "Billboard Global 200") simultaneously; it set the record for the most simultaneous top-10 entries (nine) and made Swift the first artist to occupy the entire top five.[\[131\]](#cite_note-137)

In the United States, _Midnights_ became Swift's record-extending fifth album to sell one million first-week copies after five days of availability.[\[132\]](#cite_note-138) It debuted atop the [_Billboard_ 200](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billboard_200 "Billboard 200") with first-week units of 1.578 million, consisting of 1.14 million sales and 549.26 million streams,[\[133\]](#cite_note-Caulfield-2022a-139) tying her with [Barbra Streisand](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barbra_Streisand "Barbra Streisand") for the most number-one albums for a female artist (11).[\[133\]](#cite_note-Caulfield-2022a-139) _Midnights_ was the best-selling album of 2022, the second-best-selling album of 2023, and the second-most-consumed album of both years.[\[134\]](#cite_note-140) Swift became the first artist to have a [yearly best-seller](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_best-selling_albums_by_year_in_the_United_States "List of best-selling albums by year in the United States") six times since [Luminate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luminate_\(company\) "Luminate (company)") tracked US music sales in 1991.[\[107\]](#cite_note-Caulfield-2023a-113) _Midnights_ spent six weeks atop the _Billboard_ 200,[\[125\]](#cite_note-Caulfield-2023b-131) and 68 weeks in the top 10, the longest run in the top 10 for Swift.[\[135\]](#cite_note-141) Its songs, led by "Anti-Hero", made Swift the first artist to occupy the entire top 10 of the _Billboard_ Hot 100 the same week;[\[117\]](#cite_note-Trust-2022-123) all 20 tracks from the _3am Edition_ charted in the top 45.[\[136\]](#cite_note-142) "Anti-Hero" and _Midnights_ marked the fourth time Swift had a number-one album and song simultaneously.[\[117\]](#cite_note-Trust-2022-123) It had sold 2.814 million US copies by January 2024.[\[137\]](#cite_note-143) In September 2025, the [Recording Industry Association of America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Recording_Industry_Association_of_America "Recording Industry Association of America") (RIAA) [certified](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RIAA_certification "RIAA certification") the album seven-times platinum, denoting seven million [album-equivalent units](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Album-equivalent_units "Album-equivalent units").[\[138\]](#cite_note-RIAA-144)

_Midnights_ debuted at number one on the album charts in at least 14 countries, including Belgium, Canada, Finland, France, Germany, Italy, Ireland, the Netherlands, New Zealand, Norway, and Sweden.[\[130\]](#cite_note-Young-2022-136) It was Swift's first number-one album in France and Germany[\[139\]](#cite_note-145)[\[140\]](#cite_note-146) and made her the best-selling foreign artist in China of 2022 after selling nearly 250,000 copies within one day.[\[141\]](#cite_note-147) On the [Australian charts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Australian_charts "Australian charts"), _Midnights_ was Swift's 10th consecutive number-one album,[\[142\]](#cite_note-148) and its tracks made her the first artist to have nine songs on the top 10 of the singles chart the same week.[\[143\]](#cite_note-149) In the United Kingdom, _Midnights_ sold over 140,000 units in its first three days to become the fastest-selling album of 2022.[\[144\]](#cite_note-150) It debuted atop the [UK Albums Chart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UK_Albums_Chart "UK Albums Chart") with 204,000 units, helping Swift achieve the shortest duration (10 years) for a female act to accumulate nine UK number-one albums.[\[145\]](#cite_note-151) _Midnights_ spent five weeks atop the UK Albums Chart.[\[146\]](#cite_note-152) It sold 80,000 vinyl copies in 2022, the highest annual figure for an album in the 21st century, propelling total UK vinyl sales past CD sales for the first time since 1987.[\[147\]](#cite_note-153)

According to [Universal Music Group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Universal_Music_Group "Universal Music Group"), the album crossed three million album-equivalent units in its first week and six million in two months.[\[148\]](#cite_note-154) [Bloomberg News](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bloomberg_News "Bloomberg News") reported that the album generated $230 million in sales for Universal in 2022, accounting for 3% of their annual revenue—the highest from any artist.[\[149\]](#cite_note-155) The [International Federation of the Phonographic Industry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Federation_of_the_Phonographic_Industry "International Federation of the Phonographic Industry") (IFPI) recognized _Midnights_ as the second-most-consumed album of 2022; it ranked third in pure sales (first in vinyl sales) and fifth in streams; they named Swift the [Global Recording Artist of 2022](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Global_Recording_Artist_of_the_Year "Global Recording Artist of the Year"), which made her the first act to win the accolade three times (after 2014 and 2019).[\[150\]](#cite_note-156)[\[151\]](#cite_note-157) In the IFPI's 2023 report, _Midnights_ was the year's fourth-most-consumed album (third in bot
