_**Evermore**_ (stylized in [all lowercase](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/All_lowercase "All lowercase")) is the ninth studio album by the American singer-songwriter [Taylor Swift](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taylor_Swift "Taylor Swift"). It was [surprise-released](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Surprise_album "Surprise album") on December 11, 2020, through [Republic Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republic_Records "Republic Records"). Swift conceived _Evermore_ as a "sister record" to its predecessor, _[Folklore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Folklore_\(Taylor_Swift_album\) "Folklore (Taylor Swift album)")_, which had been released in July. She recorded _Evermore_ mainly with [Aaron Dessner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aaron_Dessner "Aaron Dessner") at his Long Pond Studio in the [Hudson Valley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hudson_Valley "Hudson Valley").

_Evermore_ expands on _Folklore_'s [escapist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Escapism "Escapism") fantasy songwriting with fictional narratives and delves into the imaginary world Swift had ideated while self-isolating during the [COVID-19 pandemic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/COVID-19_pandemic "COVID-19 pandemic"). The lyrics depict uneasy emotions like longing, grief, nostalgia, and regret, which stem from unhappy endings caused by complications like forbidden love, divorce, and infidelity. _Evermore_ features an [acoustic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Acoustic_music "Acoustic music") and atmospheric [alternative pop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alternative_pop "Alternative pop"), [chamber rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chamber_rock "Chamber rock"), [folk-pop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Folk-pop "Folk-pop"), [indie folk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indie_folk "Indie folk"), and [indie rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indie_rock "Indie rock") soundscape. Its spare arrangements and [orchestrations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orchestration "Orchestration") consist of [fingerpicked](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fingerpick "Fingerpick") guitars, pianos, [strings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/String_section "String section"), subtle [synths](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Synths "Synths"), and [programmed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Programming_\(music\) "Programming (music)") drums. [Haim](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haim_\(band\) "Haim (band)"), [the National](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_National_\(band\) "The National (band)"), and [Bon Iver](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bon_Iver "Bon Iver") appear as featured artists.

_Evermore_ was supported by three [singles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Single_\(music\) "Single (music)"), each released to a different [radio format](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radio_format "Radio format") in the United States. "[Willow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Willow_\(song\) "Willow (song)")", released to [contemporary hit radio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Contemporary_hit_radio "Contemporary hit radio"), peaked atop the [_Billboard_ Hot 100](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billboard_Hot_100 "Billboard Hot 100") chart, while "[No Body, No Crime](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/No_Body,_No_Crime "No Body, No Crime")" and "[Coney Island](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coney_Island_\(Taylor_Swift_song\) "Coney Island (Taylor Swift song)")" were released to [country](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Country_radio "Country radio") and [alternative](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adult_album_alternative "Adult album alternative") radio. _Evermore_ reached number one and was [certified](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Music_recording_certification "Music recording certification") multi-platinum in Australia, Canada, New Zealand, and the United Kingdom. In the United States, it was Swift's eighth consecutive number-one debut on the [_Billboard_ 200](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billboard_200 "Billboard 200") chart and was the best-selling alternative album of 2021, being [certified](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RIAA_certification "RIAA certification") four-times platinum by the [Recording Industry Association of America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Recording_Industry_Association_of_America "Recording Industry Association of America").

[Music critics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Music_critics "Music critics") opined that _Evermore_ was musically bold and experimental while expanding on the styles of _Folklore._ Many reviews lauded Swift's songwriting, deeming the character studies intricate and the narratives well-constructed; several were more reserved in their praise and considered the album less groundbreaking than its predecessor. _Evermore_ appeared in various publications' rankings of the best albums of 2020, and some listed it alongside _Folklore_. At the [64th Annual Grammy Awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/64th_Annual_Grammy_Awards "64th Annual Grammy Awards") in 2022, _Evermore_ was nominated for [Album of the Year](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grammy_Award_for_Album_of_the_Year "Grammy Award for Album of the Year").

[Taylor Swift](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taylor_Swift "Taylor Swift") wrote and produced her eighth studio album, _[Folklore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Folklore_\(Taylor_Swift_album\) "Folklore (Taylor Swift album)")_, while self-isolating during the [COVID-19 lockdowns](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/COVID-19_lockdowns "COVID-19 lockdowns") in 2020. It was released on July 24, 2020, via [Republic Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republic_Records "Republic Records"). Swift worked on half of the album with [Jack Antonoff](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jack_Antonoff "Jack Antonoff"), whom she had collaborated with since 2014, and the other half with [Aaron Dessner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aaron_Dessner "Aaron Dessner") of [the National](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_National_\(band\) "The National (band)"), a first-time collaborator.[\[1\]](#cite_note-Doyle-2021-1) Swift had been fond of Dessner's works for the National and reached out to him to collaborate in April 2020, without requesting a specific sound. Dessner thought that the National's 2019 album [_I Am Easy to Find_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/I_Am_Easy_to_Find_\(album\) "I Am Easy to Find (album)") could have been a subconscious influence.[\[2\]](#cite_note-Rao-2020-2)

Other first-time collaborators were Dessner's brother [Bryce Dessner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bryce_Dessner "Bryce Dessner"),[\[a\]](#cite_note-3) who [orchestrated](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orchestrated "Orchestrated") several tracks; [Justin Vernon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Justin_Vernon "Justin Vernon") of the [indie folk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indie_folk "Indie folk") band [Bon Iver](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bon_Iver "Bon Iver"), and [Joe Alwyn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Alwyn "Joe Alwyn") (credited under the pseudonym William Bowery)—her boyfriend at the time—who co-wrote several songs.[\[2\]](#cite_note-Rao-2020-2) Due to lockdown restrictions, Swift recorded her vocals in her home studio in Los Angeles and sent audio files to Dessner and Antonoff, who operated from their studios on the [United States East Coast](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_East_Coast "United States East Coast"). _Folklore_'s indie folk and [alternative rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alternative_rock "Alternative rock") sounds, and its fictional songwriting with imaginary characters and narratives, were new aspects of Swift's artistry.[\[3\]](#cite_note-Light-2020-4)[\[4\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKimbro202413-5) The critical acclaim that _Folklore_ received encouraged Swift to continue experimenting with its styles.[\[5\]](#cite_note-Countryman-2020-6)

In September 2020, Swift, Antonoff, and Dessner convened to film the documentary _[Folklore: The Long Pond Studio Sessions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Folklore:_The_Long_Pond_Studio_Sessions "Folklore: The Long Pond Studio Sessions")_ in person at Dessner's Long Pond Studios in the [Hudson Valley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hudson_Valley "Hudson Valley"), one of the recording locations of _Folklore_. After filming, the three continued writing songs spontaneously during their stay at Long Pond.[\[1\]](#cite_note-Doyle-2021-1)[\[6\]](#cite_note-DessnerBB-7) Dessner described their collaboration as a "weird avalanche"[\[6\]](#cite_note-DessnerBB-7) and a natural extension of their work on _Folklore_, but with more room for experimentation, as the two did not subject themselves to limitations.[\[7\]](#cite_note-DessnerRS-8) He would send Swift instrumentals, and she would write the lyrics to them and send the songs back to him.[\[1\]](#cite_note-Doyle-2021-1)[\[7\]](#cite_note-DessnerRS-8) After Swift, Alwyn, and Vernon had written the song "Evermore", Dessner concluded that they were working on a new album.[\[7\]](#cite_note-DessnerRS-8)

## Writing and recording

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Evermore&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Writing and recording")\]

[![Aaron Dessner in a blue shirt playing a guitar onstage](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/81/Aaron_Dessner_%2828677721700%29.jpg/250px-Aaron_Dessner_%2828677721700%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Aaron_Dessner_\(28677721700\).jpg)

Swift recorded much of _Evermore_ with [Aaron Dessner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aaron_Dessner "Aaron Dessner") (pictured in 2016) at his Long Pond Studio in the [Hudson Valley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hudson_Valley "Hudson Valley").

On _Evermore_'s standard edition, Dessner produced 14 tracks (including four co-produced with Swift and one with Bryce), and Antonoff co-produced one with Swift.[\[8\]](#cite_note-Swift-2020-9) According to Dessner, he was attuned to Swift's way of structuring a song with [verses](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Verse_\(music\) "Verse (music)"), [refrains](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Refrain "Refrain"), and [bridges](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bridge_\(music\) "Bridge (music)"), and thus did not edit her outputs much. While her vocals for _Folklore_ were processed remotely, Swift recorded many of her vocals for _Evermore_ in person at Long Pond, using Dessner's [Telefunken](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Telefunken "Telefunken") microphone and [Siemens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siemens "Siemens") [preamplifiers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Preamplifier "Preamplifier").[\[1\]](#cite_note-Doyle-2021-1) In late 2020, when COVID restrictions kept studios closed in England, Dessner arranged for her to quarantine and record an extended session at Scarlet Pimpernel Studios at Marcus Mumford's home in [Devon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Devon "Devon").[\[9\]](#cite_note-Khalifeh-10)[\[10\]](#cite_note-11) According to Swift, she recorded "five or six" songs during this stay.[\[9\]](#cite_note-Khalifeh-10) Other collaborators, such as Vernon and Bryce, collaborated virtually due to pandemic restrictions.[\[5\]](#cite_note-Countryman-2020-6) Given Swift's international popularity, they recorded the album in secrecy, using passwords, [data encryption](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Data_encryption "Data encryption"), and specific communications when sharing [mixes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Audio_mixing_\(recorded_music\) "Audio mixing (recorded music)") of the tracks.[\[1\]](#cite_note-Doyle-2021-1) For songs that feature orchestration, Dessner sent Bryce [chord charts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chord_chart "Chord chart"), and Bryce orchestrated the songs from his studio in [Biarritz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Biarritz "Biarritz"), France, before sending them back to Dessner, who then coordinated other musicians to record instruments individually from their home studios.[\[1\]](#cite_note-Doyle-2021-1)[\[11\]](#cite_note-12)

Several _Evermore_ tracks were created from scratch.[\[1\]](#cite_note-Doyle-2021-1)[\[6\]](#cite_note-DessnerBB-7) Swift wrote two tracks, "Closure" and "[Dorothea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dorothea_\(song\) "Dorothea (song)")", for Dessner and Vernon's [supergroup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supergroup_\(music\) "Supergroup (music)") [Big Red Machine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Big_Red_Machine_\(band\) "Big Red Machine (band)"); the songs were eventually recorded for _Evermore_.[\[6\]](#cite_note-DessnerBB-7) For "Closure", Vernon played a drum [loop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loop_\(music\) "Loop (music)"), and Dessner added piano, imagining it as a track in [5/4 time](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/5/4_time "5/4 time"). Dessner pinpointed "Closure" as the track that opened up more possibilities for the album, in that Swift and the production team did not subject themselves to any limitations.[\[1\]](#cite_note-Doyle-2021-1) Dessner composed "Westerly", an instrumental track named after the town of [Westerly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Westerly,_Rhode_Island "Westerly, Rhode Island"), where Swift's [Rhode Island](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhode_Island "Rhode Island") home is located. Swift subsequently spent an hour writing what became "[Willow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Willow_\(song\) "Willow (song)")" on that instrumental.[\[7\]](#cite_note-DessnerRS-8) "[No Body, No Crime](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/No_Body,_No_Crime "No Body, No Crime")" is the only _Evermore_ track that Swift wrote without collaborators;[\[8\]](#cite_note-Swift-2020-9) she wrote it on a rubber-bridge guitar and sent Dessner a [voice memo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Voice_Memos "Voice Memos"), which he produced. The track's feature artist, the [pop rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pop_rock "Pop rock") band [Haim](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haim_\(band\) "Haim (band)"), recorded their vocals at [Ariel Rechtshaid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ariel_Rechtshaid "Ariel Rechtshaid")'s Los Angeles home and forwarded them to Swift and Dessner.[\[7\]](#cite_note-DessnerRS-8)

Other tracks were Dessner's works he had created for his own projects or _Folklore_.[\[6\]](#cite_note-DessnerBB-7) "['Tis the Damn Season](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/'Tis_the_Damn_Season "'Tis the Damn Season")" was a product of Swift's songwriting while she was drunk and Dessner's instrumental track, which he had written "a long time ago".[\[6\]](#cite_note-DessnerBB-7)[\[7\]](#cite_note-DessnerRS-8) "[Coney Island](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coney_Island_\(Taylor_Swift_song\) "Coney Island (Taylor Swift song)")" was based on a track that Dessner and Bryce had written for the National. Swift and Alwyn wrote the lyrics to it, and the National's lead singer, [Matt Berninger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matt_Berninger "Matt Berninger"), duetted with Swift while other members played instruments, including the drums, pocket piano, and bass.[\[7\]](#cite_note-DessnerRS-8) The bridge of "[Marjorie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marjorie_\(song\) "Marjorie (song)")" [samples](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sampling_\(music\) "Sampling (music)") the [drone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Drone_\(sound\) "Drone (sound)") from _Folklore_'s "[Peace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peace_\(Taylor_Swift_song\) "Peace (Taylor Swift song)")"; Swift wrote "Marjorie" about her maternal grandmother, [Marjorie Finlay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marjorie_Finlay "Marjorie Finlay"), whose [operatic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operatic "Operatic") vocals were also sampled.[\[12\]](#cite_note-Lowe-2020-13) Dessner had started composing "Right Where You Left Me" and "[Happiness](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Happiness_\(Taylor_Swift_song\) "Happiness (Taylor Swift song)")" for Big Red Machine in 2019. Swift finished writing and recording the two songs as the last two for _Evermore_;[\[7\]](#cite_note-DessnerRS-8) "Happiness" was completed six days before the album was [mastered](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mastered "Mastered").[\[13\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKimbro202420-14) All 17 tracks were mixed by Jonathan Low at Long Pond.[\[7\]](#cite_note-DessnerRS-8)[\[8\]](#cite_note-Swift-2020-9)

### Music and production

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Evermore&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Music and production")\]

![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/cb/Gnome-mime-audio-openclipart.svg/60px-Gnome-mime-audio-openclipart.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)

Swift envisioned _Evermore_ as a nostalgic fall and winter album, as opposed to _Folklore_ as a spring and summer record.[\[7\]](#cite_note-DessnerRS-8)[\[15\]](#cite_note-Crone-2020-16) As with _Folklore_, _Evermore_ explores atmospheric folk and [indie rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indie_rock "Indie rock") styles that were different from Swift's previous [country](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Country_music "Country music") and [synth-pop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Synth-pop "Synth-pop") releases,[\[1\]](#cite_note-Doyle-2021-1)[\[16\]](#cite_note-17) showcased through the subdued and nuanced production and relaxed pacing over straightforward, arena-friendly [hooks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hook_\(music\) "Hook (music)").[\[3\]](#cite_note-Light-2020-4)[\[17\]](#cite_note-Independent-18)[\[18\]](#cite_note-Telegraph-19)[\[19\]](#cite_note-20)[\[20\]](#cite_note-21) The album incorporates [acoustic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Acoustic_music "Acoustic music") and atmospheric [alternative pop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alternative_pop "Alternative pop"),[\[21\]](#cite_note-Wheeler-2020-22) [chamber rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chamber_rock "Chamber rock"),[\[22\]](#cite_note-LAtimes-23) [folk-pop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Folk-pop "Folk-pop"),[\[23\]](#cite_note-24) indie folk,[\[24\]](#cite_note-25) and indie rock styles,[\[25\]](#cite_note-26) with [chamber pop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chamber_pop "Chamber pop") embellishments,[\[26\]](#cite_note-Willman-2020a-27) bringing forth an introspective listening experience.[\[15\]](#cite_note-Crone-2020-16)[\[27\]](#cite_note-28)[\[28\]](#cite_note-29) The music critic [Steven Hyden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steven_Hyden "Steven Hyden") wrote in _[Uproxx](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uproxx "Uproxx")_ that the album exuded "wintery-country vibes".[\[29\]](#cite_note-Hyden-2020-30) Comparing _Evermore_ to _Folklore_, _[Stereogum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stereogum "Stereogum")_'s Tom Breihan opined that the music of _Evermore_ is straightforward "indie", while that of _Folklore_ is "indie"–styled pop music.[\[30\]](#cite_note-Breihan-2020-31)

Dessner's compositions are based on both acoustic and electronic instruments,[\[22\]](#cite_note-LAtimes-23) largely characterized by [programmed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Programming_\(music\) "Programming (music)") drum sounds using the [iOS app](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IOS_app "IOS app") FunkBox or [analog drum generators](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Analog_synthesizer "Analog synthesizer") such as the Vermona DRM1, the [Roland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roland_Corporation "Roland Corporation") TR-8 and TR-8s, and the [Teenage Engineering OP-1](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teenage_Engineering_OP-1 "Teenage Engineering OP-1"); layered electric guitars; and piano-based arrangements using a [Yamaha U1](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yamaha_Corporation "Yamaha Corporation") [upright piano](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Upright_piano "Upright piano").[\[1\]](#cite_note-Doyle-2021-1) Bryce added orchestration to 13 songs.[\[8\]](#cite_note-Swift-2020-9) Compared to _Folklore_, _Evermore_ retains the [minimal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minimal_music "Minimal music") soundscape and spare arrangements[\[31\]](#cite_note-Annie-2020-32)[\[32\]](#cite_note-Pareles-2020-33) but is less consistent and more experimental: it has a more spacious [ambience](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ambient_music "Ambient music")[\[33\]](#cite_note-Wilson-2020-34) and its songs contain looser structures and [textures](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texture_\(music\) "Texture (music)")[\[3\]](#cite_note-Light-2020-4) and use varied instruments,[\[34\]](#cite_note-Barna-2020-35) namely [fingerpicked](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fingerpick "Fingerpick") or plucked guitars, [glockenspiel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glockenspiel "Glockenspiel"), [modular synthesizers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modular_synthesizer "Modular synthesizer"), [strings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/String_instrument "String instrument"), and subtle layers of [Mellotrons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mellotron "Mellotron"), [French horns](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_horn "French horn"), and [flutes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flute "Flute").[\[35\]](#cite_note-Guardian-36)[\[26\]](#cite_note-Willman-2020a-27)[\[36\]](#cite_note-Ryan-2020a-37)

Swift's vocals in _Evermore_ are generally breathy and soft, accompanied by layered backing vocals,[\[18\]](#cite_note-Telegraph-19)[\[22\]](#cite_note-LAtimes-23) and deliver the songs in a conversational tone.[\[37\]](#cite_note-Rodgers-2020-38) In a profile for _[Sound on Sound](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sound_on_Sound "Sound on Sound")_, Tom Doyle wrote that Swift's voice "is very much front and centre and high in the mix, and generally sounds fairly dry".[\[1\]](#cite_note-Doyle-2021-1) Dessner processed Swift's vocals such that they retained what he described as a "warmth" that he found lacking in "pop-oriented records" to sound "very bright and \[...\] cut really well on the radio". The final song mixes were often the unedited mixes, such as the case of "Willow": Dessner said that the production team "settled back almost to the point where it began".[\[1\]](#cite_note-Doyle-2021-1) According to the [music theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Music_theory "Music theory") professor Alyssa Barna, both Swift's singing and the song's arrangements embrace flat [dynamics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dynamics_\(music\) "Dynamics (music)") with little shifts in tempo or volume, and a static [timbre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timbre "Timbre") that remains consistent throughout each track: her timbre sounds "breathy and bright" when she sings in her upper [register](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Register_\(music\) "Register (music)") and "full and dark" in her lower.[\[34\]](#cite_note-Barna-2020-35)

[![The cover of 1938 book Rebecca](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/5/55/Rebecca-FE.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail_unscaled)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Rebecca-FE.jpg)

[![The cover of 1925 book The Great Gatsby](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/7a/The_Great_Gatsby_Cover_1925_Retouched.jpg/250px-The_Great_Gatsby_Cover_1925_Retouched.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:The_Great_Gatsby_Cover_1925_Retouched.jpg)

_Evermore_ expanded on the imaginary world that Swift had ideated when creating _Folklore_:[\[38\]](#cite_note-SMH-39) its songs incorporate fictional narratives and characters not based on Swift's personal experience—a deviation from the autobiographical songwriting that she had been known for.[\[30\]](#cite_note-Breihan-2020-31)[\[39\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHurley2024182-40) _Evermore_ contains intertextual concepts, language, and imagery with _Folklore_, such as fragmented memories, cabin-like settings, and shifting scenes of nature, including seascapes, forests, cliffs, and cosmic phenomena.[\[39\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHurley2024182-40)[\[40\]](#cite_note-Opperman-2021-41) Also in the same vein as _Folklore_, _Evermore_ was influenced by authors of [modernist literature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modernist_literature "Modernist literature"), such as the poets [Robert Frost](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Frost "Robert Frost") ("'Tis the Damn Season") and [Emily Dickinson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emily_Dickinson "Emily Dickinson") ("Ivy"), and the writer [F. Scott Fitzgerald](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/F._Scott_Fitzgerald "F. Scott Fitzgerald") ("Happiness").[\[41\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTESmith202478–80Geary2024135-42)

In an [Apple Music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_Music "Apple Music") interview with [Zane Lowe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zane_Lowe "Zane Lowe") in December 2020, Swift detailed the relationship between _Folklore_ and _Evermore_, which she designated as "sister records": whereas _Folklore_ deals with "conflict resolution" and reconciliations, _Evermore_ explores "endings of all sorts, sizes and shapes" and the painful aftermath.[\[12\]](#cite_note-Lowe-2020-13) It details multiple themes related to unfulfilled romance—forbidden love, neglect, divorce, and infidelity[\[18\]](#cite_note-Telegraph-19)[\[42\]](#cite_note-Clash-43)—in addition to other painful endings such as fallen friendships and unrealized self-actualization.[\[43\]](#cite_note-44) Narrated from the perspectives of complicated women who construct their stories from distant or recent memories,[\[31\]](#cite_note-Annie-2020-32)[\[44\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHurley2024184-45) the songs are set in winter, particularly events related to the [Christmas and holiday season](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christmas_and_holiday_season "Christmas and holiday season") such as returning to one's hometown during a weekend, a [Christmas dinner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christmas_dinner "Christmas dinner"), and a wrenching December that leaves one "feeling unmoored", as depicted in the title track.[\[31\]](#cite_note-Annie-2020-32)

_[Slate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slate_\(magazine\) "Slate (magazine)")_'s [Carl Wilson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Wilson_\(writer\) "Carl Wilson (writer)") dubbed _Evermore_ an [anthology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anthology "Anthology") without an integrated storyline,[\[33\]](#cite_note-Wilson-2020-34) while Hyden and _[The A.V. Club](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_A.V._Club "The A.V. Club")_'s [Annie Zaleski](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Annie_Zaleski "Annie Zaleski") contended that the wintry settings established a coherent throughline.[\[29\]](#cite_note-Hyden-2020-30)[\[31\]](#cite_note-Annie-2020-32) Compared to the restraint of _Folklore_, _Evermore_ is more uninhibited and playful, demonstrated through tracks like "No Body, No Crime", "[Long Story Short](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Long_Story_Short_\(Taylor_Swift_song\) "Long Story Short (Taylor Swift song)")", and "Dorothea",[\[45\]](#cite_note-NME-46)[\[46\]](#cite_note-AllMusic-47) although most of the songs' narratives do not have [happy endings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Happy_ending "Happy ending").[\[15\]](#cite_note-Crone-2020-16)[\[47\]](#cite_note-RS-48) The overall mood of _Evermore_, nonetheless, is hopeful and warm, amidst the wintry settings and bittersweet feelings.[\[26\]](#cite_note-Willman-2020a-27)[\[31\]](#cite_note-Annie-2020-32)[\[46\]](#cite_note-AllMusic-47) In the view of the English literature scholar Maria Juko, while the title _Evermore_ suggests the lasting legacy of the tales that have become folklore, the album's content questions the concept of eternity.[\[48\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEJuko2024240-49)

_**Evermore**_ (stylized in [all lowercase](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/All_lowercase "All lowercase")) is the ninth studio album by the American singer-songwriter [Taylor Swift](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taylor_Swift "Taylor Swift"). It was [surprise-released](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Surprise_album "Surprise album") on December 11, 2020, through [Republic Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republic_Records "Republic Records"). Swift conceived _Evermore_ as a "sister record" to its predecessor, _[Folklore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Folklore_\(Taylor_Swift_album\) "Folklore (Taylor Swift album)")_, which had been released in July. She recorded _Evermore_ mainly with [Aaron Dessner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aaron_Dessner "Aaron Dessner") at his Long Pond Studio in the [Hudson Valley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hudson_Valley "Hudson Valley").

_Evermore_ expands on _Folklore_'s [escapist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Escapism "Escapism") fantasy songwriting with fictional narratives and delves into the imaginary world Swift had ideated while self-isolating during the [COVID-19 pandemic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/COVID-19_pandemic "COVID-19 pandemic"). The lyrics depict uneasy emotions like longing, grief, nostalgia, and regret, which stem from unhappy endings caused by complications like forbidden love, divorce, and infidelity. _Evermore_ features an [acoustic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Acoustic_music "Acoustic music") and atmospheric [alternative pop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alternative_pop "Alternative pop"), [chamber rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chamber_rock "Chamber rock"), [folk-pop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Folk-pop "Folk-pop"), [indie folk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indie_folk "Indie folk"), and [indie rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indie_rock "Indie rock") soundscape. Its spare arrangements and [orchestrations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orchestration "Orchestration") consist of [fingerpicked](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fingerpick "Fingerpick") guitars, pianos, [strings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/String_section "String section"), subtle [synths](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Synths "Synths"), and [programmed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Programming_\(music\) "Programming (music)") drums. [Haim](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haim_\(band\) "Haim (band)"), [the National](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_National_\(band\) "The National (band)"), and [Bon Iver](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bon_Iver "Bon Iver") appear as featured artists.

_Evermore_ was supported by three [singles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Single_\(music\) "Single (music)"), each released to a different [radio format](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radio_format "Radio format") in the United States. "[Willow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Willow_\(song\) "Willow (song)")", released to [contemporary hit radio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Contemporary_hit_radio "Contemporary hit radio"), peaked atop the [_Billboard_ Hot 100](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billboard_Hot_100 "Billboard Hot 100") chart, while "[No Body, No Crime](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/No_Body,_No_Crime "No Body, No Crime")" and "[Coney Island](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coney_Island_\(Taylor_Swift_song\) "Coney Island (Taylor Swift song)")" were released to [country](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Country_radio "Country radio") and [alternative](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adult_album_alternative "Adult album alternative") radio. _Evermore_ reached number one and was [certified](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Music_recording_certification "Music recording certification") multi-platinum in Australia, Canada, New Zealand, and the United Kingdom. In the United States, it was Swift's eighth consecutive number-one debut on the [_Billboard_ 200](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billboard_200 "Billboard 200") chart and was the best-selling alternative album of 2021, being [certified](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RIAA_certification "RIAA certification") four-times platinum by the [Recording Industry Association of America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Recording_Industry_Association_of_America "Recording Industry Association of America").

[Music critics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Music_critics "Music critics") opined that _Evermore_ was musically bold and experimental while expanding on the styles of _Folklore._ Many reviews lauded Swift's songwriting, deeming the character studies intricate and the narratives well-constructed; several were more reserved in their praise and considered the album less groundbreaking than its predecessor. _Evermore_ appeared in various publications' rankings of the best albums of 2020, and some listed it alongside _Folklore_. At the [64th Annual Grammy Awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/64th_Annual_Grammy_Awards "64th Annual Grammy Awards") in 2022, _Evermore_ was nominated for [Album of the Year](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grammy_Award_for_Album_of_the_Year "Grammy Award for Album of the Year").

[Taylor Swift](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taylor_Swift "Taylor Swift") wrote and produced her eighth studio album, _[Folklore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Folklore_\(Taylor_Swift_album\) "Folklore (Taylor Swift album)")_, while self-isolating during the [COVID-19 lockdowns](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/COVID-19_lockdowns "COVID-19 lockdowns") in 2020. It was released on July 24, 2020, via [Republic Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republic_Records "Republic Records"). Swift worked on half of the album with [Jack Antonoff](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jack_Antonoff "Jack Antonoff"), whom she had collaborated with since 2014, and the other half with [Aaron Dessner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aaron_Dessner "Aaron Dessner") of [the National](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_National_\(band\) "The National (band)"), a first-time collaborator.[\[1\]](#cite_note-Doyle-2021-1) Swift had been fond of Dessner's works for the National and reached out to him to collaborate in April 2020, without requesting a specific sound. Dessner thought that the National's 2019 album [_I Am Easy to Find_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/I_Am_Easy_to_Find_\(album\) "I Am Easy to Find (album)") could have been a subconscious influence.[\[2\]](#cite_note-Rao-2020-2)

Other first-time collaborators were Dessner's brother [Bryce Dessner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bryce_Dessner "Bryce Dessner"),[\[a\]](#cite_note-3) who [orchestrated](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orchestrated "Orchestrated") several tracks; [Justin Vernon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Justin_Vernon "Justin Vernon") of the [indie folk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indie_folk "Indie folk") band [Bon Iver](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bon_Iver "Bon Iver"), and [Joe Alwyn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Alwyn "Joe Alwyn") (credited under the pseudonym William Bowery)—her boyfriend at the time—who co-wrote several songs.[\[2\]](#cite_note-Rao-2020-2) Due to lockdown restrictions, Swift recorded her vocals in her home studio in Los Angeles and sent audio files to Dessner and Antonoff, who operated from their studios on the [United States East Coast](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_East_Coast "United States East Coast"). _Folklore_'s indie folk and [alternative rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alternative_rock "Alternative rock") sounds, and its fictional songwriting with imaginary characters and narratives, were new aspects of Swift's artistry.[\[3\]](#cite_note-Light-2020-4)[\[4\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKimbro202413-5) The critical acclaim that _Folklore_ received encouraged Swift to continue experimenting with its styles.[\[5\]](#cite_note-Countryman-2020-6)

In September 2020, Swift, Antonoff, and Dessner convened to film the documentary _[Folklore: The Long Pond Studio Sessions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Folklore:_The_Long_Pond_Studio_Sessions "Folklore: The Long Pond Studio Sessions")_ in person at Dessner's Long Pond Studios in the [Hudson Valley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hudson_Valley "Hudson Valley"), one of the recording locations of _Folklore_. After filming, the three continued writing songs spontaneously during their stay at Long Pond.[\[1\]](#cite_note-Doyle-2021-1)[\[6\]](#cite_note-DessnerBB-7) Dessner described their collaboration as a "weird avalanche"[\[6\]](#cite_note-DessnerBB-7) and a natural extension of their work on _Folklore_, but with more room for experimentation, as the two did not subject themselves to limitations.[\[7\]](#cite_note-DessnerRS-8) He would send Swift instrumentals, and she would write the lyrics to them and send the songs back to him.[\[1\]](#cite_note-Doyle-2021-1)[\[7\]](#cite_note-DessnerRS-8) After Swift, Alwyn, and Vernon had written the song "Evermore", Dessner concluded that they were working on a new album.[\[7\]](#cite_note-DessnerRS-8)

## Writing and recording

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Evermore&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Writing and recording")\]

[![Aaron Dessner in a blue shirt playing a guitar onstage](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/81/Aaron_Dessner_%2828677721700%29.jpg/250px-Aaron_Dessner_%2828677721700%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Aaron_Dessner_\(28677721700\).jpg)

Swift recorded much of _Evermore_ with [Aaron Dessner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aaron_Dessner "Aaron Dessner") (pictured in 2016) at his Long Pond Studio in the [Hudson Valley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hudson_Valley "Hudson Valley").

On _Evermore_'s standard edition, Dessner produced 14 tracks (including four co-produced with Swift and one with Bryce), and Antonoff co-produced one with Swift.[\[8\]](#cite_note-Swift-2020-9) According to Dessner, he was attuned to Swift's way of structuring a song with [verses](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Verse_\(music\) "Verse (music)"), [refrains](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Refrain "Refrain"), and [bridges](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bridge_\(music\) "Bridge (music)"), and thus did not edit her outputs much. While her vocals for _Folklore_ were processed remotely, Swift recorded many of her vocals for _Evermore_ in person at Long Pond, using Dessner's [Telefunken](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Telefunken "Telefunken") microphone and [Siemens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siemens "Siemens") [preamplifiers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Preamplifier "Preamplifier").[\[1\]](#cite_note-Doyle-2021-1) In late 2020, when COVID restrictions kept studios closed in England, Dessner arranged for her to quarantine and record an extended session at Scarlet Pimpernel Studios at Marcus Mumford's home in [Devon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Devon "Devon").[\[9\]](#cite_note-Khalifeh-10)[\[10\]](#cite_note-11) According to Swift, she recorded "five or six" songs during this stay.[\[9\]](#cite_note-Khalifeh-10) Other collaborators, such as Vernon and Bryce, collaborated virtually due to pandemic restrictions.[\[5\]](#cite_note-Countryman-2020-6) Given Swift's international popularity, they recorded the album in secrecy, using passwords, [data encryption](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Data_encryption "Data encryption"), and specific communications when sharing [mixes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Audio_mixing_\(recorded_music\) "Audio mixing (recorded music)") of the tracks.[\[1\]](#cite_note-Doyle-2021-1) For songs that feature orchestration, Dessner sent Bryce [chord charts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chord_chart "Chord chart"), and Bryce orchestrated the songs from his studio in [Biarritz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Biarritz "Biarritz"), France, before sending them back to Dessner, who then coordinated other musicians to record instruments individually from their home studios.[\[1\]](#cite_note-Doyle-2021-1)[\[11\]](#cite_note-12)

Several _Evermore_ tracks were created from scratch.[\[1\]](#cite_note-Doyle-2021-1)[\[6\]](#cite_note-DessnerBB-7) Swift wrote two tracks, "Closure" and "[Dorothea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dorothea_\(song\) "Dorothea (song)")", for Dessner and Vernon's [supergroup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supergroup_\(music\) "Supergroup (music)") [Big Red Machine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Big_Red_Machine_\(band\) "Big Red Machine (band)"); the songs were eventually recorded for _Evermore_.[\[6\]](#cite_note-DessnerBB-7) For "Closure", Vernon played a drum [loop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loop_\(music\) "Loop (music)"), and Dessner added piano, imagining it as a track in [5/4 time](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/5/4_time "5/4 time"). Dessner pinpointed "Closure" as the track that opened up more possibilities for the album, in that Swift and the production team did not subject themselves to any limitations.[\[1\]](#cite_note-Doyle-2021-1) Dessner composed "Westerly", an instrumental track named after the town of [Westerly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Westerly,_Rhode_Island "Westerly, Rhode Island"), where Swift's [Rhode Island](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhode_Island "Rhode Island") home is located. Swift subsequently spent an hour writing what became "[Willow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Willow_\(song\) "Willow (song)")" on that instrumental.[\[7\]](#cite_note-DessnerRS-8) "[No Body, No Crime](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/No_Body,_No_Crime "No Body, No Crime")" is the only _Evermore_ track that Swift wrote without collaborators;[\[8\]](#cite_note-Swift-2020-9) she wrote it on a rubber-bridge guitar and sent Dessner a [voice memo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Voice_Memos "Voice Memos"), which he produced. The track's feature artist, the [pop rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pop_rock "Pop rock") band [Haim](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haim_\(band\) "Haim (band)"), recorded their vocals at [Ariel Rechtshaid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ariel_Rechtshaid "Ariel Rechtshaid")'s Los Angeles home and forwarded them to Swift and Dessner.[\[7\]](#cite_note-DessnerRS-8)

Other tracks were Dessner's works he had created for his own projects or _Folklore_.[\[6\]](#cite_note-DessnerBB-7) "['Tis the Damn Season](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/'Tis_the_Damn_Season "'Tis the Damn Season")" was a product of Swift's songwriting while she was drunk and Dessner's instrumental track, which he had written "a long time ago".[\[6\]](#cite_note-DessnerBB-7)[\[7\]](#cite_note-DessnerRS-8) "[Coney Island](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coney_Island_\(Taylor_Swift_song\) "Coney Island (Taylor Swift song)")" was based on a track that Dessner and Bryce had written for the National. Swift and Alwyn wrote the lyrics to it, and the National's lead singer, [Matt Berninger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matt_Berninger "Matt Berninger"), duetted with Swift while other members played instruments, including the drums, pocket piano, and bass.[\[7\]](#cite_note-DessnerRS-8) The bridge of "[Marjorie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marjorie_\(song\) "Marjorie (song)")" [samples](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sampling_\(music\) "Sampling (music)") the [drone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Drone_\(sound\) "Drone (sound)") from _Folklore_'s "[Peace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peace_\(Taylor_Swift_song\) "Peace (Taylor Swift song)")"; Swift wrote "Marjorie" about her maternal grandmother, [Marjorie Finlay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marjorie_Finlay "Marjorie Finlay"), whose [operatic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operatic "Operatic") vocals were also sampled.[\[12\]](#cite_note-Lowe-2020-13) Dessner had started composing "Right Where You Left Me" and "[Happiness](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Happiness_\(Taylor_Swift_song\) "Happiness (Taylor Swift song)")" for Big Red Machine in 2019. Swift finished writing and recording the two songs as the last two for _Evermore_;[\[7\]](#cite_note-DessnerRS-8) "Happiness" was completed six days before the album was [mastered](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mastered "Mastered").[\[13\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKimbro202420-14) All 17 tracks were mixed by Jonathan Low at Long Pond.[\[7\]](#cite_note-DessnerRS-8)[\[8\]](#cite_note-Swift-2020-9)

### Music and production

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Evermore&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Music and production")\]

![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/cb/Gnome-mime-audio-openclipart.svg/60px-Gnome-mime-audio-openclipart.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)

Swift envisioned _Evermore_ as a nostalgic fall and winter album, as opposed to _Folklore_ as a spring and summer record.[\[7\]](#cite_note-DessnerRS-8)[\[15\]](#cite_note-Crone-2020-16) As with _Folklore_, _Evermore_ explores atmospheric folk and [indie rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indie_rock "Indie rock") styles that were different from Swift's previous [country](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Country_music "Country music") and [synth-pop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Synth-pop "Synth-pop") releases,[\[1\]](#cite_note-Doyle-2021-1)[\[16\]](#cite_note-17) showcased through the subdued and nuanced production and relaxed pacing over straightforward, arena-friendly [hooks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hook_\(music\) "Hook (music)").[\[3\]](#cite_note-Light-2020-4)[\[17\]](#cite_note-Independent-18)[\[18\]](#cite_note-Telegraph-19)[\[19\]](#cite_note-20)[\[20\]](#cite_note-21) The album incorporates [acoustic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Acoustic_music "Acoustic music") and atmospheric [alternative pop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alternative_pop "Alternative pop"),[\[21\]](#cite_note-Wheeler-2020-22) [chamber rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chamber_rock "Chamber rock"),[\[22\]](#cite_note-LAtimes-23) [folk-pop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Folk-pop "Folk-pop"),[\[23\]](#cite_note-24) indie folk,[\[24\]](#cite_note-25) and indie rock styles,[\[25\]](#cite_note-26) with [chamber pop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chamber_pop "Chamber pop") embellishments,[\[26\]](#cite_note-Willman-2020a-27) bringing forth an introspective listening experience.[\[15\]](#cite_note-Crone-2020-16)[\[27\]](#cite_note-28)[\[28\]](#cite_note-29) The music critic [Steven Hyden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steven_Hyden "Steven Hyden") wrote in _[Uproxx](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uproxx "Uproxx")_ that the album exuded "wintery-country vibes".[\[29\]](#cite_note-Hyden-2020-30) Comparing _Evermore_ to _Folklore_, _[Stereogum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stereogum "Stereogum")_'s Tom Breihan opined that the music of _Evermore_ is straightforward "indie", while that of _Folklore_ is "indie"–styled pop music.[\[30\]](#cite_note-Breihan-2020-31)

Dessner's compositions are based on both acoustic and electronic instruments,[\[22\]](#cite_note-LAtimes-23) largely characterized by [programmed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Programming_\(music\) "Programming (music)") drum sounds using the [iOS app](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IOS_app "IOS app") FunkBox or [analog drum generators](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Analog_synthesizer "Analog synthesizer") such as the Vermona DRM1, the [Roland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roland_Corporation "Roland Corporation") TR-8 and TR-8s, and the [Teenage Engineering OP-1](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teenage_Engineering_OP-1 "Teenage Engineering OP-1"); layered electric guitars; and piano-based arrangements using a [Yamaha U1](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yamaha_Corporation "Yamaha Corporation") [upright piano](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Upright_piano "Upright piano").[\[1\]](#cite_note-Doyle-2021-1) Bryce added orchestration to 13 songs.[\[8\]](#cite_note-Swift-2020-9) Compared to _Folklore_, _Evermore_ retains the [minimal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minimal_music "Minimal music") soundscape and spare arrangements[\[31\]](#cite_note-Annie-2020-32)[\[32\]](#cite_note-Pareles-2020-33) but is less consistent and more experimental: it has a more spacious [ambience](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ambient_music "Ambient music")[\[33\]](#cite_note-Wilson-2020-34) and its songs contain looser structures and [textures](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texture_\(music\) "Texture (music)")[\[3\]](#cite_note-Light-2020-4) and use varied instruments,[\[34\]](#cite_note-Barna-2020-35) namely [fingerpicked](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fingerpick "Fingerpick") or plucked guitars, [glockenspiel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glockenspiel "Glockenspiel"), [modular synthesizers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modular_synthesizer "Modular synthesizer"), [strings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/String_instrument "String instrument"), and subtle layers of [Mellotrons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mellotron "Mellotron"), [French horns](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_horn "French horn"), and [flutes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flute "Flute").[\[35\]](#cite_note-Guardian-36)[\[26\]](#cite_note-Willman-2020a-27)[\[36\]](#cite_note-Ryan-2020a-37)

Swift's vocals in _Evermore_ are generally breathy and soft, accompanied by layered backing vocals,[\[18\]](#cite_note-Telegraph-19)[\[22\]](#cite_note-LAtimes-23) and deliver the songs in a conversational tone.[\[37\]](#cite_note-Rodgers-2020-38) In a profile for _[Sound on Sound](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sound_on_Sound "Sound on Sound")_, Tom Doyle wrote that Swift's voice "is very much front and centre and high in the mix, and generally sounds fairly dry".[\[1\]](#cite_note-Doyle-2021-1) Dessner processed Swift's vocals such that they retained what he described as a "warmth" that he found lacking in "pop-oriented records" to sound "very bright and \[...\] cut really well on the radio". The final song mixes were often the unedited mixes, such as the case of "Willow": Dessner said that the production team "settled back almost to the point where it began".[\[1\]](#cite_note-Doyle-2021-1) According to the [music theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Music_theory "Music theory") professor Alyssa Barna, both Swift's singing and the song's arrangements embrace flat [dynamics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dynamics_\(music\) "Dynamics (music)") with little shifts in tempo or volume, and a static [timbre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timbre "Timbre") that remains consistent throughout each track: her timbre sounds "breathy and bright" when she sings in her upper [register](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Register_\(music\) "Register (music)") and "full and dark" in her lower.[\[34\]](#cite_note-Barna-2020-35)

[![The cover of 1925 book The Great Gatsby](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/7a/The_Great_Gatsby_Cover_1925_Retouched.jpg/250px-The_Great_Gatsby_Cover_1925_Retouched.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:The_Great_Gatsby_Cover_1925_Retouched.jpg)

_Evermore_ expanded on the imaginary world that Swift had ideated when creating _Folklore_:[\[38\]](#cite_note-SMH-39) its songs incorporate fictional narratives and characters not based on Swift's personal experience—a deviation from the autobiographical songwriting that she had been known for.[\[30\]](#cite_note-Breihan-2020-31)[\[39\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHurley2024182-40) _Evermore_ contains intertextual concepts, language, and imagery with _Folklore_, such as fragmented memories, cabin-like settings, and shifting scenes of nature, including seascapes, forests, cliffs, and cosmic phenomena.[\[39\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHurley2024182-40)[\[40\]](#cite_note-Opperman-2021-41) Also in the same vein as _Folklore_, _Evermore_ was influenced by authors of [modernist literature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modernist_literature "Modernist literature"), such as the poets [Robert Frost](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Frost "Robert Frost") ("'Tis the Damn Season") and [Emily Dickinson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emily_Dickinson "Emily Dickinson") ("Ivy"), and the writer [F. Scott Fitzgerald](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/F._Scott_Fitzgerald "F. Scott Fitzgerald") ("Happiness").[\[41\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTESmith202478–80Geary2024135-42)

In an [Apple Music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_Music "Apple Music") interview with [Zane Lowe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zane_Lowe "Zane Lowe") in December 2020, Swift detailed the relationship between _Folklore_ and _Evermore_, which she designated as "sister records": whereas _Folklore_ deals with "conflict resolution" and reconciliations, _Evermore_ explores "endings of all sorts, sizes and shapes" and the painful aftermath.[\[12\]](#cite_note-Lowe-2020-13) It details multiple themes related to unfulfilled romance—forbidden love, neglect, divorce, and infidelity[\[18\]](#cite_note-Telegraph-19)[\[42\]](#cite_note-Clash-43)—in addition to other painful endings such as fallen friendships and unrealized self-actualization.[\[43\]](#cite_note-44) Narrated from the perspectives of complicated women who construct their stories from distant or recent memories,[\[31\]](#cite_note-Annie-2020-32)[\[44\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHurley2024184-45) the songs are set in winter, particularly events related to the [Christmas and holiday season](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christmas_and_holiday_season "Christmas and holiday season") such as returning to one's hometown during a weekend, a [Christmas dinner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christmas_dinner "Christmas dinner"), and a wrenching December that leaves one "feeling unmoored", as depicted in the title track.[\[31\]](#cite_note-Annie-2020-32)

_[Slate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slate_\(magazine\) "Slate (magazine)")_'s [Carl Wilson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Wilson_\(writer\) "Carl Wilson (writer)") dubbed _Evermore_ an [anthology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anthology "Anthology") without an integrated storyline,[\[33\]](#cite_note-Wilson-2020-34) while Hyden and _[The A.V. Club](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_A.V._Club "The A.V. Club")_'s [Annie Zaleski](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Annie_Zaleski "Annie Zaleski") contended that the wintry settings established a coherent throughline.[\[29\]](#cite_note-Hyden-2020-30)[\[31\]](#cite_note-Annie-2020-32) Compared to the restraint of _Folklore_, _Evermore_ is more uninhibited and playful, demonstrated through tracks like "No Body, No Crime", "[Long Story Short](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Long_Story_Short_\(Taylor_Swift_song\) "Long Story Short (Taylor Swift song)")", and "Dorothea",[\[45\]](#cite_note-NME-46)[\[46\]](#cite_note-AllMusic-47) although most of the songs' narratives do not have [happy endings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Happy_ending "Happy ending").[\[15\]](#cite_note-Crone-2020-16)[\[47\]](#cite_note-RS-48) The overall mood of _Evermore_, nonetheless, is hopeful and warm, amidst the wintry settings and bittersweet feelings.[\[26\]](#cite_note-Willman-2020a-27)[\[31\]](#cite_note-Annie-2020-32)[\[46\]](#cite_note-AllMusic-47) In the view of the English literature scholar Maria Juko, while the title _Evermore_ suggests the lasting legacy of the tales that have become folklore, the album's content questions the concept of eternity.[\[48\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEJuko2024240-49)
