_**1989 (Taylor's Version)**_ is the fourth [re-recorded album](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Re-recorded_album "Re-recorded album") by the American singer-songwriter [Taylor Swift](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taylor_Swift "Taylor Swift"). It was released on October 27, 2023, through [Republic Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republic_Records "Republic Records"), as part of Swift's re-recording project following the [2019 dispute over the master recordings of her back catalog](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taylor_Swift_masters_dispute "Taylor Swift masters dispute").

A re-recording of Swift's fifth album, _[1989](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1989_\(album\) "1989 (album)")_ (2014), _1989 (Taylor's Version)_ consists of re-recorded versions of the 16 songs from _1989_'s deluxe edition and five previously unreleased "From the Vault" tracks;[\[a\]](#cite_note-1) extended editions additionally feature the re-recorded versions of the [_One Chance_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/One_Chance_\(film\) "One Chance (film)") soundtrack song "[Sweeter than Fiction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sweeter_than_Fiction "Sweeter than Fiction")" (2013) and the [Kendrick Lamar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kendrick_Lamar "Kendrick Lamar") remix of "[Bad Blood](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bad_Blood_\(Taylor_Swift_song\) "Bad Blood (Taylor Swift song)")" (2015). Swift, [Jack Antonoff](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jack_Antonoff "Jack Antonoff"), and [Christopher Rowe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christopher_Rowe_\(record_producer\) "Christopher Rowe (record producer)") produced the majority of the album; [Ryan Tedder](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ryan_Tedder "Ryan Tedder"), [Noel Zancanella](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Noel_Zancanella "Noel Zancanella"), [Shellback](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shellback_\(record_producer\) "Shellback (record producer)"), and [Imogen Heap](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imogen_Heap "Imogen Heap") reprised their production roles. A 1980s-inspired [synth-pop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Synth-pop "Synth-pop") album, _1989 (Taylor's Version)_ is characterized by [upbeat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beat_\(music\)#Downbeat_and_upbeat "Beat (music)") arrangements of [synthesizers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Synthesizer "Synthesizer") and [percussion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Percussion "Percussion").

Music critics praised _1989 (Taylor's Version)_, with emphasis on the production, Swift's vocals, and the vault tracks. The album topped [record charts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Record_chart "Record chart") in Australia, Canada, and European territories including France, Germany, Italy, Spain, and the United Kingdom. In the United States, _1989 (Taylor's Version)_ marked Swift's 13th number-one album on the [_Billboard_ 200](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billboard_200 "Billboard 200") and record-extending [sixth album to sell over one million first-week copies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_fastest-selling_albums "List of fastest-selling albums"). Seven of its songs concurrently became top-10 entries on the [_Billboard_ Hot 100](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billboard_Hot_100 "Billboard Hot 100"), with the vault tracks "[Is It Over Now?](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Is_It_Over_Now%3F "Is It Over Now?")", "[Now That We Don't Talk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Now_That_We_Don't_Talk "Now That We Don't Talk")", and "['Slut!'](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/"Slut!" "\"Slut!\"")" occupying the top three spots. In 2024, [Apple Music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_Music "Apple Music") placed the album at number 18 on its list of the [100 Best Albums](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_Music_100_Best_Albums "Apple Music 100 Best Albums").

[Taylor Swift](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taylor_Swift "Taylor Swift") released her fifth album, _[1989](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1989_\(album\) "1989 (album)")_, on October 27, 2014, under [Big Machine Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Big_Machine_Records "Big Machine Records"). Inspired by 1980s [synth-pop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Synth-pop "Synth-pop"), Swift conceived _1989_ to recalibrate her artistry to [pop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pop_music "Pop music") after promoting her first four albums to [country radio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Country_radio "Country radio").[\[1\]](#cite_note-Vinson-2014-2) The album received generally positive critical reviews and sold over 10 million copies worldwide.[\[2\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcNutt202078-3)[\[3\]](#cite_note-4) Three of its singles—"[Shake It Off](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shake_It_Off "Shake It Off")", "[Blank Space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blank_Space "Blank Space")", and "[Bad Blood](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bad_Blood_\(Taylor_Swift_song\) "Bad Blood (Taylor Swift song)")"—reached number one on the [_Billboard_ Hot 100](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billboard_Hot_100 "Billboard Hot 100").[\[4\]](#cite_note-5) At the [58th Annual Grammy Awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/58th_Annual_Grammy_Awards "58th Annual Grammy Awards"), _1989_ made Swift the first female musician to win the [Grammy Award for Album of the Year](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grammy_Award_for_Album_of_the_Year "Grammy Award for Album of the Year") twice—her first win was for _[Fearless](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fearless_\(Taylor_Swift_album\) "Fearless (Taylor Swift album)")_ in [2010](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/52nd_Annual_Grammy_Awards "52nd Annual Grammy Awards").[\[5\]](#cite_note-6)

Swift's contract with Big Machine expired in November 2018. She then withdrew from Big Machine and signed a new deal with [Republic Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republic_Records "Republic Records"), which secured her the rights to own the [masters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mastering_\(audio\) "Mastering (audio)") of any new music she would release.[\[6\]](#cite_note-7) In 2019, American music executive [Scooter Braun](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scooter_Braun "Scooter Braun") acquired Big Machine;[\[7\]](#cite_note-8) the ownership of the masters to Swift's first six albums, including _1989_, was transferred to him.[\[8\]](#cite_note-9) In August 2019, Swift spoke against Braun's purchase and announced that she would [re-record](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Re-recording_\(music\) "Re-recording (music)") her first six albums so as to own their masters herself.[\[9\]](#cite_note-10) Swift began the re-recording process in November 2020.[\[10\]](#cite_note-11) _[Fearless (Taylor's Version)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fearless_\(Taylor's_Version\) "Fearless (Taylor's Version)")_, the first of her six re-recorded albums, was released on April 9, 2021, followed by _[Red (Taylor's Version)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_\(Taylor's_Version\) "Red (Taylor's Version)")_ on November 12, 2021,[\[11\]](#cite_note-12)[\[12\]](#cite_note-13) and _[Speak Now (Taylor's Version)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now_\(Taylor's_Version\) "Speak Now (Taylor's Version)")_ on July 7, 2023; all three peaked atop the US [_Billboard_ 200](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billboard_200 "Billboard 200") chart.[\[13\]](#cite_note-14)

Swift released re-recordings of some _1989_ tracks prior to the re-recorded album; all songs feature the additional "Taylor's Version" moniker in their titles. The re-recording of "[Wildest Dreams](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wildest_Dreams_\(Taylor's_Version\) "Wildest Dreams (Taylor's Version)")" was released on September 17, 2021, after the [original version](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wildest_Dreams_\(Taylor_Swift_song\) "Wildest Dreams (Taylor Swift song)") went viral on [TikTok](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TikTok "TikTok").[\[14\]](#cite_note-15) Other tracks were used in films and series: "[This Love](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/This_Love_\(Taylor's_Version\) "This Love (Taylor's Version)")" was released on May 6, 2022, after its snippet featured in the trailer for the series [_The Summer I Turned Pretty_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Summer_I_Turned_Pretty_\(TV_series\) "The Summer I Turned Pretty (TV series)");[\[15\]](#cite_note-16) a snippet of "[Bad Blood](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bad_Blood_\(Taylor's_Version\) "Bad Blood (Taylor's Version)")" appeared in the animated film _[DC League of Super-Pets](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DC_League_of_Super-Pets "DC League of Super-Pets"),_[\[16\]](#cite_note-17) and "[Out of the Woods](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Out_of_the_Woods_\(Taylor's_Version\) "Out of the Woods (Taylor's Version)")" featured in a trailer for [_Migration_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Migration_\(2023_film\) "Migration (2023 film)").[\[17\]](#cite_note-18) On August 9, 2023, at the final Los Angeles show at [SoFi Stadium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SoFi_Stadium "SoFi Stadium") as part of Swift's [Eras Tour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eras_Tour "Eras Tour"), she performed in five new blue outfits, representing the color that Swift's fans associated _1989_ with;[\[18\]](#cite_note-19) during the half-show acoustic set, she announced _1989 (Taylor's Version)_ as her next re-recorded album, set for release on October 27, 2023, exactly nine years after the original release of _1989_.[\[19\]](#cite_note-20)[\[20\]](#cite_note-21)

## Writing and recording

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=1989_\(Taylor%27s_Version\)&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Writing and recording")\]

The standard edition of _1989 (Taylor's Version)_ comprises 21 tracks: re-recordings of the 13 songs from the standard edition of _1989_, as well as the three bonus tracks from the original deluxe edition, and five previously unreleased "From the Vault" songs that were written for the 2014 album but excluded from the final track list.[\[21\]](#cite_note-Caulfield-1M-22) Re-recordings of the "Bad Blood" remix (2015) featuring American rapper [Kendrick Lamar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kendrick_Lamar "Kendrick Lamar") and "[Sweeter than Fiction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sweeter_than_Fiction "Sweeter than Fiction")" (2013), a song Swift and [Jack Antonoff](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jack_Antonoff "Jack Antonoff") contributed to the soundtrack of _[One Chance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/One_Chance_\(film\) "One Chance (film)")_ (2013), were included on extended editions of _1989 (Taylor's Version)_ as bonus tracks.[\[22\]](#cite_note-23)[\[23\]](#cite_note-24)

Most re-recorded tracks were produced by Swift and [Christopher Rowe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christopher_Rowe_\(record_producer\) "Christopher Rowe (record producer)"). The remaining were co-produced by their original producers—Antonoff, [Ryan Tedder](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ryan_Tedder "Ryan Tedder"), [Noel Zancanella](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Noel_Zancanella "Noel Zancanella"), and [Imogen Heap](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imogen_Heap "Imogen Heap"). [Shellback](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shellback_\(record_producer\) "Shellback (record producer)"), who produced multiple songs on _1989_ alongside [Max Martin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Max_Martin "Max Martin"), only produced "Wildest Dreams (Taylor's Version)" with Swift and Rowe, while Martin was not involved in the production of the re-recording.[\[24\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTESomvilleBenoit2025243-25) All of the vault tracks were written and produced by Swift and Antonoff, except "[Say Don't Go](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Say_Don't_Go "Say Don't Go")", which was co-written by the American songwriter [Diane Warren](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diane_Warren "Diane Warren").[\[25\]](#cite_note-26) According to Antonnoff, he could not recall some original sounds that he created, so he asked for help from his [Bleachers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bleachers_\(band\) "Bleachers (band)") bandmates for certain sounds like the "soft synths".[\[26\]](#cite_note-Curto-2024-27)

_1989 (Taylor's Version)_ is a synth-pop album,[\[27\]](#cite_note-Guardian_review-28) with a production composed of upbeat [synthesizers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Synthesizer "Synthesizer") and dynamic [percussions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Percussions "Percussions").[\[28\]](#cite_note-Telegraph-29) According to _[NME](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NME "NME")_, the album has a [1980s](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1980s_in_music "1980s in music")\-inspired synth-pop sound, but is "an evolution of Swift's own sound" rather than a "kitschy pastiche" of [retro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Retro "Retro") influences.[\[29\]](#cite_note-NME_review-30) Various critics have opined that the only sonic difference between _1989_ and _1989 (Taylor's Version)_ is Swift's vocals, which have become technically stronger and richer.[\[b\]](#cite_note-33) According to _[Clash](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clash_\(magazine\) "Clash (magazine)")_'s Alex Berry, the re-recording has a "cleaner" instrumentation.[\[32\]](#cite_note-Clash_review-34) _[Slant Magazine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slant_Magazine "Slant Magazine")_'s Jonathan Keefe identified minor changes: the clicking pen noise on "Blank Space" sounds less like the spring action of a ballpoint pen, the "ah-ah-ah" vocal [hook](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hook_\(music\) "Hook (music)") of "[New Romantics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Romantics_\(song\) "New Romantics (song)")" is more [staccato](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Staccato "Staccato"), the [reverb](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reverb_effect "Reverb effect") on "[Out of the Woods](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Out_of_the_Woods "Out of the Woods")" is more prominent, and the guitar's tone on "[Style](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Style_\(Taylor_Swift_song\) "Style (Taylor Swift song)")" is altered.[\[33\]](#cite_note-Keefe-35)

### "From the Vault" songs

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=1989_\(Taylor%27s_Version\)&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: \"From the Vault\" songs")\]

As with the original album, the vault tracks incorporate production elements that evoke the 1980s-inspired pop sound: reverb, synths, [keyboards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electronic_keyboard "Electronic keyboard"), and percussions.[\[c\]](#cite_note-38) [AllMusic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AllMusic "AllMusic")'s Fred Thomas wrote that the production was reminiscent of late-1980s radio,[\[36\]](#cite_note-allmusicreview-39) and _[The Line of Best Fit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Line_of_Best_Fit "The Line of Best Fit")_'s Kelsey Barnes opined that the vault tracks featured different pop subgenres.[\[31\]](#cite_note-TLOBF_review-32) _[Variety](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Variety_\(magazine\) "Variety (magazine)")_'s Chris Willman and _[Pitchfork](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pitchfork_\(website\) "Pitchfork (website)")_'s Shaad D'Souza opined that their production elements were influenced by the music of Swift's tenth studio album, _[Midnights](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Midnights "Midnights")_ (2022).[\[37\]](#cite_note-40)[\[38\]](#cite_note-Pitchfork-41)

The title of "['Slut!'](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/"Slut!" "\"Slut!\"")" refers to the [slut-shaming](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slut-shaming "Slut-shaming") Swift experienced as a public figure, a result of the media scrutiny on her personal life and serial romantic relationships.[\[39\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTESomvilleBenoit2025244-42) In its lyrics, Swift describes a relationship that she is proud of and does not care how the outside world views it.[\[35\]](#cite_note-Lipshutz-2023-37)[\[40\]](#cite_note-RS_review-43) It is a mid-tempo synth-pop song,[\[41\]](#cite_note-44)[\[42\]](#cite_note-WoodLAT1-45) featuring layered, grainy [analog synthesizers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Analog_synthesizers "Analog synthesizers") and soft backing vocals.[\[39\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTESomvilleBenoit2025244-42)[\[32\]](#cite_note-Clash_review-34) "[Say Don't Go](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Say_Don't_Go "Say Don't Go")" is about Swift hanging on to an unfruitful relationship;[\[28\]](#cite_note-Telegraph-29) it has a reverb-heavy, [pop rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pop_rock "Pop rock") production that consists of isolated vocal patterns, [gated](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gated_reverb "Gated reverb") snare drums, synthesized [Moog bass](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moog_bass "Moog bass") and guitar, and layered keyboard sounds created with a [Mellotron](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mellotron "Mellotron") and analog synths: [Oberheim OB-Xa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oberheim_OB-Xa "Oberheim OB-Xa"), [Yamaha DX100](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yamaha_DX100_\(synthesizer\) "Yamaha DX100 (synthesizer)"), [Juno-6](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roland_Juno-60 "Roland Juno-60"), and [Korg M1](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Korg_M1 "Korg M1").[\[31\]](#cite_note-TLOBF_review-32)[\[42\]](#cite_note-WoodLAT1-45)[\[43\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTESomvilleBenoit2025245-46)

![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/cb/Gnome-mime-audio-openclipart.svg/60px-Gnome-mime-audio-openclipart.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)

The [disco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Disco "Disco") track "[Now That We Don't Talk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Now_That_We_Don't_Talk "Now That We Don't Talk")" incorporates disco [grooves](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Groove_\(music\) "Groove (music)") and [falsetto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Falsetto "Falsetto") vocals in the [chorus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Refrain "Refrain"),[\[31\]](#cite_note-TLOBF_review-32)[\[40\]](#cite_note-RS_review-43) and its lyrics see Swift moving on from an ex-lover while making fun of his lifestyle and tastes.[\[28\]](#cite_note-Telegraph-29) "[Suburban Legends](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suburban_Legends_\(song\) "Suburban Legends (song)")" depicts Swift yearning for a hopeful but unfruitful romance.[\[35\]](#cite_note-Lipshutz-2023-37) It features an insistent disco groove instrumented by layers of synth [arpeggiators](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arpeggiator "Arpeggiator"), a mix of acoustic and programmed drums, and an outro of dissipating synths.[\[35\]](#cite_note-Lipshutz-2023-37)[\[42\]](#cite_note-WoodLAT1-45)[\[44\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTESomvilleBenoit2025247-47) "[Is It Over Now?](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Is_It_Over_Now%3F "Is It Over Now?")" chronicles the end of a relationship, with lyrics about mistakes committed by both partners and the mixed feelings that ensued.[\[35\]](#cite_note-Lipshutz-2023-37)[\[32\]](#cite_note-Clash_review-34)[\[45\]](#cite_note-48) A [synthwave](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Synthwave "Synthwave")\-influenced synth-pop [power ballad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Power_ballad "Power ballad"),[\[46\]](#cite_note-Paste_review-49)[\[47\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTESomvilleBenoit2025247Zaleski2024129-50) it begins with a vocal [hook](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hook_\(music\) "Hook (music)") that resembles sounds of a seagull, created with a [Moog](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moog_synthesizer "Moog synthesizer") model D and a [Juno 6](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roland_Juno-60 "Roland Juno-60"), over atmospheric layers of synths and bass.[\[26\]](#cite_note-Curto-2024-27)[\[44\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTESomvilleBenoit2025247-47) The track progresses with a reverb-heavy soundscape composed of synths and echoing [drum machines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Drum_machines "Drum machines").[\[27\]](#cite_note-Guardian_review-28)[\[48\]](#cite_note-51)[\[30\]](#cite_note-Independent_review-31)

[![Taylor Swift wearing a blue two-piece](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/79/Taylor_Swift_The_Eras_Tour_1989_Era_Set_%2853110043448%29_%28cropped%29.jpg/250px-Taylor_Swift_The_Eras_Tour_1989_Era_Set_%2853110043448%29_%28cropped%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Taylor_Swift_The_Eras_Tour_1989_Era_Set_\(53110043448\)_\(cropped\).jpg)

Swift announced the album at the [Eras Tour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eras_Tour "Eras Tour") concert at the [SoFi Stadium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SoFi_Stadium "SoFi Stadium") on August 9, 2023.

On September 19, 2023, Swift posted a short visual on social media that depicted the characters "T-S-!-U-L" emerging from a blue vault, which fans and journalists considered to be a teaser for one of the five "From the Vault" tracks.[\[49\]](#cite_note-52) She also partnered with [Google Search](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Google_Search "Google Search") to launch a feature for solving [word puzzles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Word_puzzle "Word puzzle") to uncover the album's "From the Vault" track titles. Searching for "Taylor Swift" gave rise to an animated graphic of a blue vault, which, upon being clicked, produced one of 89 puzzles with or without an accompanying hint.[\[50\]](#cite_note-53) The track titles were set to be officially revealed once 33 million puzzles had been solved globally.[\[51\]](#cite_note-54) Although the feature crashed hours after launching, it reached the 33-million mark in less than one day.[\[52\]](#cite_note-55)[\[53\]](#cite_note-56) Four of the five vault track titles were revealed: "Is It Over Now?", "Now That We Don't Talk", "Say Don't Go", and "Suburban Legends".[\[54\]](#cite_note-57) Swift unveiled the back covers of the album, which featured the full track list, confirming "'Slut!'" as the remaining vault track.[\[55\]](#cite_note-58)

Republic Records released _1989 (Taylor's Version)_ on October 27, 2023, as Swift's fourth re-recorded album. The album was made available for [streaming](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Music_streaming_service "Music streaming service"), download, [vinyl LP](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vinyl_LP "Vinyl LP"), [cassette](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cassette_tape "Cassette tape"), and CD.[\[56\]](#cite_note-Sisario-59) The standard edition contains 21 tracks—16 are re-recorded versions of the tracks on the original album and five are vault tracks.[\[57\]](#cite_note-Unterberger-60) A deluxe edition containing the re-recorded remix of "Bad Blood" featuring Lamar was released on streaming and digital download platforms hours after the standard album.[\[58\]](#cite_note-1989TV_DLX-61)[\[59\]](#cite_note-62) The album was sold in 14 physical variants, including five vinyl editions (one of which, the Tangerine Edition, being a [Target](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Target_Corporation "Target Corporation") exclusive containing the re-recording of "Sweeter than Fiction"), eight CD editions (each with folded posters or photographs), and a multi-colored cassette.[\[57\]](#cite_note-Unterberger-60)[\[d\]](#cite_note-editions-64) The standard cover is a photograph of Swift in red lipstick with a background of a blue sky and seagulls flying in the distance.[\[61\]](#cite_note-65) _[Exclaim!](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Exclaim! "Exclaim!")_ listed the album cover as the 15th worst of the year, saying that Swift "could afford to hire a professional graphic designer" to design the cover, and that the cover looks like a fan design on [Canva](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canva "Canva").[\[62\]](#cite_note-66) [Universal Music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Universal_Music "Universal Music") released "'Slut!'" to Italian radio on October 27,[\[63\]](#cite_note-67) and Republic Records released "Is It Over Now?" as a single to US [contemporary hit radio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Contemporary_hit_radio "Contemporary hit radio") on October 31.[\[64\]](#cite_note-68)[\[65\]](#cite_note-69)

_**1989 (Taylor's Version)**_ is the fourth [re-recorded album](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Re-recorded_album "Re-recorded album") by the American singer-songwriter [Taylor Swift](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taylor_Swift "Taylor Swift"). It was released on October 27, 2023, through [Republic Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republic_Records "Republic Records"), as part of Swift's re-recording project following the [2019 dispute over the master recordings of her back catalog](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taylor_Swift_masters_dispute "Taylor Swift masters dispute").

A re-recording of Swift's fifth album, _[1989](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1989_\(album\) "1989 (album)")_ (2014), _1989 (Taylor's Version)_ consists of re-recorded versions of the 16 songs from _1989_'s deluxe edition and five previously unreleased "From the Vault" tracks;[\[a\]](#cite_note-1) extended editions additionally feature the re-recorded versions of the [_One Chance_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/One_Chance_\(film\) "One Chance (film)") soundtrack song "[Sweeter than Fiction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sweeter_than_Fiction "Sweeter than Fiction")" (2013) and the [Kendrick Lamar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kendrick_Lamar "Kendrick Lamar") remix of "[Bad Blood](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bad_Blood_\(Taylor_Swift_song\) "Bad Blood (Taylor Swift song)")" (2015). Swift, [Jack Antonoff](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jack_Antonoff "Jack Antonoff"), and [Christopher Rowe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christopher_Rowe_\(record_producer\) "Christopher Rowe (record producer)") produced the majority of the album; [Ryan Tedder](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ryan_Tedder "Ryan Tedder"), [Noel Zancanella](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Noel_Zancanella "Noel Zancanella"), [Shellback](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shellback_\(record_producer\) "Shellback (record producer)"), and [Imogen Heap](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imogen_Heap "Imogen Heap") reprised their production roles. A 1980s-inspired [synth-pop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Synth-pop "Synth-pop") album, _1989 (Taylor's Version)_ is characterized by [upbeat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beat_\(music\)#Downbeat_and_upbeat "Beat (music)") arrangements of [synthesizers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Synthesizer "Synthesizer") and [percussion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Percussion "Percussion").

Music critics praised _1989 (Taylor's Version)_, with emphasis on the production, Swift's vocals, and the vault tracks. The album topped [record charts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Record_chart "Record chart") in Australia, Canada, and European territories including France, Germany, Italy, Spain, and the United Kingdom. In the United States, _1989 (Taylor's Version)_ marked Swift's 13th number-one album on the [_Billboard_ 200](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billboard_200 "Billboard 200") and record-extending [sixth album to sell over one million first-week copies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_fastest-selling_albums "List of fastest-selling albums"). Seven of its songs concurrently became top-10 entries on the [_Billboard_ Hot 100](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billboard_Hot_100 "Billboard Hot 100"), with the vault tracks "[Is It Over Now?](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Is_It_Over_Now%3F "Is It Over Now?")", "[Now That We Don't Talk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Now_That_We_Don't_Talk "Now That We Don't Talk")", and "['Slut!'](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/"Slut!" "\"Slut!\"")" occupying the top three spots. In 2024, [Apple Music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_Music "Apple Music") placed the album at number 18 on its list of the [100 Best Albums](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_Music_100_Best_Albums "Apple Music 100 Best Albums").

[Taylor Swift](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taylor_Swift "Taylor Swift") released her fifth album, _[1989](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1989_\(album\) "1989 (album)")_, on October 27, 2014, under [Big Machine Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Big_Machine_Records "Big Machine Records"). Inspired by 1980s [synth-pop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Synth-pop "Synth-pop"), Swift conceived _1989_ to recalibrate her artistry to [pop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pop_music "Pop music") after promoting her first four albums to [country radio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Country_radio "Country radio").[\[1\]](#cite_note-Vinson-2014-2) The album received generally positive critical reviews and sold over 10 million copies worldwide.[\[2\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcNutt202078-3)[\[3\]](#cite_note-4) Three of its singles—"[Shake It Off](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shake_It_Off "Shake It Off")", "[Blank Space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blank_Space "Blank Space")", and "[Bad Blood](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bad_Blood_\(Taylor_Swift_song\) "Bad Blood (Taylor Swift song)")"—reached number one on the [_Billboard_ Hot 100](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billboard_Hot_100 "Billboard Hot 100").[\[4\]](#cite_note-5) At the [58th Annual Grammy Awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/58th_Annual_Grammy_Awards "58th Annual Grammy Awards"), _1989_ made Swift the first female musician to win the [Grammy Award for Album of the Year](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grammy_Award_for_Album_of_the_Year "Grammy Award for Album of the Year") twice—her first win was for _[Fearless](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fearless_\(Taylor_Swift_album\) "Fearless (Taylor Swift album)")_ in [2010](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/52nd_Annual_Grammy_Awards "52nd Annual Grammy Awards").[\[5\]](#cite_note-6)

Swift's contract with Big Machine expired in November 2018. She then withdrew from Big Machine and signed a new deal with [Republic Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republic_Records "Republic Records"), which secured her the rights to own the [masters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mastering_\(audio\) "Mastering (audio)") of any new music she would release.[\[6\]](#cite_note-7) In 2019, American music executive [Scooter Braun](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scooter_Braun "Scooter Braun") acquired Big Machine;[\[7\]](#cite_note-8) the ownership of the masters to Swift's first six albums, including _1989_, was transferred to him.[\[8\]](#cite_note-9) In August 2019, Swift spoke against Braun's purchase and announced that she would [re-record](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Re-recording_\(music\) "Re-recording (music)") her first six albums so as to own their masters herself.[\[9\]](#cite_note-10) Swift began the re-recording process in November 2020.[\[10\]](#cite_note-11) _[Fearless (Taylor's Version)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fearless_\(Taylor's_Version\) "Fearless (Taylor's Version)")_, the first of her six re-recorded albums, was released on April 9, 2021, followed by _[Red (Taylor's Version)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_\(Taylor's_Version\) "Red (Taylor's Version)")_ on November 12, 2021,[\[11\]](#cite_note-12)[\[12\]](#cite_note-13) and _[Speak Now (Taylor's Version)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now_\(Taylor's_Version\) "Speak Now (Taylor's Version)")_ on July 7, 2023; all three peaked atop the US [_Billboard_ 200](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billboard_200 "Billboard 200") chart.[\[13\]](#cite_note-14)

Swift released re-recordings of some _1989_ tracks prior to the re-recorded album; all songs feature the additional "Taylor's Version" moniker in their titles. The re-recording of "[Wildest Dreams](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wildest_Dreams_\(Taylor's_Version\) "Wildest Dreams (Taylor's Version)")" was released on September 17, 2021, after the [original version](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wildest_Dreams_\(Taylor_Swift_song\) "Wildest Dreams (Taylor Swift song)") went viral on [TikTok](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TikTok "TikTok").[\[14\]](#cite_note-15) Other tracks were used in films and series: "[This Love](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/This_Love_\(Taylor's_Version\) "This Love (Taylor's Version)")" was released on May 6, 2022, after its snippet featured in the trailer for the series [_The Summer I Turned Pretty_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Summer_I_Turned_Pretty_\(TV_series\) "The Summer I Turned Pretty (TV series)");[\[15\]](#cite_note-16) a snippet of "[Bad Blood](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bad_Blood_\(Taylor's_Version\) "Bad Blood (Taylor's Version)")" appeared in the animated film _[DC League of Super-Pets](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DC_League_of_Super-Pets "DC League of Super-Pets"),_[\[16\]](#cite_note-17) and "[Out of the Woods](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Out_of_the_Woods_\(Taylor's_Version\) "Out of the Woods (Taylor's Version)")" featured in a trailer for [_Migration_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Migration_\(2023_film\) "Migration (2023 film)").[\[17\]](#cite_note-18) On August 9, 2023, at the final Los Angeles show at [SoFi Stadium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SoFi_Stadium "SoFi Stadium") as part of Swift's [Eras Tour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eras_Tour "Eras Tour"), she performed in five new blue outfits, representing the color that Swift's fans associated _1989_ with;[\[18\]](#cite_note-19) during the half-show acoustic set, she announced _1989 (Taylor's Version)_ as her next re-recorded album, set for release on October 27, 2023, exactly nine years after the original release of _1989_.[\[19\]](#cite_note-20)[\[20\]](#cite_note-21)

## Writing and recording

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=1989_\(Taylor%27s_Version\)&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Writing and recording")\]

The standard edition of _1989 (Taylor's Version)_ comprises 21 tracks: re-recordings of the 13 songs from the standard edition of _1989_, as well as the three bonus tracks from the original deluxe edition, and five previously unreleased "From the Vault" songs that were written for the 2014 album but excluded from the final track list.[\[21\]](#cite_note-Caulfield-1M-22) Re-recordings of the "Bad Blood" remix (2015) featuring American rapper [Kendrick Lamar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kendrick_Lamar "Kendrick Lamar") and "[Sweeter than Fiction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sweeter_than_Fiction "Sweeter than Fiction")" (2013), a song Swift and [Jack Antonoff](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jack_Antonoff "Jack Antonoff") contributed to the soundtrack of _[One Chance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/One_Chance_\(film\) "One Chance (film)")_ (2013), were included on extended editions of _1989 (Taylor's Version)_ as bonus tracks.[\[22\]](#cite_note-23)[\[23\]](#cite_note-24)

Most re-recorded tracks were produced by Swift and [Christopher Rowe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christopher_Rowe_\(record_producer\) "Christopher Rowe (record producer)"). The remaining were co-produced by their original producers—Antonoff, [Ryan Tedder](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ryan_Tedder "Ryan Tedder"), [Noel Zancanella](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Noel_Zancanella "Noel Zancanella"), and [Imogen Heap](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imogen_Heap "Imogen Heap"). [Shellback](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shellback_\(record_producer\) "Shellback (record producer)"), who produced multiple songs on _1989_ alongside [Max Martin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Max_Martin "Max Martin"), only produced "Wildest Dreams (Taylor's Version)" with Swift and Rowe, while Martin was not involved in the production of the re-recording.[\[24\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTESomvilleBenoit2025243-25) All of the vault tracks were written and produced by Swift and Antonoff, except "[Say Don't Go](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Say_Don't_Go "Say Don't Go")", which was co-written by the American songwriter [Diane Warren](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diane_Warren "Diane Warren").[\[25\]](#cite_note-26) According to Antonnoff, he could not recall some original sounds that he created, so he asked for help from his [Bleachers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bleachers_\(band\) "Bleachers (band)") bandmates for certain sounds like the "soft synths".[\[26\]](#cite_note-Curto-2024-27)

_1989 (Taylor's Version)_ is a synth-pop album,[\[27\]](#cite_note-Guardian_review-28) with a production composed of upbeat [synthesizers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Synthesizer "Synthesizer") and dynamic [percussions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Percussions "Percussions").[\[28\]](#cite_note-Telegraph-29) According to _[NME](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NME "NME")_, the album has a [1980s](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1980s_in_music "1980s in music")\-inspired synth-pop sound, but is "an evolution of Swift's own sound" rather than a "kitschy pastiche" of [retro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Retro "Retro") influences.[\[29\]](#cite_note-NME_review-30) Various critics have opined that the only sonic difference between _1989_ and _1989 (Taylor's Version)_ is Swift's vocals, which have become technically stronger and richer.[\[b\]](#cite_note-33) According to _[Clash](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clash_\(magazine\) "Clash (magazine)")_'s Alex Berry, the re-recording has a "cleaner" instrumentation.[\[32\]](#cite_note-Clash_review-34) _[Slant Magazine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slant_Magazine "Slant Magazine")_'s Jonathan Keefe identified minor changes: the clicking pen noise on "Blank Space" sounds less like the spring action of a ballpoint pen, the "ah-ah-ah" vocal [hook](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hook_\(music\) "Hook (music)") of "[New Romantics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Romantics_\(song\) "New Romantics (song)")" is more [staccato](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Staccato "Staccato"), the [reverb](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reverb_effect "Reverb effect") on "[Out of the Woods](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Out_of_the_Woods "Out of the Woods")" is more prominent, and the guitar's tone on "[Style](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Style_\(Taylor_Swift_song\) "Style (Taylor Swift song)")" is altered.[\[33\]](#cite_note-Keefe-35)

### "From the Vault" songs

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=1989_\(Taylor%27s_Version\)&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: \"From the Vault\" songs")\]

As with the original album, the vault tracks incorporate production elements that evoke the 1980s-inspired pop sound: reverb, synths, [keyboards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electronic_keyboard "Electronic keyboard"), and percussions.[\[c\]](#cite_note-38) [AllMusic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AllMusic "AllMusic")'s Fred Thomas wrote that the production was reminiscent of late-1980s radio,[\[36\]](#cite_note-allmusicreview-39) and _[The Line of Best Fit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Line_of_Best_Fit "The Line of Best Fit")_'s Kelsey Barnes opined that the vault tracks featured different pop subgenres.[\[31\]](#cite_note-TLOBF_review-32) _[Variety](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Variety_\(magazine\) "Variety (magazine)")_'s Chris Willman and _[Pitchfork](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pitchfork_\(website\) "Pitchfork (website)")_'s Shaad D'Souza opined that their production elements were influenced by the music of Swift's tenth studio album, _[Midnights](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Midnights "Midnights")_ (2022).[\[37\]](#cite_note-40)[\[38\]](#cite_note-Pitchfork-41)

The title of "['Slut!'](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/"Slut!" "\"Slut!\"")" refers to the [slut-shaming](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slut-shaming "Slut-shaming") Swift experienced as a public figure, a result of the media scrutiny on her personal life and serial romantic relationships.[\[39\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTESomvilleBenoit2025244-42) In its lyrics, Swift describes a relationship that she is proud of and does not care how the outside world views it.[\[35\]](#cite_note-Lipshutz-2023-37)[\[40\]](#cite_note-RS_review-43) It is a mid-tempo synth-pop song,[\[41\]](#cite_note-44)[\[42\]](#cite_note-WoodLAT1-45) featuring layered, grainy [analog synthesizers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Analog_synthesizers "Analog synthesizers") and soft backing vocals.[\[39\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTESomvilleBenoit2025244-42)[\[32\]](#cite_note-Clash_review-34) "[Say Don't Go](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Say_Don't_Go "Say Don't Go")" is about Swift hanging on to an unfruitful relationship;[\[28\]](#cite_note-Telegraph-29) it has a reverb-heavy, [pop rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pop_rock "Pop rock") production that consists of isolated vocal patterns, [gated](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gated_reverb "Gated reverb") snare drums, synthesized [Moog bass](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moog_bass "Moog bass") and guitar, and layered keyboard sounds created with a [Mellotron](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mellotron "Mellotron") and analog synths: [Oberheim OB-Xa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oberheim_OB-Xa "Oberheim OB-Xa"), [Yamaha DX100](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yamaha_DX100_\(synthesizer\) "Yamaha DX100 (synthesizer)"), [Juno-6](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roland_Juno-60 "Roland Juno-60"), and [Korg M1](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Korg_M1 "Korg M1").[\[31\]](#cite_note-TLOBF_review-32)[\[42\]](#cite_note-WoodLAT1-45)[\[43\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTESomvilleBenoit2025245-46)

Swift announced the album at the [Eras Tour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eras_Tour "Eras Tour") concert at the [SoFi Stadium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SoFi_Stadium "SoFi Stadium") on August 9, 2023.

On September 19, 2023, Swift posted a short visual on social media that depicted the characters "T-S-!-U-L" emerging from a blue vault, which fans and journalists considered to be a teaser for one of the five "From the Vault" tracks.[\[49\]](#cite_note-52) She also partnered with [Google Search](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Google_Search "Google Search") to launch a feature for solving [word puzzles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Word_puzzle "Word puzzle") to uncover the album's "From the Vault" track titles. Searching for "Taylor Swift" gave rise to an animated graphic of a blue vault, which, upon being clicked, produced one of 89 puzzles with or without an accompanying hint.[\[50\]](#cite_note-53) The track titles were set to be officially revealed once 33 million puzzles had been solved globally.[\[51\]](#cite_note-54) Although the feature crashed hours after launching, it reached the 33-million mark in less than one day.[\[52\]](#cite_note-55)[\[53\]](#cite_note-56) Four of the five vault track titles were revealed: "Is It Over Now?", "Now That We Don't Talk", "Say Don't Go", and "Suburban Legends".[\[54\]](#cite_note-57) Swift unveiled the back covers of the album, which featured the full track list, confirming "'Slut!'" as the remaining vault track.[\[55\]](#cite_note-58)

Republic Records released _1989 (Taylor's Version)_ on October 27, 2023, as Swift's fourth re-recorded album. The album was made available for [streaming](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Music_streaming_service "Music streaming service"), download, [vinyl LP](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vinyl_LP "Vinyl LP"), [cassette](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cassette_tape "Cassette tape"), and CD.[\[56\]](#cite_note-Sisario-59) The standard edition contains 21 tracks—16 are re-recorded versions of the tracks on the original album and five are vault tracks.[\[57\]](#cite_note-Unterberger-60) A deluxe edition containing the re-recorded remix of "Bad Blood" featuring Lamar was released on streaming and digital download platforms hours after the standard album.[\[58\]](#cite_note-1989TV_DLX-61)[\[59\]](#cite_note-62) The album was sold in 14 physical variants, including five vinyl editions (one of which, the Tangerine Edition, being a [Target](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Target_Corporation "Target Corporation") exclusive containing the re-recording of "Sweeter than Fiction"), eight CD editions (each with folded posters or photographs), and a multi-colored cassette.[\[57\]](#cite_note-Unterberger-60)[\[d\]](#cite_note-editions-64) The standard cover is a photograph of Swift in red lipstick with a background of a blue sky and seagulls flying in the distance.[\[61\]](#cite_note-65) _[Exclaim!](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Exclaim! "Exclaim!")_ listed the album cover as the 15th worst of the year, saying that Swift "could afford to hire a professional graphic designer" to design the cover, and that the cover looks like a fan design on [Canva](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canva "Canva").[\[62\]](#cite_note-66) [Universal Music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Universal_Music "Universal Music") released "'Slut!'" to Italian radio on October 27,[\[63\]](#cite_note-67) and Republic Records released "Is It Over Now?" as a single to US [contemporary hit radio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Contemporary_hit_radio "Contemporary hit radio") on October 31.[\[64\]](#cite_note-68)[\[65\]](#cite_note-69)

_**Speak Now (Taylor's Version)**_ is the third [re-recorded album](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Re-recorded_album "Re-recorded album") by the American singer-songwriter [Taylor Swift](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taylor_Swift "Taylor Swift"). It was released on July 7, 2023, through [Republic Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republic_Records "Republic Records"), as part of Swift's re-recording project following the [2019 dispute over the master recordings of her back catalog](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taylor_Swift_masters_dispute "Taylor Swift masters dispute"). The album is a re-recording of Swift's third studio album, _[Speak Now](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now "Speak Now")_ (2010). She announced the re-recording at the first [Nashville](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nashville "Nashville") concert of her sixth concert tour, [the Eras Tour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Eras_Tour "The Eras Tour"), on May 5, 2023.

_Speak Now (Taylor's Version)_ consists of songs written solely by Swift. She produced the re-recorded versions of 16 tracks from the deluxe edition of _Speak Now_ with [Christopher Rowe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christopher_Rowe_\(record_producer\) "Christopher Rowe (record producer)"), and six previously unreleased "From the Vault" tracks with [Jack Antonoff](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jack_Antonoff "Jack Antonoff") and [Aaron Dessner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aaron_Dessner "Aaron Dessner"). Two vault tracks respectively feature [Fall Out Boy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_Out_Boy "Fall Out Boy") and [Hayley Williams](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hayley_Williams "Hayley Williams"). A [country pop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Country_pop "Country pop") and [pop rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pop_rock "Pop rock") album, _Speak Now (Taylor's Version)_ incorporates various [rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rock_music "Rock music") styles such as [emo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emo "Emo"), [pop-punk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pop-punk "Pop-punk"), and [alternative rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alternative_rock "Alternative rock"). Its sound is characterized by prominent [electric guitars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electric_guitar "Electric guitar"), dynamic drums, and [strings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/String_section "String section"). Reflecting Swift's adolescence, the songs document emotions of affection, grievance, and heartbreak, forming a loose [concept album](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Concept_album "Concept album") of unspoken confessions.

Music critics praised Swift's emotionally engaging songwriting in the album and the matured tone of her vocal performances, although the alteration to a lyric in the track "[Better than Revenge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Better_than_Revenge "Better than Revenge")" had a mixed response. _Speak Now (Taylor's Version)_ reached number one on the album charts of Australia, Canada, Spain, Sweden, and the United Kingdom, among others. In the United States, it was Swift's 12th album to top the [_Billboard_ 200](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billboard_200 "Billboard 200") chart, breaking [Barbra Streisand](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barbra_Streisand "Barbra Streisand")'s all-time record for the most number-one albums by a female artist. It was later [certified](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RIAA_certification "RIAA certification") four-times platinum by the [Recording Industry Association of America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Recording_Industry_Association_of_America "Recording Industry Association of America"). All 22 of its tracks charted on the [_Billboard_ Hot 100](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billboard_Hot_100 "Billboard Hot 100"), with "[I Can See You](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/I_Can_See_You_\(song\) "I Can See You (song)")", which was accompanied by a music video, becoming the highest-peaking at number five.

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/6e/Taylor_Swift_2011crop.jpg/250px-Taylor_Swift_2011crop.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Taylor_Swift_2011crop.jpg)

Swift performing on the [Speak Now World Tour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now_World_Tour "Speak Now World Tour") (2011–2012)

[Taylor Swift](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taylor_Swift "Taylor Swift") signed a recording contract with [Big Machine Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Big_Machine_Records "Big Machine Records"), an [independent record label](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Independent_record_label "Independent record label") based in [Nashville](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nashville "Nashville"), in 2005.[\[1\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTESpencer201027-1) As part of the contract, Big Machine released Swift's first six studio albums, from [_Taylor Swift_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taylor_Swift_\(album\) "Taylor Swift (album)") (2006) to [_Reputation_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reputation_\(album\) "Reputation (album)") (2017).[\[2\]](#cite_note-2) Swift wrote the standard edition of her third studio album, _[Speak Now](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now "Speak Now")_, entirely herself and produced it with [Nathan Chapman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nathan_Chapman_\(record_producer\) "Nathan Chapman (record producer)"), who had produced both of her previous albums.[\[3\]](#cite_note-wsj_int-3)[\[4\]](#cite_note-SoS-4) The album was released on October 25, 2010, by Big Machine.[\[5\]](#cite_note-US-5) It expands on the [country pop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Country_pop "Country pop") style of her past albums with more aggressive elements of mainstream [pop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pop_music "Pop music")[\[6\]](#cite_note-AllMusic-6) and [rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rock_music "Rock music") styles from the 1970s and 1980s, such as [pop rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pop_rock "Pop rock"), [arena rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arena_rock "Arena rock"), and [new wave rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_wave_rock "New wave rock").[\[7\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPerone201729,_42-7) _Speak Now_ registered in the 2010 _[Guinness World Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guinness_World_Records "Guinness World Records")_ as the fastest-selling US digital album by a female artist[\[8\]](#cite_note-8) and was nominated for [Best Country Album](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Best_Country_Album "Best Country Album") at the [54th Grammy Awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/54th_Grammy_Awards "54th Grammy Awards") in 2012.[\[9\]](#cite_note-9) _[The New York Times](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_New_York_Times "The New York Times")_ wrote in 2010 that the album's strong sales proved Swift "has transcended the limitations of genre and become a pop megastar".[\[10\]](#cite_note-nytimes_sales-10)

By August 2018, Swift's contract with Big Machine had expired; she signed a new contract with [Republic Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republic_Records "Republic Records"), a division of [Universal Music Group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Universal_Music_Group "Universal Music Group"), which secured her the rights to own the [masters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mastering_\(audio\) "Mastering (audio)") of the new music she would release.[\[11\]](#cite_note-11) In 2019, the talent manager [Scooter Braun](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scooter_Braun "Scooter Braun") and his company, Ithaca Holdings, acquired Big Machine Records. The masters of Swift's Big Machine-released albums were effectively transferred to Braun, which resulted in a [public dispute](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taylor_Swift_masters_dispute "Taylor Swift masters dispute") between Swift and Braun.[\[12\]](#cite_note-12) Swift denounced the purchase and began [re-recording](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Re-recording_\(music\) "Re-recording (music)") her first six studio albums in November 2020.[\[13\]](#cite_note-13)[\[14\]](#cite_note-14) By re-recording the albums, Swift had full ownership of the new masters, which enabled her to control the licensing of her songs for [commercial use](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Synchronization_rights "Synchronization rights") and therefore substituted the Big Machine–owned masters.[\[15\]](#cite_note-Shah-2021-15)

Swift released the first two re-recorded albums in 2021: _[Fearless (Taylor's Version)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fearless_\(Taylor's_Version\) "Fearless (Taylor's Version)")_ in April and _[Red (Taylor's Version)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_\(Taylor's_Version\) "Red (Taylor's Version)")_ in November; the former is the re-recording of Swift's second studio album, [_Fearless_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fearless_\(Taylor_Swift_album\) "Fearless (Taylor Swift album)") (2008), and the latter is of her fourth, [_Red_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_\(Taylor_Swift_album\) "Red (Taylor Swift album)") (2012). In addition to reproduced versions of the original songs subtitled "Taylor's Version", each album includes several previously unreleased tracks denoted as "From the Vault".[\[a\]](#cite_note-16) After their release, both re-recorded albums performed better in commercial metrics than their original counterparts did.[\[16\]](#cite_note-17) At the first Nashville show of her sixth headlining concert tour, [the Eras Tour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Eras_Tour "The Eras Tour"), on May 5, 2023, Swift announced the third installment in her re-recording project, _Speak Now (Taylor's Version)_.[\[17\]](#cite_note-18)

[![Fall Out Boy performing](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c6/Fall_Out_Boy_Rock_am_Ring_2014_%284%29.JPG/250px-Fall_Out_Boy_Rock_am_Ring_2014_%284%29.JPG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Fall_Out_Boy_Rock_am_Ring_2014_\(4\).JPG)

[![Hayley Williams singing onto a red mic](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/20/Hayley_Williams_-_concierto_de_Paramore_en_Bogot%C3%A1%2C_Colombia_%282011%29_-_5569060233.jpg/120px-Hayley_Williams_-_concierto_de_Paramore_en_Bogot%C3%A1%2C_Colombia_%282011%29_-_5569060233.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Hayley_Williams_-_concierto_de_Paramore_en_Bogotá,_Colombia_\(2011\)_-_5569060233.jpg)

_Speak Now (Taylor's Version)_ contains 22 tracks written solely by Swift, 16 of which are re-recorded versions of songs from the 2010 deluxe edition of _Speak Now_, save for "[If This Was a Movie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/If_This_Was_a_Movie "If This Was a Movie")", which was re-recorded and released separately.[\[18\]](#cite_note-19)[\[19\]](#cite_note-20) Six tracks were denoted as "From the Vault", which Swift had written and intended to include in the original album but ultimately did not.[\[20\]](#cite_note-Pitchfork2-21) [Fall Out Boy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_Out_Boy "Fall Out Boy") features on the vault track "[Electric Touch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electric_Touch_\(song\) "Electric Touch (song)")", and [Hayley Williams](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hayley_Williams "Hayley Williams") on "[Castles Crumbling](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Castles_Crumbling "Castles Crumbling")".[\[21\]](#cite_note-Willman-2023-22)

Swift shared via social media that re-recording _Speak Now_ made her reminisce about it as an album that "tells a tale of growing up, flailing, flying and crashing ... and living to speak about it",[\[22\]](#cite_note-23) influenced by her adolescence to encapsulate "brutal honesty, unfiltered diaristic confessions and wild wistfulness".[\[23\]](#cite_note-24) The songs on _Speak Now (Taylor's Version)_ reflect on Swift's transition from adolescence to adulthood; they employ autobiographical songwriting to explore the sentiments stemming from love and life, such as enchantment, heartbreak,[\[24\]](#cite_note-Johnston-2023-25) and teenage angst.[\[25\]](#cite_note-Olivier-2023-26) Some songs were inspired by Swift's celebrity.[\[26\]](#cite_note-Guardian_review-27) They altogether constitute a loose concept of unspoken things Swift wanted to deliver to the subjects of her songs.[\[25\]](#cite_note-Olivier-2023-26)[\[26\]](#cite_note-Guardian_review-27) All re-recorded tracks retain their original lyrics, except "[Better than Revenge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Better_than_Revenge "Better than Revenge")", whose line "She's better known for the things that she does on the mattress" in the chorus was replaced with "He was a moth to the flame, she was holding the matches".[\[27\]](#cite_note-28)

Swift produced all tracks on _Speak Now (Taylor's Version)_. The re-recorded tracks were produced with [Christopher Rowe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christopher_Rowe_\(record_producer\) "Christopher Rowe (record producer)"),[\[28\]](#cite_note-29) and the vault tracks with [Aaron Dessner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aaron_Dessner "Aaron Dessner") and [Jack Antonoff](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jack_Antonoff "Jack Antonoff"), who were each credited on three tracks.[\[29\]](#cite_note-30) _Speak Now (Taylor's Version)_ is a country pop[\[30\]](#cite_note-Sputnikmusic-2023-31)[\[31\]](#cite_note-32) and pop rock album.[\[21\]](#cite_note-Willman-2023-22) It incorporates elements of various rock styles,[\[25\]](#cite_note-Olivier-2023-26) such as [pop-punk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pop-punk "Pop-punk"),[\[26\]](#cite_note-Guardian_review-27) [emo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emo "Emo"),[\[32\]](#cite_note-RS_UK_review-33) and [alternative rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alternative_rock "Alternative rock"). In the re-recorded version, all of the original tracks are heavier compared to the original.[\[33\]](#cite_note-AS_review-34) _[Clash](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clash_\(magazine\) "Clash (magazine)")_'s Alex Berry described the album as a blend of rock, [country](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Country_music "Country music"), and pop,[\[34\]](#cite_note-Clash_review-35) and [_Spin_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spin_\(magazine\) "Spin (magazine)")'s Bobby Olivier attributed the rock sounds to the production elements of "rousing electric guitars, heavier drums, volatile choruses".[\[25\]](#cite_note-Olivier-2023-26) In _[Rolling Stone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rolling_Stone "Rolling Stone")_, [Maura Johnston](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maura_Johnston "Maura Johnston") said that Swift's songwriting exhibits country roots while drawing influences from the pop-rock sound popular around the time she was writing the original album;[\[24\]](#cite_note-Johnston-2023-25) this idea was shared by [_Variety_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Variety_\(magazine\) "Variety (magazine)")'s Chris Willman, who described the overall sound Swift was pursuing as "the organic pop-rock band sound" that captured "the stylistic spirit of 2010".[\[21\]](#cite_note-Willman-2023-22)

### "From the Vault" tracks

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Speak_Now_\(Taylor%27s_Version\)&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: \"From the Vault\" tracks")\]

![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/87/Gnome-mime-sound-openclipart.svg/60px-Gnome-mime-sound-openclipart.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)

"Electric Touch" featuring Fall Out Boy is a pop rock[\[25\]](#cite_note-Olivier-2023-26) and pop-punk track[\[32\]](#cite_note-RS_UK_review-33) that is instrumented by electric guitar [riffs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riff "Riff") and [crescendoing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crescendo "Crescendo") drums.[\[35\]](#cite_note-:0-36) In it, Swift duets with Fall Out Boy's frontman, [Patrick Stump](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patrick_Stump "Patrick Stump").[\[25\]](#cite_note-Olivier-2023-26) The lyrics are about the conflicting feelings such as anxieties, pessimism, excitement, hope, and self-doubt over a newfound romance.[\[21\]](#cite_note-Willman-2023-22)[\[24\]](#cite_note-Johnston-2023-25) "[When Emma Falls in Love](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/When_Emma_Falls_in_Love "When Emma Falls in Love")" is a mellow [piano ballad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Piano_ballad "Piano ballad")[\[36\]](#cite_note-Lipshutz-2023-37) that also incorporates [banjo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Banjo "Banjo"),[\[30\]](#cite_note-Sputnikmusic-2023-31) exhibiting elements of country and pop.[\[36\]](#cite_note-Lipshutz-2023-37) In the lyrics, Swift's character observes a friend's love life and character.[\[37\]](#cite_note-Indp_review-38)[\[32\]](#cite_note-RS_UK_review-33) "[I Can See You](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/I_Can_See_You_\(song\) "I Can See You (song)")" has a [groove](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Groove_\(music\) "Groove (music)") that is instrumented by a rhythmic electric guitar,[\[21\]](#cite_note-Willman-2023-22) featuring elements of [indie rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indie_rock "Indie rock")[\[37\]](#cite_note-Indp_review-38) and [surf rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Surf_rock "Surf rock").[\[36\]](#cite_note-Lipshutz-2023-37) The lyrics contain sexually suggestive innuendos.[\[26\]](#cite_note-Guardian_review-27)[\[36\]](#cite_note-Lipshutz-2023-37)

"Castles Crumbling" is a duet between Swift and Williams.[\[38\]](#cite_note-TLOBF_review-39) It is a piano ballad[\[25\]](#cite_note-Olivier-2023-26) about dealing with the pressures of fame and potentially losing the interest of fans.[\[21\]](#cite_note-Willman-2023-22)[\[30\]](#cite_note-Sputnikmusic-2023-31) "Foolish One" is about self-criticism for one's naivety in love.[\[26\]](#cite_note-Guardian_review-27) It is a country pop song driven by acoustic guitar strums and [programmed drums](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Drum_machine "Drum machine").[\[21\]](#cite_note-Willman-2023-22)[\[39\]](#cite_note-Pitchfork-40) In the closing ballad "Timeless", Swift finds old photos of couples in an antique shop and superimposes herself in their lives,[\[26\]](#cite_note-Guardian_review-27) imagining herself longing for a lover who has gone to war.[\[26\]](#cite_note-Guardian_review-27) The song's arrangement mainly consists of acoustic guitars and [organ](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Organ_\(music\) "Organ (music)"), with accents of [ukulele](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ukulele "Ukulele") and [flute](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flute "Flute").[\[21\]](#cite_note-Willman-2023-22)

After a month of the album's announcement, Swift unveiled its track listing via social media on June 5, 2023.[\[20\]](#cite_note-Pitchfork2-21) On June 9, the French newspaper _[Ouest-France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ouest-France "Ouest-France")_ reported that a temporary worker from [Le Mans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Le_Mans "Le Mans"), France, was arrested for stealing 10 vinyl records of _Speak Now (Taylor's Version)_ from a warehouse and selling them on [Leboncoin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leboncoin "Leboncoin"), a [classified ads](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Classified_ads "Classified ads") website. The worker was sentenced to eight months in prison. The [public prosecutor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Public_prosecutor "Public prosecutor") stated that only the eight unsold LPs were retrieved from the worker; the whereabouts of the two sold copies remain unknown.[\[40\]](#cite_note-41)[\[41\]](#cite_note-42)

Swift released a snippet of the re-recorded version of "[Mine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mine_\(Taylor_Swift_song\) "Mine (Taylor Swift song)")" via social media on June 24,[\[42\]](#cite_note-43) and "[Back to December](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Back_to_December "Back to December")" in the trailer for the [Amazon Prime Video](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amazon_Prime_Video "Amazon Prime Video") series _[The Summer I Turned Pretty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Summer_I_Turned_Pretty_\(TV_series\) "The Summer I Turned Pretty (TV series)")_ on June 29.[\[43\]](#cite_note-44) _Speak Now (Taylor's Version)_ was released on July 7, 2023.[\[44\]](#cite_note-45) The standard vinyl edition of _Speak Now (Taylor's Version)_ is a set of three [marbled](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marbleizing "Marbleizing") violet [LP records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/LP_record "LP record").[\[45\]](#cite_note-46) Two additional lilac and orchid marbled variants were also released.[\[46\]](#cite_note-47)[\[47\]](#cite_note-48) [Universal Music Japan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Universal_Music_Japan "Universal Music Japan") released two Japanese exclusive physical versions, a standard CD and a deluxe 7–inch jacket, on August 16, 2023.[\[48\]](#cite_note-49)

When the album was released on July 7, Swift premiered the music video for "I Can See You" at the first [Kansas City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kansas_City,_Missouri "Kansas City, Missouri") show on the Eras Tour.[\[49\]](#cite_note-50) The following day, it was released to her YouTube channel.[\[50\]](#cite_note-51) Directed and written by Swift, the video stars her alongside [Taylor Lautner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taylor_Lautner "Taylor Lautner"), [Joey King](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joey_King "Joey King"), and [Presley Cash](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presley_Cash "Presley Cash"); the latter two previously appeared in Swift's video for "[Mean](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mean_\(song\) "Mean (song)")" (2011).[\[51\]](#cite_note-52) On July 13, 2023, Swift released a digital deluxe edition of the album, featuring live recordings of "[Dear John](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dear_John_\(Taylor_Swift_song\) "Dear John (Taylor Swift song)")" and "Last Kiss" from the [Minneapolis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minneapolis "Minneapolis") and Kansas City shows of the Eras Tour, respectively.[\[52\]](#cite_note-u467-53)
